items.explanation_markdown:
You get home, and the bicycle that was leaning against the fence this morning is standing upright against the wall, chained in place. You didn't do that. Your roommate did, earlier, and now the state of it — parked, secured — is just sitting there as a fact about the world. That's the feeling てある captures: not someone doing something, but something someone did, on display.

## How it works

てある attaches to the te-form of a **transitive** verb (one that takes a direct object — the person doing the action acts *on* something) and adds ある, the verb for existence of things. Together they describe a state that exists *because* someone deliberately set it up that way.

```jp
窓[まど]が開[あ]けてある。
```

*The window has been opened (and left that way).*

Notice the marker: it's が, not を, even though 開[あ]ける is a transitive verb and 窓[まど] is what got opened. Once てある turns the sentence into a description of a state, が marks what that state belongs to — the same shift you'd expect from any sentence about how something *is*.

```jp
名[な]前[まえ]が書[か]いてある。
```

*A name is written (there).*

```jp
机[つくえ]の上[うえ]に手[て]紙[がみ]が置[お]いてある。
```

*There's a letter placed on the desk.*

The verb conjugates exactly like it does before いる in ている — drop る, add て — then ある just tacks on.

```jp
止[と]める → 止[と]めてある
```

## Rules and exceptions

The whole pattern depends on the verb being transitive. 止[と]める (to stop something — a car, a machine) works because there's an agent doing the stopping. Its intransitive twin, 止[と]まる (to stop, on its own), can't take てある at all — there's no one whose deliberate setup you'd be describing.

> てある almost always implies a person set the state up on purpose. If nothing planted an intentional state, てある sounds wrong to a native ear — plain ている is what you want for something that just happened on its own.

```jp
自[じ]転[てん]車[しゃ]が止[と]めてある。
```

*The bicycle has been parked.*

Because the emphasis is on the *result being ready for someone*, てある often shows up when the state matters to the speaker right now — a door left open for a guest, a seat saved, food set out. Simply stating that a transitive action happened isn't enough; you need the outcome to still be sitting there, relevant.

## Casual speech

In casual explanations, てある often picks up んだ instead of the more formal んです — you're not changing the pattern itself, just how you frame it as an aside. 電[でん]気[き]がつけてあるんだ ("the light's on, see" — someone left it on) reads far more natural in conversation than the plain sentence alone.

```jp
電[でん]気[き]がつけてある。
```

*The light has been left on.*

## Contrast

You already have ている doing two jobs: progressive ("in the middle of") and resultant state for **intransitive** verbs. てある is the transitive half of that second job — same idea, "something is in a state," but now there's a person behind it.

```jp
自[じ]転[てん]車[しゃ]が止[と]まっている。
```

*The bicycle is stopped (it's just sitting there, stopped).*

Line that up against 自[じ]転[てん]車[しゃ]が止[と]めてある above: both describe a parked bike, but 止[と]まっている only tells you the bike isn't moving — it says nothing about who parked it or why. 止[と]めてある insists someone put it there on purpose, and that fact is still true.

```jp
ドアが閉[し]めてある。
```

*The door has been shut.*

Swap in ドアが閉[し]まっている and you'd only be reporting that the door is closed right now, no hint of intent behind it — useful if you don't know or don't care who closed it.

That distinction — a bare fact about how something is, versus a fact plus someone's fingerprints on it — is what you're listening for every time you meet these two side by side. Hold onto てある; you'll want it again soon when you learn ておく, which is the *moment before* this state gets set up on purpose.
caution_notes: てある needs a transitive verb behind it — an intransitive twin like 止まる can't take this pattern at all.
The object of the original action is marked with が, not を, once てある turns the sentence into a state description.
てある implies a person deliberately set the state up; don't reach for it when nothing and no one caused the state on purpose, like a flower blooming.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend is coming over tonight, and right now the room is a mess and the fridge is empty. You've got a couple of hours before they show up, which means everything you do now is really *for later* — you're not cleaning because someone's watching, you're cleaning so that later, when they arrive, it's already done.

Japanese has a dedicated way to mark that kind of action: te-form + おく.

```jp
部屋[へや]を掃[そう]除[じ]しておく。
```
*I'll clean the room ahead of time.*

The cleaning happens now, but the sentence's whole point is the *later* — you're doing it so that future-you doesn't have to.

## How it works

`おく` on its own is a normal verb meaning "to put / place" (置[お]く — you'll have seen 置[お]く with this exact kanji). Attach the te-form of any verb to it, and the meaning shifts from "put something down" to "do this now, for a reason that shows up later."

```jp
ビールを買[か]っておく。
```
*I'll buy beer in advance.*

The structure is mechanical: take the te-form you already know, then add おく. 買[か]う → 買[か]って → 買[か]っておく. Nothing about the te-form itself changes — おく just rides on the back of it.

```jp
窓[まど]を開[あ]けておく。
```
*I'll leave the window open (ahead of time).*

Notice something here: with an already-open-ended verb like 開[あ]ける, ておく can land on either of two related jobs — "do this in preparation" (I'll open it before the guests arrive) or "do this and then leave it that way" (I'm opening it and not touching it again). Context decides which one you're hearing; the grammar itself doesn't distinguish them.

```jp
お金[かね]を持[も]っておく。
```
*I'll have money on me (just in case).*

That "just in case" flavor is common — ておく covers not just "prepare for a known event" but also "take care of this now so I'm not caught out later," a slightly broader net than "prepare" alone suggests.

## Rules and exceptions

おく conjugates exactly like the plain verb 置[お]く does, because that's what it is — a u-verb ending in く. So you get おく → おかない → おきます → おいて, all the ordinary patterns. The only thing special is that it's riding on a te-form host, not standing alone.

> A very common wrong guess is treating おく like an auxiliary that doesn't conjugate — writing something like `掃除しておくます` instead of 掃[そう]除[じ]しておきます. おく still takes its own conjugation ending; only the verb in front of it stays frozen in te-form.

ておく wants a *deliberate* action with a *purpose* pointing forward. It's a poor fit for things that are simply true or that just happened to end up a certain way — for that job you already have てある and ている, which we'll get to in the contrast section below.

## Casual speech

In relaxed spoken Japanese, ておく contracts hard — the て and おく fuse into とく. It's extremely common; you'll hear it constantly among friends and family.

```jp
窓[まど]、開[あ]けとく。
```
*I'll leave the window open.*

Same meaning as 窓[まど]を開[あ]けておく, just faster and more casual — drop the と for です/ます-level speech, since とく reads as clearly informal.

## Contrast

You've met てある for "has been done, and the result is sitting there" — the difference is *whose intention the sentence is tracking*. てある describes the state as a fact you're reporting; ておく describes the deliberate act of setting that state up, with your reason for doing so implied.

```jp
窓[まど]が開[あ]けてある。
```
*The window has been left open.*

Compare that to 窓[まど]を開[あ]けておく from earlier — same window, same open state, but that version is about *you doing the opening on purpose, now, for later*. てある just notes that it's open; it doesn't care why or by whom.

ている (progressive) is a different trap entirely — it's about an action unfolding in real time, not something staged for the future.

```jp
今[いま]、部屋[へや]を掃[そう]除[じ]している。
```
*I'm cleaning the room right now.*

Swap しておく in for している here and the sentence stops describing what's happening this second — it starts describing something you're doing *because of what comes next*, which is a completely different scene.

ておく is the one you reach for whenever the real content of the sentence is "I'm doing this now so that later goes smoothly" — hold onto that shape, because てしまう later covers the flip side: doing something now and living with the consequences, whether you meant to or not.
caution_notes: おく still conjugates on its own as a regular u-verb (おかない, おきます, おいて) — only the verb in front of it stays frozen in te-form.
とく is the casual, spoken contraction of ておく; don't write it anywhere formal.
ておく needs a deliberate action aimed at a later purpose — for a state that simply exists or just happened, use てある or ている instead.
With verbs like 開ける, ておく can mean either 'do it now to prepare' or 'do it and leave it that way' — only context tells you which.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're describing your day to a friend, but every sentence carries a little sigh — you forgot the homework, you ate all the snacks you were supposed to save, you lost your wallet. In English you'd just say "I forgot" or "I ate it all," but Japanese has a whole grammar pattern built for that sigh: てしまう.

```jp
宿[しゅく]題[だい]を忘[わす]れてしまう。
```
*I end up forgetting the homework.*

That しまう on the end isn't decoration — it's doing real work. It's telling the listener: this happened in full, and the speaker wishes it hadn't.

## How it works

てしまう attaches to the te-form of any verb, exactly like ている or ておく do. Take the verb, drop it into its te-form, and add しまう.

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べてしまう
```
*to eat → to eat up / end up eating*

Once you've got te-form + しまう, that whole chunk conjugates like any regular verb: past, non-past, and so on, just like a normal verb.

```jp
お菓[か]子[し]を全[ぜん]部[ぶ]食[た]べてしまう。
```
*I end up eating all the snacks.*

Notice what しまう adds that 食[た]べた alone wouldn't: it wasn't supposed to happen, or it happened faster or more thoroughly than intended. 食[た]べた is neutral. 食[た]べてしまう has a story behind it.

```jp
財[さい]布[ふ]を無[な]くしてしまう。
```
*I end up losing my wallet.*

## Rules and exceptions

てしまう actually carries two related meanings, and context decides which one you're hearing:

1. **An unwanted result** — something went wrong, and you (or someone) is stuck with it. That's the wallet, the snacks, the homework you forgot.
2. **Emphatic completion** — the action ran all the way through, with no bad feeling at all, just emphasis that nothing was left undone.

```jp
宿[しゅく]題[だい]を全[ぜん]部[ぶ]してしまう。
```
*I get all the homework done.*

Same grammar, opposite mood — here it just means "done, every last bit of it," maybe even with relief. Which reading you get depends entirely on the situation and the speaker's tone, not on the grammar itself.

> てしまう attaches only to verbs — you can't put it on an adjective or a noun directly. `暑いてしまう` is not a sentence; there's no equivalent shortcut for adjectives. Keep it to the te-form of verbs.

A common beginner habit is reaching for てしまう every time something is simply "done," the way learners overuse plain past tense on its own. Save it for moments where thoroughness or an unwanted outcome is actually the point — otherwise plain past tense does the job.

## Casual speech

In fast, casual speech, てしまう almost always contracts. てしまう becomes ちゃう, and でしまう (after ん-stem verbs like 遊[あそ]ぶ) becomes じゃう.

```jp
忘[わす]れちゃう。
```
*I totally forget.*

```jp
遊[あそ]んじゃう。
```
*I go and play (when I shouldn't).*

You'll hear ちゃう constantly between friends and almost never in polite writing — treat it like any other casual contraction: fine to recognize everywhere, risky to use with your teacher.

## Contrast

You've already met ておく — te-form + おく — for doing something *in advance*, so it's ready later. てしまう points the opposite direction: it looks *back* at something already fully done, often with a reaction attached.

```jp
明日[あした]の準[じゅん]備[び]をしておきました。
```
*I got tomorrow's preparations done in advance.*

```jp
明日[あした]の準[じゅん]備[び]をしてしまう。
```
*I go and do tomorrow's preparations (before I meant to).*

Swap おく for しまう and the meaning shifts from "I set this up ahead of time, on purpose" to a completed action with a reaction attached — the forward-planning feel disappears entirely.

ている, by contrast, marks something still in progress or a state that has settled in. てしまう marks a point where the action stops because there's nothing left to do.

Homework you've already turned in and can't get back, snacks you can't unsnack — that's the shape of てしまう. Hold onto that finality; you'll want the opposite feeling again once ていく and てくる show up, since those describe change that's still underway.
caution_notes: てしまう attaches only to verb te-forms — it cannot attach directly to an adjective or a noun.
The same grammar can read as either an unwanted result or plain emphatic completion — the feeling comes from context, not the words themselves.
ちゃう and じゃう are casual contractions of てしまう and でしまう — avoid them in polite or written Japanese.
Don't reach for てしまう for every finished action — plain past tense is usually enough unless thoroughness or an unwanted outcome is the point.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're back in your hometown after a year away, and your friend meets you at the station. 「大[おお]きくなったね」isn't the sentence you reach for — what you actually notice is *change still happening*, something that was one way and is sliding toward another. Japanese has a pair of endings built exactly for that: **ていく** and **てくる**. They turn any verb into a story about direction — away from now, or toward now.

```jp
天[てん]気[き]がだんだん暖[あたた]かくなってくる。
```

*The weather is gradually getting warmer (and it's happening right now, moving toward us).*

## How it works

Both endings attach to the **te-form** of a verb, then add 行[い]く (いく, to go) or 来[く]る (くる, to come). That's the whole structure: te-form + いく, or te-form + くる. The "go / come" meaning is mostly bleached out — what's left is a sense of *direction*, either away from the present moment (**ていく**) or toward it (**てくる**).

Think of it on a timeline with "now" as a fixed point. **てくる** describes something arriving at now, coming closer, building up to this point. **ていく** describes something leaving now, heading off, continuing on from here.

```jp
子[こ]供[ども]はだんだん大[おお]きくなっていく。
```

*The child keeps growing bigger and bigger (moving forward from now).*

```jp
彼[かれ]は毎[まい]晩[ばん]遅[おそ]く帰[かえ]ってくる。
```

*He comes home late every night (repeatedly arriving back, toward here).*

This works with plain motion verbs too, and there the "go/come" sense is much more literal — it just adds the direction relative to the speaker.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]がこちらへ歩[ある]いてくる。
```

*My friend is walking this way (toward me).*

```jp
私[わたし]は駅[えき]まで歩[ある]いていく。
```

*I'll walk to the station (away from here).*

The same logic covers actions that aren't physical movement at all — a habit, a change, a process that keeps going. 仕[し]事[ごと]を続[つづ]ける (to continue work) plus ていく says the continuing is aimed at the future.

```jp
彼[かの]女[じょ]は仕[し]事[ごと]を続[つづ]けていく。
```

*She's going to keep going with her work (carrying it forward from here).*

## Rules and exceptions

Both endings need the verb's te-form first — there's no shortcut version that skips it. `大きいてくる` is not a real word; you need `大きくなってくる`, because it's なる (to become) that's carrying the ていく/てくる, not the adjective itself.

> 来[く]る itself can take てくる: 来[き]てくる. It looks redundant — "come and come" — but it's genuinely rare and > mostly shows up with other movement verbs stacked on top, so don't reach for it as your default てくる example.

The direction reading (away vs. toward) is the default with change-of-state verbs like なる, but with plain motion verbs like 歩[ある]く or 走[はし]る, ていく/てくる simply mark which way the person is heading relative to whoever's talking. Context tells you which flavor you're getting — there's no separate grammar for it.

```jp
犬[いぬ]が公[こう]園[えん]から走[はし]ってくる。
```

*The dog comes running out of the park (heading toward the speaker).*

## Casual speech

In relaxed conversation, ていく often shrinks to てく — the い drops out, the same way ている shrinks to てる. てくる doesn't contract the same way; it usually stays whole even in casual speech.

- Neutral: 私[わたし]は駅[えき]まで歩[ある]いていく。
- Casual: 私[わたし]は駅[えき]まで歩[ある]いてく。

## Contrast

You already know ている for an action in progress or a state that's settled in — it freezes a moment. ていく/てくる instead point at *movement between* moments: where something is coming from, or where it's headed. 大[おお]きくなっている says a child is currently in a bigger state; 大[おお]きくなっていく says the growing is still going to keep happening from here on.

You also know てしまう for finishing something completely, often with a note of regret. てしまう closes a door; ていく/てくる describe someone walking through one, mid-step, either arriving or leaving.

Hold onto that "toward now / away from now" picture — it comes back once you meet ても and てはいけない, where the same te-form is doing a completely different job, but the habit of reading a te-form ending as a small grammatical hinge will already feel familiar.
caution_notes: Both endings require the te-form first — an adjective like 大きい cannot take てくる directly; you need the verb なる carrying the ending, as in 大きくなってくる.
てくる with 来る itself (来てくる) is grammatically valid but very rare — don't treat it as the standard pattern.
With plain motion verbs (歩く, 走る), ていく/てくる mark literal direction relative to the speaker, not a change over time — read the verb first to know which sense applies.
てくる rarely contracts in casual speech the way ていく shrinks to てく — don't force a casual shortening onto てくる.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're supposed to meet a friend at the park at six. At five-thirty it starts raining, hard. You text them anyway: 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]っても、公[こう]園[えん]を歩[ある]く。 Rain or no rain, you're going. That flip — "no matter what happens, the plan holds" — is what ても does. It bolts onto the te-form you already know and turns any verb or adjective into "even if / even though X."

## How it works

The base is the same te-form you've been using for ている, てある, ておく, and the rest — you're just handing it to a new job. Take the te-form, add も (the word that works like *even / also*), and you get "even if / even though."

```jp
忙[いそが]しくても、毎[まい]日[にち]勉[べん]強[きょう]する。
```

*Even if I'm busy, I study every day.*

With verbs, the te-form does all the work — も just rides on the end. With い-adjectives, drop the い, add くて, then も:

```jp
忙[いそが]しい → 忙[いそが]しくて → 忙[いそが]しくても
```

For な-adjectives and nouns, the connector is で, and ても becomes でも (the same shape as the word for "but" — more on that below):

```jp
元[げん]気[き]でも、今日[きょう]は休[やす]む。
```

*Even though I'm fine, I'm resting today.*

```jp
元[げん]気[き] → 元[げん]気[き]で → 元[げん]気[き]でも
```

One more shape worth knowing early: pair ても with a question word like 何[なん]回[かい] (how many times) and you get "no matter how many times."

```jp
何[なん]回[かい]聞[き]いても、分[わ]からない。
```

*No matter how many times I ask, I don't understand.*

That's the whole mechanic. One connector, four flavors depending on what it's attached to — verb, い-adjective, な-adjective/noun, or a question word.

## Rules and exceptions

ても doesn't care whether the outcome is good or bad, expected or not — it just says "this condition doesn't change the result." Compare that to から (for reasons) or ので (softer reasons), which you'll meet elsewhere: those explain *why* something happens. ても explains why something *doesn't stop* happening.

```jp
高[たか]くても、あの時計[とけい]を買[か]う。
```

*Even if it's expensive, I'll buy that watch.*

Nobody's giving a reason here — 高[たか]い isn't the cause of buying the watch, it's the obstacle that fails to change the decision. That's the whole flavor of ても: expect it wherever a sentence in English has "even if," "no matter," or "however X is."

> A common first-week slip is dropping the も and just leaving the te-form alone: `忙しくて、毎日勉強する` reads as "I'm busy, and so I study every day" — a plain reason, the opposite of what you meant. The も is not optional decoration; it's the whole concession.

でも after a noun or な-adjective looks exactly like でも the conjunction meaning "but" (the one sitting in your vocabulary list already). They really are the same word wearing two hats: sentence-initial でも contrasts two whole sentences, while attached でも at the end of a noun or な-adjective contrasts a single condition against its result. Context tells them apart fast — one starts a sentence, the other ends a clause.

## Contrast

You already know a handful of jobs the te-form can do: ている marks something in progress, てしまう marks something finished (often with a little regret), ていく and てくる track a change moving away from or toward you. ても is another one of those jobs, and it's worth keeping straight from the others precisely because the *shape* is so similar — te-form plus one more piece.

The difference is what that piece asks. ている, てしまう, ていく, and てくる all describe what's happening *to the action itself* — is it ongoing, complete, moving. ても doesn't touch the action's own status at all; it's entirely about the relationship between a condition and a result that refuses to budge. 忙[いそが]しくても勉[べん]強[きょう]する isn't telling you anything about the studying being finished or ongoing — it's telling you the studying happens *regardless* of the business.

## Closing thought

Every time you reach for ても, you're saying "here's the obstacle, and here's the outcome that ignores it." Hold onto that shape — you'll want it again soon, when てもいい turns the same connector into asking permission instead of describing defiance.
caution_notes: Dropping the も and leaving only the te-form turns a concession into a plain reason, so 忙しくて means 'because I'm busy,' not 'even though I'm busy.'
でも attached to a noun or な-adjective is the same word as the conjunction でも (but) — only its position in the sentence tells you which job it's doing.
ても does not explain a cause the way から or ので do; it says a condition failed to change the outcome, not why the outcome happened.

items.explanation_markdown:
It's late, you're at the desk with your textbook open, and your eyelids have that heavy pull that means you're one blink away from losing the fight. You're not asleep yet — you catch yourself right on the edge of it. Japanese has one small pattern built exactly for that edge, the instant before something happens: そうになる.

```jp
寝[ね]る → 寝[ね]そうになる
```

*to sleep → to be right on the edge of falling asleep*

## How it works

そうになる attaches to the stem of a verb — the same stem you already strip off before adding other endings. For an ichidan verb like 寝[ね]る, drop the る to get 寝[ね]そうになる. For a godan verb, swap the final u-sound for its i-row partner first: 忘[わす]れる is actually ichidan too (忘[わす]れそうになる, not 忘[わす]れるそうになる), but a true godan verb like 泣[な]く becomes 泣[な]きそうになる instead of 泣[な]くそうになる. Whatever the verb, the meaning is the same shape: the subject was right at the threshold of that action or state, close enough to feel it, before it either happened or was caught in time.

```jp
授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]で寝[ね]そうになりました。
```

*In class, I nearly fell asleep.*

Most of the time you'll meet this pattern in the past tense, そうになった, because you're reporting a close call after the fact — the moment has already passed by the time you're telling someone about it.

```jp
約[やく]束[そく]を忘[わす]れそうになりました。
```

*I nearly forgot the appointment.*

## Rules and exceptions

そうになる almost always describes something the subject didn't actually want — falling, crying, forgetting, being late. Nothing in the grammar forces that, but in real use it's overwhelmingly the pattern for near misses you're glad didn't fully land.

> Don't confuse そうになる with the appearance pattern そうだ ("it looks like it's about to rain," 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]りそうだ). そうだ is a guess about something you're watching from outside; そうになる is the subject itself standing right at the edge of an event. The stem attachment looks similar, but the meaning is not interchangeable.

The other trap is attaching it to the wrong form. The stem loses its dictionary-form る or u-ending before そうになる goes on — `食べるそうになる` is wrong; it has to be 食[た]べそうになる. If you can say the plain stem on its own and it sounds incomplete, that's the piece そうになる wants.

```jp
電[でん]車[しゃ]に遅[おく]れそうになりました。
```

*I nearly missed the train.*

```jp
階[かい]段[だん]で落[お]ちそうになりました。
```

*I nearly fell on the stairs.*

```jp
悲[かな]しい映[えい]画[が]を見[み]て、泣[な]きそうになりました。
```

*I watched a sad movie and nearly cried.*

## Contrast: そうになる vs ていく・てくる

You already know ていく and てくる for change that unfolds over a stretch of time — something drifting steadily in one direction. そうになる is the opposite shape: not a stretch, a single moment right at the tipping point. Put them side by side and the difference is obvious.

```jp
荷[に]物[もつ]がだんだん重[おも]くなっていく。
```

*The luggage keeps getting heavier and heavier.*

```jp
でも、今日[きょう]は重[おも]くて、道[みち]で落[お]ちそうになった。
```

*But today it was so heavy that I nearly dropped it in the street.*

The first sentence describes a slow slide that's still going; the second is one sharp instant inside that slide, the point where it almost got away from you.

## Closing thought

そうになる is for the instant something almost happens to you — the near miss, caught right before it lands. Later on you'll meet ようにする, which is the deliberate opposite: not something that almost happens to you, but something you push yourself to make happen on purpose.
caution_notes: そうになる attaches to the verb stem, not the dictionary form — 食べるそうになる is wrong; it must be 食べそうになる.
Don't confuse そうになる (the subject is right at the edge of an event) with そうだ (a guess about something you're observing).
そうになる almost always describes an unwanted near miss, even though nothing in the grammar itself requires that.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend leans over during lunch and asks what you're doing this weekend. You already know the answer — you're not guessing, you're not hoping, you've already decided. What you need is the phrase for *I'm planning to*, and that's exactly what つもり gives you. It takes a plain verb and turns it into a stated intention, something you're announcing as your own decision rather than a fact about the world.

```jp
週[しゅう]末[まつ]、映[えい]画[が]を見[み]るつもりです。
```

*This weekend, I'm planning to watch a movie.*

## How It Works

つもり attaches straight onto the dictionary form of a verb — the plain, unconjugated form you'd find listed in a dictionary. There's no te-form, no stem change, nothing to memorize beyond the shape you already know. You say the verb exactly the way you'd think it to yourself, and つもり rides along right after it.

```jp
明日[あした]、図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で勉[べん]強[きょう]するつもりだ。
```

*Tomorrow, I'm planning to study at the library.*

Notice the だ sitting at the end there. That's the plain copula (the word that works like *is/am/are*), and its job is to turn つもり from a bare noun-like word — closer to "intention" on its own — into a complete sentence: "it's my intention." Drop だ entirely and bare つもり still reads as a finished statement in speech; swap だ for です and the sentence gets politer without the meaning shifting even slightly.

```jp
来[らい]年[ねん]、日本[にほん]語[ご]を勉[べん]強[きょう]するつもりです。
```

*Next year, I'm planning to study Japanese.*

So つもり, つもりだ, and つもりです are all accepted, and choosing between them is purely a question of how formal the room is — a plain つもり with friends, つもりです with your teacher or a stranger. The dictionary form doing the heavy lifting in front of it is really the whole grammar lesson here.

```jp
見[み]る → 見[み]るつもり
```

*see → planning to see*

Whatever the plain form looks like — 見[み]る, 勉[べん]強[きょう]する, 帰[かえ]る, 引[ひ]っ越[こ]す — that's exactly what goes in front of つもり. No exceptions, no irregular attachments to track.

## Rules and Exceptions

Here's the part that's easy to miss at first: つもり describes what's inside your head *right now*, not a fact about how the future will actually go. That's a real difference from a fixed schedule — つもり can describe an intention that quietly falls apart later, and saying it doesn't promise anything actually happens. It just reports your current resolve, honestly, at the moment you say it.

That subjective feel matters even more when you're talking about someone else's plans instead of your own.

> Using つもり to describe someone else's intention can sound like you're speaking for them with total certainty. Among close friends who talk about everything, that's completely normal — toward someone you barely know, it can come across as oddly presumptuous, like you're announcing their decision before they have.

```jp
彼[かれ]はもう帰[かえ]るつもりだ。
```

*He's already planning to go home.*

A common wrong guess, especially early on, is trying to attach つもり directly to a noun or a plain adjective, the way `静かつもり` gets typed by someone reaching for "I intend to be quiet." That doesn't work — つもり only follows the dictionary form of a verb, full stop, never a bare noun or adjective standing on its own.

## Casual Speech

In relaxed conversation, だ often gets swapped for だよ, which softens a flat, declarative statement into something warmer and more conversational — roughly the effect "you know" has tacked onto the end of an English sentence.

```jp
今日[きょう]は早[はや]く寝[ね]るつもりだよ。
```

*I'm planning to go to bed early today, you know.*

That だよ isn't required and it isn't more "correct" than だ — it's just the sound of someone talking to a friend instead of reading off a form.

## Contrast: つもり vs なければならない

You already know なければならない for the things you have no real choice about — homework due tomorrow, a deadline nobody's moving for you. つもり lives in completely different territory: it's the plan *you* chose, not the obligation life handed you. Swap one pattern for the other in an otherwise identical sentence and the entire feel of it flips.

```jp
明日[あした]、宿[しゅく]題[だい]をしなければならない。
```

*I have to do my homework tomorrow.*

```jp
明日[あした]、宿[しゅく]題[だい]をするつもりだ。
```

*I'm planning to do my homework tomorrow.*

Same homework, same day, same person saying it — but the first sentence carries the weight of a burden, and the second sounds like someone quietly proud of a decision they've already made. That contrast is worth sitting with, because English "I'm going to do my homework" flattens a distinction Japanese keeps sharply separate.

```jp
私[わたし]は来[らい]月[げつ]引[ひ]っ越[こ]すつもりです。
```

*I'm planning to move next month.*

つもり is how you tell someone what's already settled in your own head, whether or not the day itself ever cooperates. Hold onto that self-directed, decision-first feel — it's exactly the muscle ようにする leans on later, once the intention needs ongoing upkeep instead of a single statement.
caution_notes: つもり states your current intention, not a guarantee — the plan itself can still fall through.
Stating someone else's つもり as fact can sound presumptuous unless you know them well.
つもり attaches only to the dictionary form of a verb, never directly to a noun or a plain adjective.
Ending with だ, です, or nothing at all after つもり only changes politeness, not the meaning.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your doctor takes one look at your blood sugar numbers and tells you plainly: cut back on sweets. You don't need a magic diet, you need a habit — a small deliberate effort, repeated. That's exactly the shape ようにする was built for.

```jp
毎[まい]朝[あさ]、野[や]菜[さい]を食[た]べるようにしている。
```
*I make a point of eating vegetables every morning.*

That sentence isn't reporting what you did once. It's reporting a standing effort — something you've set up as a rule for yourself and keep chasing, even on the days you fall short.

## How it works

ようにする attaches straight onto the dictionary form of a verb for a habit you're aiming for, or the ない form for one you're trying to avoid. Nothing else changes — no te-form, no stem-shaving, just the plain form plus ようにする.

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べるようにする
```
*to eat → to make it a habit to eat*

```jp
食[た]べない → 食[た]べないようにする
```
*to not eat → to make it a habit not to eat*

する here is doing its ordinary job — the word for "to do" — so it conjugates exactly like every other する verb you already know: past ようにした, negative ようにしない, and so on.

The form you'll meet constantly is ようにしている — the て-form of する plus いる, the same "ongoing state" marker you already use for continuous actions. ようにする by itself is closer to a decision you're making right now; ようにしている is the report that the effort has been running for a while.

```jp
甘[あま]い物[もの]を食[た]べないようにしている。
```
*I try not to eat sweets.*

```jp
毎[まい]晩[ばん]早[はや]く寝[ね]るようにする。
```
*I'm going to make a habit of going to bed early.*

Notice the difference: the sweets sentence is a lifestyle you've already built (しています), while the early-bedtime one is you announcing the plan today, before the habit exists yet.

## Rules and exceptions

ようにする is for effort toward a repeated behavior, not for a single one-off action. "I made sure to lock the door this one time" isn't this pattern — that's just a plain past-tense sentence. ようにする wants something you're trying to keep doing, day after day, whether or not you always succeed.

> The "try" is doing real work here. ようにする never promises the outcome — it promises the attempt. Someone can say 野[や]菜[さい]を食[た]べるようにしている and still skip vegetables some days; the sentence is honest about that built-in slack.

A common wrong guess is treating ようにする like a flat statement of fact, the way you'd use する alone. `野菜を食べるにする` drops the necessary よう and just sounds broken — the よう isn't optional decoration, it's the part that turns "do" into "orient yourself toward doing."

## Contrast: ようにする vs つもり

You already have つもり for stating a plan — 野[や]菜[さい]を食[た]べるつもりだ, "I intend to eat vegetables." That's a single decision, and it says nothing about follow-through or repetition; you could mean tonight, once.

```jp
野[や]菜[さい]を食[た]べるつもりだ。
```
*I intend to eat vegetables.*

```jp
野[や]菜[さい]をもっと食[た]べるようにしている。
```
*I make a point of eating more vegetables.*

Swap the two and the sentence changes shape, not just tone: つもり is a plan you're holding in your head; ようにしている is a habit you can already point to evidence for, because you've been doing the work.

```jp
毎[まい]日[にち]散[さん]歩[ぽ]するようにしている。
```
*I make a point of taking a walk every day.*

## Closing thought

ようにする is the grammar of trying on purpose, day after day, not the grammar of a single decision — hold onto that distinction, because ことにする, when you meet it, looks deceptively similar but marks a one-time choice instead of a standing effort.
caution_notes: ようにする describes a repeated effort, not a single one-off action — don't use it for something you only did once.
The よう is required — dropping it (as in `食べるにする`) isn't a shortcut, it's a mistake.
ようにしている reports an effort already underway; ようにする by itself is closer to announcing the plan today.
Don't confuse this with つもり — つもり is a plan you're holding, ようにする is an effort you're actively building.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your doctor just told you your blood pressure is a little high, and you're sitting in the waiting room deciding what to actually do about it. Not "I should probably think about maybe cutting back" — an actual decision, made right now, that you're committing to. That's the job ことにする does: it turns a choice you've just made into a sentence.

```jp
明日[あした]から毎[まい]朝[あさ]早[はや]く起[お]きることにする。
```
*I've decided to start getting up early every morning from tomorrow.*

The moment you say that sentence, the decision exists. Nobody made it for you, nothing forced it — you weighed it and chose it, and ことにする is the grammar that records the choice.

## How it works

こと is a **nominalizer** — a little word that turns a whole verb phrase into a thing you can talk about, the way "going" turns "go" into something you can point at. ことにする then works with に + する (to do) — literally something like "make it the thing of going," which is a clunky translation but explains why the whole phrase reads as *deciding on* an action.

The attachment point is the plain dictionary form of the verb, exactly as it appears in a dictionary, right before こと.

```jp
今年[ことし]は日本[にほん]語[ご]を習[なら]うことにしました。
```
*I've decided to learn Japanese this year.*

When the choice is to stop or avoid something instead, the ない form goes in that same slot.

```jp
甘[あま]い物[もの]を食[た]べないことにする。
```
*I've decided not to eat sweets.*

する verbs behave exactly the same way — the する in 食[しょく]事[じ]をする is just doing its normal job as "to do," and the whole phrase still slots in front of ことにする like any other dictionary form.

```jp
週[しゅう]末[まつ]はレストランで食[しょく]事[じ]をすることにしました。
```
*I've decided to have a meal at a restaurant this weekend.*

Both tenses matter here, and they carry a real difference. ことにする, left in the present, sounds like the decision is happening as you speak — you're announcing it. ことにしました, in the past, reports a decision you already made and are now living by. Most of the time you'll reach for ことにしました, because you're usually telling someone about a choice you settled on earlier, not narrating it live.

## Rules and exceptions

> ことにする is strictly about **your own** decision. If the outcome was decided by someone else, by circumstances, or by a rule, this pattern is the wrong tool — that job belongs to ことになる, which you'll meet soon.

A common wrong guess is reaching for the て-form or the ます-stem before こと. Neither works. It has to be the plain dictionary form for "I will do this" or the plain ない form for "I won't do this" — nothing in between.

```jp
飲[の]む → 飲[の]まないことにする
```

That arrow is the whole rule in miniature: take the dictionary form, negate it if the decision is to stop doing something, then attach ことにする. Nothing else changes.

## Contrast

You already have つもり for stating an intention — "I plan to." つもり can be looser than ことにする; it can describe something you're leaning toward without having fully committed.

```jp
来[らい]月[げつ]旅[りょ]行[こう]するつもりです。
```
*I plan to travel next month.*

Swap that つもり for ことにする and the sentence tightens: it stops sounding like a plan you're still holding loosely and starts sounding like a decision you've closed the door on.

よう にする lives in a nearby but different space too — it's about the ongoing effort to make something a habit, not the single moment of deciding.

```jp
毎[まい]日[にち]野[や]菜[さい]を食[た]べるようにする。
```
*I'm making it a habit to eat vegetables every day.*

ことにする is the decision itself, made once. ようにする is the standing effort you keep applying afterward — you might say ことにする the day you decide to change your diet, then describe the follow-through with ようにする for months after.

```jp
お酒[さけ]を飲[の]まないことにしました。
```
*I've decided not to drink alcohol.*

That's the shape you'll use constantly once you start noticing it — someone announcing a resolution, big or small, about their own behavior.

Hold onto this one: ことになる looks almost identical on the page but flips who's behind the wheel — it shows up next, for decisions and outcomes that land on you rather than ones you make.
caution_notes: ことにする reports a decision the speaker themselves made — use ことになる instead when the outcome was decided by someone else or by circumstances.
The slot before ことにする takes only the plain dictionary form or the plain ない form, never the て-form or the ます-stem.
ことにしました describes a decision already made and being kept, while ことにする can sound like the decision is happening at the moment of speaking.
Don't confuse this with つもり — つもり is a loose intention you might still change, while ことにする is the closed decision itself.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your company just told you you're being transferred. Nobody asked what you wanted — the decision landed on your desk already finished, and now you're the one explaining it to your family. In Japanese, you wouldn't say 私[わたし]は新[あたら]しい会[かい]社[しゃ]で働[はたら]きます, as if the whole thing were your idea. You'd reach for the phrase that makes the decision sound like it arrived from somewhere else, because it did.

```jp
来[らい]月[げつ]、新[あたら]しい会[かい]社[しゃ]で働[はたら]くことになりました。
```
*Next month, it's been decided that I'll work at a new company.*

ことになる is built from こと — a nominalizer, a little grammatical word that takes a whole verb phrase (新[あたら]しい会[かい]社[しゃ]で働[はたら]く, "to work at a new company") and turns it into a thing you can talk about, almost like wrapping it in quotation marks — plus なる, "to become." Put together, the verb phrase itself becomes the outcome: it isn't that you decided to work there, it's that working there became the state of affairs. You're reporting a fact that formed around you, not a plan you made. That's the whole logic of the pattern in miniature, and once it clicks, you'll start noticing ことになる everywhere — memos, announcements, casual updates about anyone's life.

## How it works

The base attachment point is the plain dictionary form of a verb — no て-form, no ます, nothing conjugated first:

```jp
来[らい]年[ねん]から宿[しゅく]題[だい]が増[ふ]えることになる。
```
*Starting next year, it turns out homework increases.*

Nobody sat down and personally decided that homework should increase — but ことになる still fits, because the pattern covers two overlapping ideas at once: an outcome someone else arranged, and an outcome that simply turns out to be true given how things are. Both share the same emotional shape — this wasn't your call, and honestly it wasn't really anyone's individual call either.

When the outcome is that something *won't* happen, the negative sits on the verb, not on なる. Turn the verb into its ない form first, then attach ことになる as usual:

```jp
明日[あした]は会[かい]社[しゃ]に行[い]かないことになりました。
```
*It's been decided that I won't go to the company tomorrow.*

行[い]く becomes 行[い]かない, and ことになりました rides on top of that — never `行くないことになりました`, which puts the negative in the wrong place entirely. Past tense, ことになりました, is the form you'll meet constantly, because you're almost always reporting a decision after it's already settled, not narrating one as it happens.

There's a third shape worth learning early: swap ました for ている, and the sentence stops describing one piece of news and starts describing a standing arrangement — the kind of thing that's simply how the schedule works, not something anyone announced today.

```jp
毎[まい]週[しゅう]月[げつ]曜[よう]日[び]に会[かい]議[ぎ]があることになっている。
```
*There's a standing arrangement that there's a meeting every Monday.*

Nobody sent a memo about this particular Monday. It's just the rule, repeating quietly in the background. That's the real difference between ことになりました (one decision, reported once, usually past) and ことになっている (an ongoing arrangement, always true, no matter when you check).

## Rules and exceptions

ことになる needs an outside cause standing behind it — a company, a school, a group, circumstance in general. It doesn't stretch to cover plain wants or feelings, because wanting something isn't a fact that gets decided for you. You wouldn't say `お茶が欲しいことになりました` for "I ended up wanting tea" — nobody arranges a craving.

> Japanese speakers reach for ことになりました even when the news is obviously their own doing — a couple announcing their wedding, someone accepting a job they applied for themselves. Framing the outcome as something that "came to be decided," rather than "I decided," reads as modest instead of self-congratulatory, and it shows up constantly in exactly these personal-announcement moments.

```jp
私[わたし]たち、結[けっ]婚[こん]することになりました。
```
*We're getting married.*

Nobody forced this couple together — but ことになりました is still the natural way to share it. Saying ことにしました instead ("we decided to get married") would sound almost transactional, businesslike where the moment calls for warmth.

This is worth sitting with, because a beginner's instinct is to reach for whichever verb feels literally true — "I decided" means ことにする, right? Not always. Politeness culture often outranks literal accuracy here, and ことになる wins even when everyone in the room knows exactly whose decision it was.

The same softening shows up when you're the one turning something down. Baldly saying 話[はな]しません ("I won't speak") reads as a personal refusal and can land harder than intended; wrapping the same fact in ことになりました makes it sound like circumstances settled the matter, not you.

```jp
その会[かい]議[ぎ]で話[はな]さないことになりました。
```
*It's been decided that I won't speak at that meeting.*

## Contrast

The pattern's closest relative is ことにする, and mixing them up is easy — same skeleton, dictionary or ない form plus こと plus a verb. The difference is entirely about who's driving. する is something you actively do; なる is something that happens to you. ことにする is a resolution you made yourself; ことになる is one that reached you from outside, whether that outside force is a person, an institution, or plain circumstance.

```jp
私[わたし]は日本[にほん]語[ご]を勉[べん]強[きょう]することにしました。
```
*I decided to study Japanese.*

That's a personal resolution — nobody assigned this, the speaker chose it. Keep the exact same activity but let a university set the requirement instead, and the sentence's whole feel shifts even though barely a word changed:

```jp
大[だい]学[がく]で日本[にほん]語[ご]を勉[べん]強[きょう]することになりました。
```
*It was decided that I'd study Japanese at university.*

Same subject, same verb, completely different source behind the decision. Whenever you're unsure which one to reach for, ask yourself whose choice it actually was — the honest answer picks the verb for you every time.

Hold onto ことになった: pair it with 〜ばかり later and you'll be able to say something was decided *just now*, freshly, before you've even had the chance to tell anyone — ことになったばかり。
caution_notes: Reserve ことになる for outcomes decided by someone or something else — for your own choice, use ことにする instead.
The negative goes on the verb (行かないことになる), never on なる itself.
Japanese speakers often announce even personal news — a marriage, a job offer they applied for — with ことになりました rather than ことにしました, because it sounds modest rather than self-congratulatory.
ことになっている describes a standing rule or arrangement, not a one-time decision — use ことになりました for news you're reporting once.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're sitting in the yard with your family after dinner, looking up, and it slips out: 毎[まい]晩[ばん]星[ほし]を見[み]たものだ。You don't mean "I watched stars every night" the way you'd read a fact off a form. You mean it with a little sigh — back then, this was just what you did, over and over, and some part of you misses it. That sigh is もの. Drop it and the sentence goes flat; keep it and the listener hears exactly how you're holding that memory.

もの is a small word that, on its own, just means "thing." Tacked onto the end of a sentence like this, though, it stops naming an object and starts coloring the whole sentence — it tells the listener *how* to feel about what you just said, not *what* you said. English does something similar with a tag like "...those were the days," except もの is built into the grammar instead of added as an afterthought, and it does double duty: sometimes it's nostalgia, sometimes it's a half-defensive reason.

You'll hear もの most often from people looking backward — a parent talking about raising their kids, a friend catching up after years apart, someone explaining why they did something the way they did. It's less about the facts of the memory and more about the feeling that's still attached to it. Learn to recognize that feeling first; the grammar rules underneath it are actually short.

## How it works

The nostalgic use is the one you'll reach for most often. Take a verb in its plain past form — the casual た-form you already use for "I did X" — and add ものだ.

```jp
毎[まい]晩[ばん]星[ほし]を見[み]たものだ。
```

*I used to watch the stars every night.*

見[み]た is just the plain past of 見[み]る, nothing new there. ものだ is what turns "I watched" into "I used to watch, and it meant something." The pattern works the same way with any verb once it's sitting in that plain past shape:

```jp
弟[おとうと]とよく公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]んだものだ。
```

*My little brother and I used to play in the park a lot.*

```jp
母[はは]はよく歌[うた]を歌[うた]ったものだ。
```

*My mother used to sing songs often.*

Notice both of those lean on よく ("often"). もの itself doesn't mean "repeatedly" — but it almost always shows up describing something that happened over and over, because a single one-off memory rarely gets the wistful treatment. If your sentence is about something that happened exactly once, もの usually isn't the tool you want; save it for the kind of thing you did so many times it became part of who you were.

There's also a quiet assumption baked into every one of these sentences: you don't do this anymore, or at least not the way you used to. 弟[おとうと]とよく公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]んだものだ carries the sense that those park afternoons belong to a chapter that's closed now — you and your brother grew up, moved on, stopped going. Swap in a habit you still keep up today and もの starts to feel wrong, because there's no distance yet for the nostalgia to sit in.

The second job もの does is give a reason, and the flavor is emotional rather than logical — closer to "well, I was busy, okay?" than to a calm から explanation. This もの closes the sentence, often after だって ("but, well"). Here the plain form comes straight from an い-adjective, and もの attaches with nothing in between:

```jp
だって、忙[いそが]しかったもの。
```

*Well, I was busy, okay?*

忙[いそが]しかった is already a complete plain-form adjective, so もの just clips onto the end. You're not reporting your schedule to a stranger; you're defending yourself a little, the way you would to someone who already half-knows the excuse.

The two uses share more than they look like they do. In both cases もの is pointing at something the listener can't argue with directly — a memory that already happened, or a feeling that's already true. から would let someone push back on your logic; もの just states the fact of the feeling and leaves it there.

## Rules and exceptions

For nouns and な-adjectives, you can't attach もの straight onto the plain form the way you can with an い-adjective — you need だ in between, giving you だもの:

```jp
まだ分[わ]からないよ。子[こ]供[ども]だもの。
```

*They still don't understand. They're a kid, after all.*

子[こ]供[ども] is a noun, so it needs だ before もの can land. Think of だもの as one fused unit for nouns and な-adjectives, the same way ものだ is one fused unit closing off a nostalgic verb sentence — the だ moves to whichever side keeps the whole thing sounding complete.

> もの carries real feeling, so it resists cold, purely informational sentences. Saying 毎[まい]日[にち]会[かい]社[しゃ]に行[い]くものだ to mean nothing more than "I go to the office every day" sounds strange — there's no wistfulness and nothing to defend in that statement, so もの has no feeling to attach to.

A guess that trips people up: because もの looks like an ordinary noun, learners sometimes try to conjugate it as if it followed the polite ます-form, writing something like `見ますもの`. もの only ever follows the *plain* form — the ます-form never sits in front of it. Another trap: もの doesn't work well in questions or orders, since you're stating a memory or defending a feeling rather than asking or commanding anyone.

So the checklist, once you strip away the categories, is short: verbs and い-adjectives take もの with nothing between them; nouns and な-adjectives insert だ first. The だ isn't decoration — without it, `子供もの` sounds broken, the same way "kid thing" sounds broken in English where "it's a kid thing" doesn't.

## Casual speech

In relaxed conversation, もの often shrinks to もん. The meaning doesn't change at all, only the register does — the same way わからない can shrink to わかんない among friends.

```jp
だって、忙[いそが]しかったもの。
だって、忙[いそが]しかったもん。
```

*Well, I was busy, okay?*
*Well, I was busy, okay?*

Say the first one to your teacher and the second one to your little brother. Same excuse, same grammar underneath, different company.

You'll hear もん a lot from kids and from adults talking to people they're close to — it has a slightly pouty, self-justifying ring to it even in writing. The nostalgic ものだ almost never contracts this way; もん belongs to the reason-giving side of the pattern, where the emotional register is already higher.

## Contrast

You've already met ことがある for talking about the past — "I've done X, at least once." Compare it against the park sentence from earlier:

```jp
公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]んだことがある。
```

*I've played in the park before.*

That sentence is a checkbox: this happened, at some point, full stop. There's no feeling attached, and it doesn't matter whether it happened once or fifty times. 弟[おとうと]とよく公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]んだものだ, on the other hand, insists on the repetition and the mood behind it — it's a memory you're replaying, not an item you're confirming. If someone asks whether you've ever done something, reach for ことがある; if you're the one bringing up the memory unprompted, with a little weight behind it, that's もの's job.

Try the swap test when you're not sure which one fits: if the sentence would still make sense as an answer to "have you ever...?", ことがある is doing the work. If the sentence only makes sense as something you'd say unprompted, half to yourself, もの is the one you want.

もの won't come up again for a while, but keep an ear out for the same reflective, slightly self-justifying tone once you meet ところ later — except ところ freezes a single instant in the middle of an action, while もの looks back on a whole stretch of time that's already over.
caution_notes: もの needs genuine wistfulness or self-justification behind it — using it on a flat, purely factual statement sounds off.
もの follows the plain form only; it never attaches after the polite ます-form.
Nouns and な-adjectives need だ before もの (だもの); い-adjectives and verbs take もの directly.
もの doesn't fit questions or commands — it states a memory or a feeling, not a request.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your host family's little brother has a bowl of お菓[か]子[し] in front of him every single time you walk into the kitchen — breakfast, lunch, it doesn't matter. Vegetables sit on the plate untouched, day after day, and eventually you want to say it out loud, the way you'd say "he only eats sweets" in English. That's the job ばかり does: it plants itself right after a noun and announces "nothing else, just this — and it's been going on."

```jp
弟[おとうと]はお菓[か]子[し]ばかり食[た]べている。
```

*My younger brother eats nothing but sweets.*

Notice what's missing from that sentence: no negative verb, no extra word bolted on to spell out the exclusion. ばかり does the whole job by itself, and it leans a little judgmental while it does it — you're not neutrally reporting a diet, you're complaining about one, and native listeners will hear that complaint whether you meant to put it there or not.

That single word is doing two jobs at once, and it's worth separating them before you go any further, because mixing them up is the single most common mistake with this pattern. One job is about *what*: out of everything that could be true, only this one thing is. The other job, which you'll meet a little further down, is about *when*: something happened, and it happened so recently that it still feels like news. Both jobs share the same name and the same little word, but they attach to different pieces of grammar, and only context tells you which one a given sentence means.

## How it works

ばかり attaches directly to a noun, no particle needed in between most of the time — though a topic marker like は often rides along outside it, the way it did in that first sentence, marking who the whole comment is about. The meaning underneath is always "nothing but X": whatever else could reasonably be happening instead is conspicuously absent, and that absence is the point.

Your own week can look the same some months. Think back to a stretch where every evening after class disappeared into one activity and nothing else got touched — that's exactly the shape ばかり is built for.

```jp
私[わたし]は宿[しゅく]題[だい]ばかりしている。
```

*I'm doing nothing but homework.*

That sentence works because ばかり sits directly on 宿[しゅく]題[だい], the thing being done exclusively. It doesn't matter whether that's actually true down to the minute — you slept, you ate, you did other things too — ばかり is about what stands out when you look back on the stretch as a whole. That's the flavor: not a literal 100%, but "this is what defined the period."

ばかり has a second job that looks completely different on the surface: bolt it onto the Ta-form — the plain past form you already know from -た, like 起[お]きた for "woke up" — and it stops meaning "nothing but" and starts meaning "just did." The trigger switches from exclusivity to timing: this thing finished so recently that it's still fresh, close enough that mentioning it feels current rather than historical.

```jp
起[お]きる → 起[お]きた → 起[お]きたばかり
```

*wake up → woke up → just woke up*

Same verb, three stages: dictionary form, plain past, and plain past plus ばかり for "moments ago." Once ばかり lands on the Ta-form, it almost always shows up with です or だ closing the sentence out, because the whole point is usually a comment about right now — someone asking what's going on, and you answering with what just happened.

```jp
今[いま]、起[お]きたばかりです。
```

*I just woke up.*

The same shape works for anything that recently wrapped up, not just waking up. Picture texting a friend who's clearly stressed and finding out why: it turns out they only clocked in for the first time yesterday, so of course everything still feels overwhelming.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]は仕[し]事[ごと]を始[はじ]めたばかりだ。
```

*My friend just started the job.*

## Rules and exceptions

The Ta-form requirement for the "just did" reading is not optional, and this is where the two jobs of ばかり can genuinely trip you up. Attach ばかり to a dictionary-form verb hoping for "just do" and you don't get that meaning at all — you get something that doesn't parse the way you intended, because ばかり on its own carries no sense of completion. The completion has to already be sitting in the Ta-form before ばかり arrives to comment on how recent it was.

> Don't reach for `起きるばかり` when you mean "just woke up" — the Ta-form (起[お]きた) is what carries the "this already happened" meaning; ばかり only adds "and it happened recently." Drop the Ta-form and there's nothing left for ばかり to attach its timing to.

There's also a nuance trap on the noun side, and it trips up learners in the opposite direction — not a grammar mistake, but a tone one. Noun + ばかり is technically neutral; it just states an exclusive fact about what's happening. But in real conversation it almost always carries a complaint, the same way English "all he does is..." sounds annoyed even though it's, strictly speaking, just a true statement. There's no way to keep the same word and strip the attitude back out — the raised eyebrow comes bundled in, every time.

The "just did" reading has one more sharp edge worth naming: "recently" is a feeling, not a stopwatch. Whether たばかり sounds natural depends on how the speaker sees the gap, not on an actual number of minutes. Someone who moved cities a month ago might still say 引[ひ]っ越[こ]したばかりだ if the boxes are still unpacked and the new routine hasn't settled in — the sentence is really about how fresh the change still feels to the person saying it, not a strict cutoff you can look up.

## Casual speech

In relaxed conversation, ばかり often stretches into ばっかり — same meaning, heavier emphasis, the kind of sound you'd expect from someone who's genuinely fed up rather than just reporting a fact. 弟[おとうと]はお菓[か]子[し]ばっかり食[た]べてるよ carries the exact same complaint as the very first example in this lesson, just with the volume turned up: ばかり lengthens into ばっかり, and ている contracts down to てる the way it usually does when people are talking quickly. Save ばっかり for friends and family. Written Japanese, and anything even slightly formal, wants the fuller ばかり.

## Contrast

You already have ことがある for talking about experience — something you've done at some undefined point in your life, with no particular claim about when. Ta-form plus ばかり looks almost identical on the page, since both sit on the exact same Ta-form starting point, but the two constructions are answering completely different questions: not "has this ever happened to you," but "did this happen just moments ago."

```jp
日本[にほん]に行[い]ったことがある。
```

*I have been to Japan before.*

```jp
私[わたし]は日本[にほん]に行[い]ったばかりだ。
```

*I just went to Japan.*

Same verb, same destination, same Ta-form beginning — and the two endings send the sentence to opposite ends of a timeline. ことがある points backward with no particular date attached, a fact filed away in your personal history. たばかり points at right now, looking back over its shoulder at something that only just wrapped up. Swap one ending for the other and you've swapped "at some point in my life" for "as of a few minutes ago," which is exactly why this pair is worth slowing down on the first few times you meet it.

Hold onto that "just wrapped up" feeling — you're about to meet ところ, a cousin construction that covers the same general territory from a few different angles at once: about to happen, happening right now, or just finished, all wrapped into one word. ばかり only ever handles that last piece, the "just finished" edge, but it's good preparation for seeing how much more ground ところ ends up covering.
caution_notes: ばかり only gives the 'just did' meaning when it follows the Ta-form — attaching it to a dictionary-form verb doesn't work.
Noun + ばかり almost always sounds like a complaint in real conversation, even though it's grammatically just a neutral statement of exclusivity.
ばっかり is a casual stretch of ばかり — save it for friends, not for anything formal or written.
Don't confuse たばかり (something just happened) with ことがある (something has happened at some point) — they share the same Ta-form but answer different questions.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your phone buzzes. A friend texts: 出[で]かける？ You already have your かばん in one hand and your 靴[くつ] on your feet, standing right by the ドア, keys warm from your palm. There's only one honest answer, and it isn't a statement of general intent — it's a report on exactly where you are, right this second.

```jp
今[いま]、出[で]るところです。
```

*I'm just about to leave.*

Not 出[で]ます, which only states a plan with no sense of *when*. ところ does something narrower and more useful: it freezes the clock and names the exact instant you're standing in — a beat before an action starts, right in the thick of it, or a beat after it's already ended. You've probably met ところ before as a plain noun meaning "place" — 図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]の近[ちか]くのところ, roughly "the area near the library." This grammar use borrows that same idea and narrows it, from physical space down to a single point in time: not where you're standing, but where you're standing *inside the action*.

## How it works

### The moment before: dictionary form + ところ

Attach ところ straight onto a verb's plain dictionary form and you get the instant right before the action starts. Everything is lined up for it — you've decided, your body is already halfway into motion — but nothing has actually happened yet. That's the shape in the opening line above, 今[いま]、出[で]るところです. Here's the same shape with a different verb.

```jp
今[いま]、電[でん]話[わ]するところです。
```

*I'm just about to make a phone call.*

You can feel why 出[で]ます and 出[で]るところです land so differently now. 出[で]ます could be true at any point today. 出[で]るところです is only true for the few seconds you're actually saying it.

### The middle: ~ているところ

Swap in ている, the ongoing-action form you already know from describing habits and states, and ところ moves right along with it. Now you're not standing before the action — you're inside it, mid-motion, and someone asking you a question would be interrupting.

```jp
今[いま]、勉[べん]強[きょう]しているところです。
```

*I'm right in the middle of studying.*

```jp
今[いま]、掃[そう]除[じ]しているところです。
```

*I'm right in the middle of cleaning.*

This is the version you'll reach for most in daily conversation, because "I'm doing X right now" is a far more common thing to report than "I'm about to" or "I just did." Notice that ている alone would already mean roughly the same thing — ところ just sharpens the focus onto this precise moment, the way pointing at a spot on a map is sharper than gesturing at a whole city.

### The moment after: た-form + ところ

Use the plain past た-form you already know from ことがある, and ところ steps to the other side of the action — the instant right after it ended, close enough that there's no real gap between finishing and speaking.

```jp
今[いま]、朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べたところです。
```

*I just finished eating breakfast.*

```jp
今[いま]、宿[しゅく]題[だい]をしたところです。
```

*I just finished my homework.*

Say either of these an hour late and something feels off, the way it feels off to say "I just woke up" at three in the afternoon. たところ is honest about the clock — it only works when the gap really is close to zero.

The shape never changes once you know which side of the action you're describing: keep whichever verb form fits the moment, then set ところ right after it.

```jp
出[で]る → 出[で]るところ
```

*leave → about to leave*

## Rules and exceptions

ところ describes one instant, not a stretch of time, and it doesn't get along with words that imply repetition, like 毎[まい]日[にち] (every day). Something that happens over and over isn't a single moment you can point at — `毎日勉強しているところです` reads like a contradiction, because "every day" pulls toward a habit while ところ insists on right now, once, and nowhere else.

> ところ only ever follows a conjugated verb — never a plain adjective sitting on its own. `暑いところです` isn't a way to say "it's hot right now"; for that you just need the adjective and です by themselves (今[いま]、暑[あつ]いです).

In casual speech, the です at the end can drop the way it does after most plain-form sentences, so a friend might just say 今[いま]、出[で]るところ with the sentence trailing off. But ところ itself never contracts or shortens — it's the polite ending around it that relaxes, not the word doing the actual work.

## Contrast

You already know ばかり for "just did" — Ta-form + ばかり. It sits close enough to たところ that it's easy to reach for the wrong one without noticing. たところ insists on zero gap: you're speaking in almost the same breath as the action ending. ばかり is looser — the action could have wrapped up a few minutes ago, even longer, and you'd still reach for it as long as it still feels recent to you.

```jp
宿[しゅく]題[だい]をしたばかりです。
```

*I only just finished my homework (and it still feels recent).*

Say it the instant the last page closes, and 宿[しゅく]題[だい]をしたところです is exact. Say it an hour later, still a little pleased with yourself, and 宿[しゅく]題[だい]をしたばかりです is the one that's honest — たところ at that point would be quietly lying about the clock, claiming a freshness that's already worn off.

ところ is a stopwatch, not a calendar — it only ever names the instant you're standing in, whether that's a beat before an action, right inside it, or a beat after it lets go of you. Hold onto that instinct for freezing a single moment; you'll want it again soon, when 間[あいだ] asks you to describe not one instant but the whole stretch of time something else was happening around it.
caution_notes: ところ marks a single instant, not a stretch of time, so it clashes with repeated or habitual phrasing like 毎日勉強しているところです.
ところ only attaches after a conjugated verb, never directly after a plain adjective, so 暑いところです is not a way to talk about right now.
たところ and ばかり look similar but aren't interchangeable — たところ claims zero gap between the action and the moment of speaking, while ばかり tolerates a small gap.
ところです can drop its です in casual speech, but ところ itself never changes shape or contracts.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at your desk with headphones on, working through kanji flashcards while your family is out running errands. By the time they get back, you've gone through half the deck — for the entire stretch they were gone, you were studying. In Japanese, saying "for this whole period, this other thing was also true" is exactly the job of 間[あいだ]・間[あいだ]に (あいだ・あいだに), a phrase that turns a stretch of time into a container you can put another action inside.

```jp
私[わたし]が勉[べん]強[きょう]している間[あいだ]、猫[ねこ]は寝[ね]ていた。
```

*While I was studying, the cat was sleeping.*

Both halves of that sentence cover the same stretch — my studying and the cat's napping ran side by side, start to finish. That's plain 間[あいだ] doing its job: it says "for this whole period," and both clauses are describing something that lasted the entire time.

This pattern shows up constantly once you start listening for it, because so much of ordinary conversation is about two things happening around the same stretch of time — someone cooking while someone else sets the table, rain falling while you wait at a station, a phone staying silent while you're in a meeting. English usually reaches for "while" or "during" without thinking twice about which one; Japanese wants you to decide something more specific first.

## How it works

間[あいだ] (あいだ) is the ordinary word for "interval" or "the space between two things" — you'll also meet it on its own, meaning "between," in phrases like 家[いえ]と駅[えき]の間[あいだ] (between the house and the station). As a grammar pattern, it attaches after a verb in its ている form, or after a plain noun with の, and either way it names a block of time that the rest of the sentence gets placed against.

```jp
勉[べん]強[きょう]する → 勉[べん]強[きょう]している間[あいだ]
```

*to study → while studying*

Dictionary form → て-form + いる → add 間[あいだ]. The ている step matters: 間[あいだ] wants an ongoing state, not a single completed action, because it's marking off a *span*, and a span needs something continuous running across it — a state you could freeze at any point in the middle and still be true.

Add に right after 間[あいだ] and the meaning shifts in a small but important way. 間[あいだ] alone says "this whole stretch"; 間[あいだ]に says "at some point within this stretch, one thing happened."

```jp
私[わたし]が勉[べん]強[きょう]している間[あいだ]に、猫[ねこ]が窓[まど]から出[で]た。
```

*While I was studying, the cat went out through the window.*

The cat didn't spend the whole study session climbing out — it happened once, at some moment inside that stretch. に is doing the work of pinning a single event somewhere inside the block of time, instead of spreading it across the whole thing the way 間[あいだ] alone would.

The same split shows up with nouns, no verb required. Attach の間[あいだ](に) straight onto a noun that names a period, and you get the same two flavors again — the whole stretch, or one moment somewhere inside it.

```jp
会[かい]議[ぎ]の間[あいだ]、電[でん]話[わ]を消[け]した。
```

*During the meeting, I turned off my phone.*

```jp
会[かい]議[ぎ]の間[あいだ]に、雨[あめ]が降[ふ]った。
```

*It started raining sometime during the meeting.*

My phone stayed off for the entire meeting, start to finish — that's plain 間[あいだ]. The rain wasn't a condition that lasted the whole meeting; it started at some unspecified point inside it, so 間[あいだ]に is the one that fits. Notice that neither sentence needed a verb before 間[あいだ] at all — の間[あいだ] sits directly on the noun, the same way ことがある sits on a verb but もの can sit on a plain adjective; each pattern has its own attachment rule, and this one is a noun's.

That noun version is worth pausing on, because it's the one you'll reach for most in casual talk about your day. Any word that names a period with a clear start and end — 会[かい]議[ぎ], 授[じゅ]業[ぎょう], 週[しゅう]末[まつ] — can slot straight into の間[あいだ](に) without any conjugation at all. You don't need to know how to turn 会[かい]議[ぎ] into a verb, because you don't; the noun already names the block of time you need.

## Rules and exceptions

The whole system comes down to one question: is the main-clause event a *stretched-out state*, or a *single occurrence*? 間[あいだ] wants the first. 間[あいだ]に wants the second. It sounds abstract until you test it against a sentence where the main clause is neither a verb nor an obvious action.

```jp
授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]の間[あいだ]、教[きょう]室[しつ]はとても静[しず]かだった。
```

*During class, the classroom was very quiet.*

"Very quiet" isn't a one-off event — it's a condition that held for the entire class period, so plain 間[あいだ] is correct, matching the same logic as the ている examples even though there's no verb in sight. As long as the described state covers the whole span, plain 間[あいだ] belongs there.

> Mixing these two up is the single most common mistake with this pattern. Writing `勉強している間、猫が窓から出た。` sounds like the cat was somehow going out through the window continuously for the entire study session, which doesn't make sense — going out is something that happens once, not something you can stretch across an hour. The fix is just adding に:

```jp
勉[べん]強[きょう]している間[あいだ]に、猫[ねこ]が窓[まど]から出[で]た。
```

*While I was studying, the cat went out.*

One more edge worth knowing: because 間[あいだ] needs an ongoing predicate, you generally can't drop it straight onto a verb that names a sudden, single change — something like 出[で]る (to go out) — without ている first. ている is what turns a one-shot action into a state you can stretch a block of time around; without it, there's nothing for 間[あいだ] to measure.

There's also a smaller trap hiding in sentences like the meeting example. Nothing stops you from writing a sentence where *both* halves are stretched-out states, which is exactly the shape 間[あいだ] wants — but it's easy to reach for に out of habit anyway, because English "during" doesn't force you to think about duration versus a single moment the way Japanese does. Whenever you catch yourself about to add に, stop and ask what the main-clause verb or adjective is actually describing: a state that fills the whole block, or an event you could point to on a clock. In casual conversation this pattern doesn't contract or drop politeness the way です/だ pairs do — 間[あいだ] and 間[あいだ]に sound exactly the same whether you're texting a friend or writing a report, which is one less thing to track while you're getting the duration-versus-moment choice right.

## Contrast

You already know ところ for catching an action mid-process — 出[で]かけるところ, "just about to head out," or 出[で]かけているところ, "in the middle of heading out." ところ zooms in on one specific point along that process, almost like pausing a video. 間[あいだ] does the opposite: it steps back and treats the whole process, start to finish, as a single block of time you can talk about. 出[で]かけるところ is a freeze-frame; 出[で]かけている間[あいだ] is the whole clip playing start to end.

That difference matters because the two aren't interchangeable just because they can follow the same verbs. If your friend calls you exactly as you're stepping out the door, that's a ところ moment — one instant, caught mid-action. If your friend calls at some unspecified point while you're out for an hour, that's an 間[あいだ]に moment — the interval itself is doing the work, not one exact instant inside a single motion.

Take the meeting sentences from earlier and imagine swapping in ところ instead: `会議のところ` doesn't really work the way 会[かい]議[ぎ]の間[あいだ] does, because ところ needs something with a clear "middle" to catch you in — a verb in progress, not a noun that just names a block of time. That's the giveaway when you're unsure which one to reach for: if you can point to a single instant and say "right there, that's the point," ところ is available; if you're describing a whole stretch, or something landing anywhere inside that stretch, 間[あいだ] or 間[あいだ]に is what you want. 間[あいだ] and 間[あいだ]に don't compete with ところ so much as sit on a different scale of time — ところ is a point, 間[あいだ] is a stretch, and 間[あいだ]に is a point that happens to land somewhere inside a stretch.

Keep that distinction in mind, because a close cousin of 間[あいだ] is coming soon: うちに, which also frames a stretch of time but adds a sense of urgency — "while it's still true, before it stops being true." For now, 間[あいだ]・間[あいだ]に stays neutral: no ticking clock, just two things that happened to share the same stretch of time.
caution_notes: Use plain 間 only when the main clause describes a state or action that fills the entire stretch of time, not something that happens once.
Use 間に when the main-clause event is a single occurrence landing somewhere inside the background stretch, not something continuous.
間 needs an ongoing predicate before it — a verb in ている form or a plain noun with の — never a bare single-shot action.
ところ marks one specific point in a process, while 間 marks the whole span around it, so the two are not interchangeable even after similar verbs.
