items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend just poured you tea, and it's exactly the kind you love — hot enough to fog the cup, poured straight from the kettle. You get pulled into conversation, thirty seconds pass, and now it's lukewarm and a little sad. The move isn't "drink your tea" — it's drink it *now*, because this particular window is closing whether you notice or not.

```jp
お茶[ちゃ]が熱[あつ]いうちに飲[の]んだ方[ほう]がいいですよ。
```
*You should drink the tea while it's still hot.*

That's うちに — a pattern for describing a state that's true right now but won't stay true, paired with something you need to squeeze in before it changes. The textbook gloss is "while" or "during," but that undersells it. The real feeling is closer to: there's a clock running, and everyone in the sentence knows it.

## How it works

うちに attaches to a plain-form clause — the same shape you already use in front of ことにする or ところ (the plain form is just the casual, unconjugated shape of a verb or adjective: 食[た]べる, not 食[た]べます). い-adjectives take it directly:

```jp
熱[あつ]い → 熱[あつ]いうちに
```

The window here is "however long the tea stays hot." Once that's over, so is your chance.

Verbs usually show up in their ている shape in front of うちに, because the window this pattern points at is almost always an ongoing state, not a single finished action:

```jp
子[こ]供[ども]が寝[ね]ているうちに掃[そう]除[じ]しましょう。
```
*Let's clean while the child is sleeping.*

The child being asleep is the window. It's open right now, it's temporary, and the sentence tells you exactly what to do with it before it shuts.

The other shape you'll meet constantly is negative: ない form + うちに, meaning "before [something that hasn't happened yet happens]." This one might actually be more common in daily speech than the plain affirmative version, because "do this before that" is a shape people reach for all the time.

```jp
忘[わす]れないうちに名[な]前[まえ]を書[か]いた。
```
*I wrote down the name before I could forget it.*

```jp
忘[わす]れる → 忘[わす]れないうちに
```

The logic flips slightly here: the window is "the stretch where you still remember," and it slams shut the instant you forget. 忘[わす]れないうちに is close to a set phrase in Japanese — people reach for it constantly, well beyond any one grammar lesson.

うちに also attaches to na-adjectives with な (元[げん]気[き]なうちに, "while you're still healthy") and to nouns with の, which turns a whole stretch of time into the window itself:

```jp
若[わか]いうちにたくさん旅[りょ]行[こう]した方[ほう]がいい。
```
*You should travel a lot while you're young.*

"Young" isn't one instant — it's a stretch of years quietly running out the whole time you have it, which is exactly the shape of thing うちに was built for.

## Rules and exceptions

The state inside the うちに clause has to still be open. That means the nonpast plain form, or ている for something ongoing — never the た-form. `寝たうちに` isn't something a native speaker would say: た marks something already finished, and うちに needs a window that hasn't shut yet. Once the state is over, うちに has nothing left to point at.

> うちに usually assumes the window is closing on its own — daylight fading, tea cooling, someone falling asleep — not because of anything the main-clause action does. If the action you're describing is what actually ends the state (you wake the child up by cleaning loudly, say), the sentence starts working against itself. Pick a different action, or a different pattern.

It also doesn't fit a state with no end in sight. You wouldn't use it for something permanent, because there's no clock to race — and racing a clock is the entire reason this pattern exists.

## Contrast

You already know 間[あいだ]・間[あいだ]に for "during" — noun+の or verb+ている間[あいだ](に). Run the same scenario through both, and the difference becomes obvious:

```jp
週[しゅう]末[まつ]の間[あいだ]に宿[しゅく]題[だい]をした。
```
*I did my homework during the weekend.*

```jp
週[しゅう]末[まつ]のうちに宿[しゅく]題[だい]をした。
```
*I got my homework done while it was still the weekend.*

Same two nouns, same event, very different feeling. 間[あいだ]に is just reporting a timeframe — no urgency, no sense that anything was about to slip away. うちに frames the weekend as a window with an expiration date, and the sentence carries a quiet "I made it in time." Whenever the scenario has that flavor of racing a deadline — real or implied — うちに is the one doing the work; 間[あいだ]に would flatten the sentence into a plain fact.

Next time something around you is fading — the tea, the daylight, someone's patience — you've got the phrase for racing it. That same instinct, "this window won't stay open forever," is exactly what you'll need for たびに later, except たびに handles windows that reopen again and again instead of closing for good.
caution_notes: うちに needs the state in its clause to still be open, so pair it with the nonpast plain form or ている — never the た-form, since a finished state has no window left to race.
Reach for the negative shape (ない form + うちに) when you mean 'before X happens' — it's the version you'll hear far more often than the plain affirmative.
Don't let the main-clause action be what closes the うちに window itself (like waking someone up by cleaning near them) — that turns the sentence into a contradiction.
うちに carries a sense of racing a closing window, while 間・間に is neutral about timing — swap in 間に when there's no urgency to the timeframe.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your little sister visits for an hour, and by the time she leaves, the cat has vanished under the bed again. Not because of today's visit specifically — this happens every single time she comes over. You want a sentence that captures the whole pattern, not just today's incident, and Japanese has a tidy tool built exactly for that job.

```jp
妹[いもうと]が来[く]るたびに、猫[ねこ]が逃[に]げる。
```

*Every time my little sister comes over, the cat runs away.*

たびに is doing the heavy lifting in that sentence. It takes what sounds like a one-time news report — she came, the cat ran — and turns it into a standing fact about how these two things relate: every single time A happens, B follows, no exceptions worth mentioning.

## How it works

たびに attaches straight onto the dictionary form (the plain, unconjugated form you would look up in a dictionary) of a verb. No extra conjugation, no special stem, nothing to remember beyond taking the verb as it already is and adding たびに.

```jp
来[く]る → 来[く]るたびに
```

*to come → every time (someone) comes*

That's the entire mechanic for verbs. Whatever the dictionary form already looks like — 買[か]う, 見[み]る, 話[はな]す — that's exactly the shape that sits in front of たびに.

Nouns work differently, because a bare noun can't glue onto たびに on its own. You need の in between — the same connecting の that links any two nouns together, the way it does in 私[わたし]の本[ほん], meaning my book. Think of の as the piece that turns a noun into something たびに can attach to.

```jp
旅[りょ]行[こう]のたびに、新[あたら]しい靴[くつ]を買[か]う。
```

*Every trip, I buy new shoes.*

The same shape covers events you attend, not just trips you take:

```jp
会[かい]議[ぎ]のたびに、彼[かれ]は遅[おく]れる。
```

*Every meeting, he's late.*

If you already know 度[ど] as the counter for counting how many times something happened, たびに is written with that same kanji, just read differently. That's not a coincidence — both readings point at the same idea: counting occasions one by one, and saying something holds true of every single one you'd count.

Notice what the two halves of these sentences are doing. 来[く]るたびに and 旅[りょ]行[こう]のたびに just name the recurring trigger — the thing that keeps happening. The rest of the sentence is whatever reliably tags along whenever that trigger fires. The subject of each half doesn't even have to match: in 会[かい]議[ぎ]のたびに、彼[かれ]は遅[おく]れる, the meeting itself doesn't have a particular doer, but 彼[かれ] is the one arriving late every time it rolls around.

## Rules and exceptions

The clause right before たびに — the trigger — stays in dictionary form no matter what tense the rest of the sentence lands on. Even when you're describing a pattern that played out entirely in the past, resist pulling that first verb into the past tense along with it.

```jp
彼[かれ]が来[く]るたびに、猫[ねこ]が逃[に]げた。
```

*Every time he came, the cat ran away.*

> The sentence is unmistakably about the past — 逃[に]げた closes it out — but 来[く]る stays in dictionary form. Writing `来たたびに` feels like it should match, and that instinct is exactly what trips people up; たびに simply never follows a past-tense verb.

The mirror-image mistake shows up with nouns: dropping の because the sentence already feels long enough. `旅行たびに` looks like a shortcut, but it isn't one — a noun always needs の to lead into たびに, the same way it needs の in front of any other noun phrase.

たびに also only earns its keep when something genuinely keeps happening. It's for the pattern you'd notice after the third or fourth time, not a single moment where this happened and then that happened. If you're only reporting one specific occasion, this word is off the table.

One thing you don't need to worry about: たびに doesn't shrink or contract in casual speech the way です or the negative forms do. You'll hear it exactly like this whether you're talking to a friend or writing something formal.

## Contrast: たびに vs 間[あいだ]に

You've already met 間[あいだ]に for while, during the interval — one particular stretch of time, with something happening once inside it. たびに is built for the opposite shape: not one window, but every window, each one counted on its own.

```jp
彼[かれ]が話[はな]している間[あいだ]に、私[わたし]は宿[しゅく]題[だい]をした。
```

*While he was talking, I did my homework.*

```jp
彼[かれ]が話[はな]すたびに、私[わたし]は笑[わら]う。
```

*Every time he talks, I laugh.*

The first sentence is about one occasion: he talked, and sometime during that stretch, the homework got done. Swap in たびに there and you'd suddenly be claiming this happens every time he talks — a far bigger claim than just this once. The second sentence is the opposite: a standing rule about every occasion. Swap in 間[あいだ]に there and the sentence collapses into describing a single conversation, which misses the entire point — the reason it's worth saying is that it happens over and over.

That distinction — one window versus every window — is worth sitting with, because it's easy to reach for whichever pattern you learned first out of habit. Ask yourself whether you're describing something that happened once during a stretch of time, or something that happens reliably, every single time. That question alone tells you which of the two you need.

Hold onto that repeating-pattern feeling. You'll meet it again from a different angle once と comes up for automatic, general results — when X happens, Y always follows, built into the grammar of a single clause rather than named from the outside. たびに says here's a pattern I've noticed; と will let you build that same inevitability directly into one sentence. For now, whenever you catch yourself thinking this always happens when, that's your cue to reach for たびに.
caution_notes: Keep the verb right before たびに in dictionary form even when the whole sentence is about the past — たびに itself never follows a past-tense verb.
Don't drop の when a noun leads into たびに; 旅行のたびに needs that の the same way any noun phrase does.
Save たびに for something that genuinely repeats — a pattern you'd notice after several occasions, not a single one-off event.
間に describes one window of time where something happens once; swapping it for たびに turns a single occasion into a standing, repeating rule.

items.explanation_markdown:
Picture this: you're texting a friend about tomorrow's hike, but the forecast is shaky. You don't want to promise it'll rain — you just want to cover what happens if it does. That's the shape 場[ば]合[あい] is built for. It doesn't predict anything. It labels a possible scenario and lets you say what you'll do if that one turns out to be the one that happens.

Japanese has plenty of ways to talk about conditions, and you'll meet more of them soon. 場[ば]合[あい] is the one for laying out a specific case — this situation, as opposed to some other one — and then responding to it directly.

## How it works

場[ば]合[あい] (ばあい) is itself a noun meaning "case" or "instance." You build the scenario in front of it, then treat the whole thing as a launching point for what comes next. With a verb, the clause in front just stays in plain form — the same shape you'd use to end a sentence on its own.

```jp
電[でん]車[しゃ]が遅[おく]れる場[ば]合[あい]は、連[れん]絡[らく]してください。
```

*If the train is late, please contact me.*

Notice 遅[おく]れる sits there completely unchanged, present-tense and plain, the way it would if you were just saying "the train is late" to a friend. 場[ば]合[あい]は then turns that into "in the case where that happens."

With a noun in front, you can't jump straight to 場[ば]合[あい] — you need の bridging the two nouns first, the same の that links 友[とも]達[だち]の家[いえ] or 私[わたし]の傘[かさ].

```jp
雨[あめ] → 雨[あめ]の場[ば]合[あい]
```

*rain → in the case of rain*

```jp
雨[あめ]の場[ば]合[あい]、傘[かさ]を持[も]って行[い]きます。
```

*In case of rain, I'll bring an umbrella.*

Past and negative clauses slot in exactly the same way, because they're still plain forms — 場[ば]合[あい] doesn't care about timing, only about the shape of what's in front of it.

```jp
分[わ]からない場[ば]合[あい]は、先[せん]生[せい]に聞[き]いてください。
```

*If you don't understand, please ask the teacher.*

```jp
財[さい]布[ふ]を無[な]くした場[ば]合[あい]、警[けい]官[かん]に言[い]います。
```

*If I lose my wallet, I'll tell a police officer.*

That second one is worth sitting with — 無[な]くした is past tense, describing a scenario that hasn't happened yet. That feels backwards in English, but in Japanese the past form there just marks the loss as a completed event *within* the hypothetical, the way "if I've lost my wallet" reads more naturally than "if I lose my wallet" once you notice it.

## Rules and exceptions

The の between a noun and 場[ば]合[あい] isn't optional style — it's structural.

> `病気場合` isn't a sentence a Japanese speaker would produce. It has to be `病気の場合` — の is doing real grammatical work, not sitting there for decoration.

は after 場[ば]合[あい] is common but not required. Reach for it when you're contrasting this case against some other one you're aware of; skip it when you're simply laying out one scenario on its own.

```jp
病[びょう]気[き]の場[ば]合[あい]、学[がっ]校[こう]を休[やす]みます。
```

*If I'm sick, I take the day off school.*

```jp
忙[いそが]しい場[ば]合[あい]は、手伝[てつだ]ってください。
```

*If you're busy, please help me.*

One more trap worth naming early: even when the scenario you're describing is about something that might happen later, the clause in front of 場[ば]合[あい] stays plain present or plain past — never a guessing form like `遅れるだろう場合`. 場[ば]合[あい] wants a fact-shaped clause sitting in front of it; the hedging about whether it'll actually happen lives outside the grammar, in your tone and context, not baked into the sentence itself.

## 場[ば]合[あい] vs たびに

You've already met たびに for "every time X happens, Y happens" — a pattern that repeats on schedule with its trigger. On the page, たびに and 場[ば]合[あい] look like cousins: both sit after a plain-form clause or noun+の. But they're answering different questions. たびに says *this happens every single time, without fail*. 場[ば]合[あい] says *if this particular thing comes up, here's my plan* — with no claim at all about how often, or whether, it actually will.

```jp
雨[あめ]が降[ふ]るたびに、傘[かさ]を忘[わす]れます。
```

*Every time it rains, I forget my umbrella.*

Set that next to the 雨[あめ]の場[ば]合[あい] line from earlier. 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]るたびに is basically a confession about a pattern in your life — it keeps happening, and the same thing follows every time. 雨[あめ]の場[ば]合[あい] makes no claim about how often it rains at all; it just says, should that be the case today, here's the plan. Swap one for the other and you've swapped a running joke about your own forgetfulness for a calm, one-off contingency plan.

Hold onto that distinction — 場[ば]合[あい] sets up a scenario without committing to it coming true, and that's exactly the territory と will move into soon, for situations where one thing leads to another automatically, no maybe about it.
caution_notes: Between a noun and 場合 you always need の — `病気場合` is wrong; it must be `病気の場合`.
場合 lays out a possible scenario without claiming it will happen, so don't dress the clause in front of it with a guessing form like だろう.
場合 and たびに aren't interchangeable — たびに means every single time without exception, while 場合 just names one particular scenario, with no claim about frequency.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're staying at a friend's place, and their phone starts buzzing on the table. Before anyone reaches for it, their cat leaps a foot in the air and knocks a cup off the shelf. Every single time, without fail, that's how it goes — the phone rings, the cat panics. There's no discussion involved, no choice, no "maybe" about it. That's exactly the shape of と: it connects two things where the first one triggers the second automatically, the way a light switch is wired straight to a bulb.

```jp
電[でん]話[わ]が鳴[な]ると、猫[ねこ]が驚[おどろ]く。
```

*The phone rings, and the cat gets startled.*

That's と doing its real job — not describing a one-off event, but describing how things just go, every time, without anyone stepping in to decide anything. English blurs "if" and "when" together in a dozen different ways, but と narrows the range on purpose: reach for it only when the second half isn't up for debate.

Think of と as a wire, not a suggestion. Once you connect the two ends, current flows whether anyone's watching or not. A friend's cat isn't consulted before it flinches, and neither is the weather, the season, or your own face after a drink — those are exactly the situations と was built for, and the rest of this lesson is mostly about learning to spot them.

## How it works

と attaches directly to the plain, present-tense form of whatever leads into it — the same casual form you'd use to end a sentence on its own. と itself never conjugates, and it doesn't care about politeness levels; whatever comes before it just needs to already be in plain present shape, and everything else builds off that one clause.

```jp
窓[まど]を開[あ]けると、風[かぜ]が入[はい]る。
```

*Open the window, and wind comes in.*

窓[まど]を開[あ]ける is already plain present ("open"), so と simply hooks onto the end of it. Whatever follows と has to be something that occurs as a direct, mechanical consequence of the first half — never something you're planning, arranging, or deciding to do. Open the window, wind arrives; there's no gap in between for anyone to weigh in.

い-adjectives slot in the same way — the plain present form of an い-adjective is just the adjective itself, no extra piece needed before と:

```jp
お酒[さけ]を飲[の]むと、顔[かお]が赤[あか]くなる。
```

*Drink this, and your face turns red.*

赤[あか]くなる is 赤[あか]い (red) reshaped into 赤[あか]く and paired with なる ("to become") — a bodily reaction nobody has to choose, it just happens. This くなる/になる + と combination shows up constantly with seasons and general changes in the world, because seasons and bodies don't ask permission either:

```jp
冬[ふゆ]になると、雪[ゆき]が降[ふ]る。
```

*When winter comes, snow falls.*

```jp
春[はる]になると、暖[あたた]かくなる。
```

*When spring comes, it turns warm.*

Both sentences use になる or くなる as the "turns into" hinge, then chain the result on with と. Seasons arriving, temperatures shifting, routines kicking in — と is the natural home for all of it, because none of it is a decision anyone makes. Worth pausing on one small trap here: 鳴[な]る (to ring, from the phone example) and なる (to become) sound identical but are completely different words written with different kanji. Context sorts them out fast once you've seen a few of each, but the first week they can blur together.

と has a second job worth knowing: reporting something you found out the moment the first action wrapped up.

```jp
家[いえ]に帰[かえ]ると、雨[あめ]だった。
```

*I got home, and it was raining.*

Here the second half sits in the past (雨[あめ]だった), because you're reporting a discovery, not stating a standing rule — you walked in the door and, huh, it turns out it's raining. The half in front of と still has to stay present plain regardless of when the whole sentence is set — 帰[かえ]る, never 帰[かえ]った, even though the story itself already happened.

## Rules and exceptions

Here's where と gets strict: the second half has to be something that just happens on its own — never something anyone requests, invites, orders, or plans. Requests, invitations, suggestions, and stated intentions are all off-limits after と, no matter how naturally they'd translate into English with "when" or "if."

> Something like `忙しいと、手伝ってください` doesn't work. Being busy doesn't automatically produce a request for help the way a phone ringing automatically startles a cat — a request is a choice someone makes, not a reflex, so と can't carry it.

For that kind of sentence, 場[ば]合[あい] does the job instead — it was built to hold plans, requests, and advice, which is exactly what と refuses to hold:

```jp
忙[いそが]しい場[ば]合[あい]、手伝[てつだ]ってください。
```

*If you're busy, please help.*

場[ば]合[あい] marks a particular situation and leaves plenty of room for a decision, a request, or a plan tied to it. と refuses that room on purpose — it's reserved for the automatic and the inevitable, the sentences where nobody is actually choosing anything.

## Contrast: と vs 場[ば]合[あい]

You already know 場[ば]合[あい] for flagging "in the case of X" before advice or a plan. と looks similar on the surface — both sit after a plain clause and set up a second half — but they carry very different weight. 場[ば]合[あい] describes a scenario someone is reasoning about ahead of time; と describes something that simply keeps happening, rain or shine, decision or no decision.

```jp
雨[あめ]の場[ば]合[あい]、公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]かない。
```

*If it rains, we won't go to the park.*

```jp
雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ると、公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]かない。
```

*When it rains, we don't go to the park.*

Both sentences land on the same outcome, but they sound different. The 場[ば]合[あい] version reads like a plan somebody worked out in advance — "in the case that it rains, here's what we've decided." The と version reads like a fact about how things go — rain shows up, the park trip just doesn't happen, every time, no planning involved, almost like a rule of the household rather than a choice anyone is making today. Swap them and you swap the flavor: と turns a decision into a law of nature, 場[ば]合[あい] turns a law of nature back into a choice.

This is also why と sentences tend to sound more confident, almost blunt, next to their 場[ば]合[あい] counterparts. Saying 雨[あめ]の場[ば]合[あい]、公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]かない leaves a little space — maybe circumstances change, maybe someone reconsiders. Saying 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ると、公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]かない closes that space entirely. If you've ever wondered why a textbook example with と can sound oddly matter-of-fact in translation, this is usually why: the grammar itself is doing the work of removing doubt, not just describing a sequence of events.

One more small thing worth knowing: unlike some connectors you've seen, と doesn't shrink or shift in casual speech. Friends talking quickly still say と exactly as written — there's no shortened version to learn here, so once the plain-present-plus-と shape is solid, you already have the whole pattern in every register.

Reach for と when you're stating something automatic, habitual, or freshly discovered. Reach for 場[ば]合[あい] the moment a request, a suggestion, or a real decision needs to sit in the second half. Keeping that line clear is most of what と actually asks of you — and it's the same instinct you'll lean on again once から shows up for reasons that are simply true, rather than reasons someone is asking you to accept.

One last thing worth carrying forward: と rewards paying attention to what kind of sentence you're actually building before you reach for it. If you catch yourself about to type a request, an invitation, or a plan right after と, that's the signal to stop and swap in 場[ば]合[あい] instead — not a sign that と is broken, just a sign it's the wrong tool for that particular sentence. Get comfortable with that swap and the rest of the pattern mostly takes care of itself.
caution_notes: Never put a request, invitation, order, or suggestion in the clause after と — for those, use 場合 instead.
The clause right before と must stay in plain present form even when the second half describes something in the past, like a discovery.
と states something automatic or habitual; if the outcome is really a plan or decision someone made, 場合 is the better fit.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're texting a friend to bail on plans tonight. "忙[いそが]しいから、行[い]けない" — busy, so no. Blunt, quick, done. Now picture writing your teacher the reason you missed class. Same idea, "because," but that same から would land like you're arguing with them. You reach for something softer instead: ので.

That's the whole tension in this lesson. から and ので both mean "because," they attach to sentences in nearly the same way, and one of them is going to sound rude in a room where the other sounds completely normal. Time to learn which is which.

## How it works

Both patterns follow the plain form of whatever caused the situation, with the reason first and the result second.

```jp
忙[いそが]しいから、行[い]けない。
```
*Busy, so [I] can't go.*

Verbs and い-adjectives don't need anything extra — the plain, dictionary-style form attaches straight to both patterns, no changes required.

```jp
忙[いそが]しい → 忙[いそが]しいから
```
*busy → because [I'm] busy*

Nouns and な-adjectives are where the two patterns split from each other. から wants the plain copula だ in front of it, exactly like any other plain-form sentence. ので wants な instead — the だ disappears completely.

```jp
静[しず]か → 静[しず]かなので
```
*quiet → since [it's] quiet*

```jp
静[しず]かだから、ここが好[す]きです。
```
*Because it's quiet, [I] like this place.*

```jp
静[しず]かなので、ここが好[す]きです。
```
*Since it's quiet, [I] like this place.*

Read those last two sentences side by side. The meaning barely moves — that's the whole point of this lesson. What actually changes is the room you can say each one in.

## Rules and exceptions

The real difference between から and ので isn't grammar, it's stance. から presents the reason as *yours* — an opinion, a decision, something you're standing behind and ready to defend if someone pushes back. ので presents the reason as a plain fact of the situation, something anyone in the room would agree with, which is exactly why it lands as more polite: you're not arguing your case, you're just reporting what's true.

That's also why ので shows up constantly in notes to teachers, apologies, and formal requests, while から shows up in casual talk and in sentences where you're explaining yourself or trying to persuade someone. Compare 忙[いそが]しいから、休[やす]みます (I'm taking the day off — busy, that's my call) against 忙[いそが]しいので、休[やす]みます (I'm taking the day off; I'm busy, as you can see) — same words, same day off, a completely different feel.

```jp
頭[あたま]が痛[いた]いので、休[やす]みます。
```
*My head hurts, so I'll rest today.*

> Commands, invitations, and "let's" sentences almost always want から, not ので. `危ないので、走らないで` reads like you're trying to sound polite while telling someone what to do, and it comes out strange. から is built for that job.

```jp
危[あぶ]ないから、走[はし]らないで。
```
*It's dangerous, so don't run.*

The だ/な split from the last section is the easiest place to slip — writing `静かだので` or `静かなから` will sound off to a Japanese ear immediately, even when every other piece of the sentence is right.

## Casual speech

In relaxed speech, ので often shrinks to んで. The meaning doesn't change at all — it's just faster to say.

```jp
忙[いそが]しいんで、行[い]けない。
```
*Busy, so [I] can't go.* (casual)

から doesn't contract the same way. It stays から whether you're texting a friend or writing something formal — the word itself never softens; only the situation you choose to use it in does.

## Contrast

You've already met と for describing something that happens automatically once a condition is met. と can't carry a decision or an opinion the way から can — 病[びょう]気[き]だから、休[やす]む is you choosing to rest, while と would need the resting to just follow on its own, with no room for you deciding anything. から and ので are both about a reason someone is putting forward; と isn't really about a reason at all, it's about an automatic result.

So the real question with から and ので was never "which one is more correct" — it's "am I stating a fact, or standing behind an opinion." Keep that instinct close, because it comes back almost unchanged when というより shows up later: instead of restating a reason, it lets you correct one you already gave.
caution_notes: ので presents a reason as a plain fact you're reporting, not an opinion you're pushing — reach for it in notes, apologies, and requests instead of から.
Commands, invitations, and volitional sentences almost always take から; ので sounds strange right in front of them.
Nouns and な-adjectives take だ before から but な before ので — mixing the two, like 静かだので or 静かなから, is the single most common slip.
から never contracts, but casual ので often shortens to んで in relaxed speech.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your mother always makes dinner, but tonight she got stuck at the office. Someone still has to cook, and right now that someone is you — not because you're taking over her job for good, just for tonight, standing in her usual spot at the stove.

```jp
母[はは]の代[か]わりに、私[わたし]が晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]を作[つく]ります。
```

*Instead of my mother, I'll make dinner.*

That little phrase, 代[か]わりに, is doing something specific in that sentence. It isn't a reason — you're not cooking *because* your mother is busy; that's a separate fact you could mention on its own, with a totally different word. And it isn't just "and also," stacking one fact on top of another. It marks a swap: one person, or one action, is taking the seat that was meant for another. Once you can hear that swap, 代[か]わりに starts showing up everywhere — someone covering a shift, someone answering a question that wasn't addressed to them, someone paying a bill that wasn't theirs to begin with.

## How it works

The most common shape is **Noun + の + 代[か]わりに**. You name whoever, or whatever, is being stood in for, attach の — the same の that links two nouns, like 私[わたし]の本[ほん] — and then 代[か]わりに. The person actually doing the substitute action shows up separately in the sentence, usually as its subject. It helps to think of 代[か]わりに as a kind of place-marker: の代[か]わりに is literally "in the spot of," and everything after it describes who or what is currently occupying that spot.

```jp
兄[あに]が忙[いそが]しいから、兄[あに]の代[か]わりに弟[おとうと]が働[はたら]きます。
先[せん]生[せい]が忙[いそが]しいから、先[せん]生[せい]の代[か]わりに生[せい]徒[と]が答[こた]えました。
```

*Because my older brother is busy, my younger brother works in his place.*
*Because the teacher is busy, the student answered in the teacher's place.*

Notice the の never drops, no matter how short the sentence gets. 代[か]わりに always needs something to hang off — a noun it's replacing, or, in the next pattern, a whole action it's replacing. That's a useful thing to hold onto, because in casual speech a lot of particles get dropped or slurred together, but this の is load-bearing. Drop it, and the sentence stops parsing as a substitution at all.

That second pattern is **dictionary form + 代[か]わりに** — the dictionary form being the plain, unconjugated shape you'd look a verb up under, like 行[い]く or 食[た]べる. Here 代[か]わりに isn't swapping one person for another; it's swapping one action for another, inside the same person's own choices. You do B instead of doing A, and both A and B belong to you.

```jp
電[でん]話[わ]する代[か]わりに、手[て]紙[がみ]を書[か]きました。
医[い]者[しゃ]に行[い]く代[か]わりに、薬[くすり]を飲[の]みました。
```

*Instead of calling, I wrote a letter.*
*Instead of going to the doctor, I took medicine.*

Both halves of each sentence belong to the same person. Nobody else enters the picture — it's a private substitution, this action instead of that one, and the dictionary form is what marks the road not taken. You'll notice that the verb before 代[か]わりに doesn't care about tense at all; even if the letter got written yesterday, 電[でん]話[わ]する stays in the dictionary form, and only the final verb — 書[か]きました — carries the past tense for the whole sentence.

代[か]わりに has a second life beyond straight substitution: it can mark a trade, something given back in return for something else. The shape is identical — dictionary form + 代[か]わりに — but the feel shifts from "instead of" to "in return for."

```jp
傘[かさ]を貸[か]す代[か]わりに、少[すこ]しお金[かね]をもらいます。
```

*In exchange for lending the umbrella, I get a little money.*

Nothing in the grammar itself tells you which reading is meant; the situation does. Lending an umbrella and getting money back is obviously a trade, not a replacement — nobody assumes you lent the umbrella *instead of* doing something else. Context carries the weight here, the same way it does with a lot of everyday Japanese: the words hand you a shape, and the scene fills in what that shape means.

## Rules and exceptions

> The の is not optional with nouns. `父代わりに行きます` is wrong — 代[か]わりに cannot bolt straight onto a noun. It has to be 父[ちち]の代[か]わりに行[い]きます.

With verbs, the attachment point is just as fixed: always the dictionary form, never the て-form and never the plain stem. `食べて代わりに` isn't a sentence anyone would say — it has to be 食[た]べる代[か]わりに. If you catch yourself reaching for a て-form right before 代[か]わりに, treat that as a signal to swap back to the dictionary form; the て-form belongs to a different family of patterns entirely, and 代[か]わりに just doesn't take it, no matter how natural it feels to chain て-forms together elsewhere.

代[か]わりに also doesn't need a noun or a verb attached to it at all — it can open a brand-new sentence on its own, pointing back at something you already said.

```jp
今日[きょう]は忙[いそが]しいです。
代[か]わりに、明日[あした]会[あ]いましょう。
```

*Today I'm busy.*
*Instead, let's meet tomorrow.*

Used this way, it works almost like a spoken aside — "instead," full stop — leaning entirely on the sentence before it for its meaning. That's worth knowing, because this is the form you'll actually hear most in casual conversation: tucked at the front of a reply, not buried in the middle of one long sentence. You don't need to reconstruct a noun or a verb after it in your head; the previous sentence already did that work for you.

## Contrast: 代[か]わりに vs から

You already know から for stating a reason — *because* X, Y happens. It's tempting to think 代[か]わりに is doing the same job, since both often turn up in sentences about someone stepping in for someone else. They don't overlap, though. から explains *why* something is happening; 代[か]わりに tells you *who or what got swapped in*. You can have either one without the other, and plenty of real sentences only need one of them.

```jp
姉[あね]が忙[いそが]しいから、妹[いもうと]が晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]を作[つく]ります。
姉[あね]が忙[いそが]しいから、姉[あね]の代[か]わりに妹[いもうと]が晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]を作[つく]ります。
```

*Because my older sister is busy, my younger sister makes dinner.*
*Because my older sister is busy, my younger sister makes dinner in her place.*

The first sentence only tells you why the younger sister is cooking — maybe she always cooks anyway, busy sister or not. The second makes a stronger claim: she's specifically doing a job that would otherwise have fallen to her sister. Same reason clause, different claim about whose turn it really was. That gap between the two sentences is the whole point of learning 代[か]わりに separately from から — without it, you can explain why something happened, but you can't say whose role got taken over to make it happen.

That distinction — swapping an actor versus just stating a reason — is exactly the kind of thing that stays blurry the first few times you meet it, so don't worry if your early 代[か]わりに sentences feel like they could've stopped at から instead. There's a rough test: if you can ask "instead of whom, or instead of what?" and get a real answer out of the sentence, 代[か]わりに belongs there. If there's no real answer to that question, you're probably just looking at a reason, and から is doing all the work on its own.

代[か]わりに earns its keep because Japanese cares a lot about naming exactly whose role got taken, and から alone can't do that job — it only ever tells you why, never who was supposed to be there first.

Hold onto that "stand-in" feeling. Later on you'll meet というより, which swaps not people or actions but *descriptions* — for when you want to correct how something was framed, rather than settle who actually did it.
caution_notes: 代わりに never attaches directly to a noun — always insert の first (兄の代わりに, not 兄代わりに).
With verbs, 代わりに attaches only to the dictionary form, never to the て-form or the stem.
The same 代わりに sentence can read as substitution or as a trade — only the situation tells you which, not the grammar.
から explains why something happens; 代わりに names who or what was swapped in — they answer different questions even in the same sentence.

items.explanation_markdown:
You are telling a friend about today's Japanese exam. 難[むずか]しい, you start to say — difficult. Except that's not quite right. Every question was written in oddly indirect language, the time limit was tight, and by the end your hand hurt from writing — none of that is really what 難[むずか]しい points at. What you actually mean is closer to annoying, and you want to say so without pretending you never said 難[むずか]しい at all.

That is the exact job というより does. It does not erase the first word — it upgrades it. You put the first guess down, mark it as a rough draft with というより, and follow it with the sharper word.

```jp
この試[し]験[けん]は難[むずか]しいというより面[めん]倒[どう]くさい。
```

*This exam isn't so much difficult as it is annoying.*

You could of course just say 面[めん]倒[どう]くさい and stop there, dropping 難[むずか]しい entirely. But that loses something real: the listener never finds out that 難[むずか]しい was your first, natural reaction, and that you're now sharpening it on purpose. というより keeps both words in play and shows the correction happening in real time, which is exactly why it shows up so often in casual conversation — it's how people actually think out loud.

This is a small but useful trick for a learner, too. You don't always need the perfect word on the first try. Say the word you already know, then reach for というより and a second, closer word — the sentence still lands, and it sounds more natural than pausing mid-thought to hunt for the ideal adjective before you say anything at all.

## How it works

というより attaches to the plain form — the same shape you already use in front of から and と. If the word in front of it is an i-adjective or a verb, you don't touch it at all; you just tack というより straight onto the end.

It helps to see where the pattern comes from. という is built from と (a quoting particle — the little word that marks what someone said or thought) plus いう (to say), so というより literally reads something like more than saying that. より is the same より you'd use in a plain comparison. Put them together and you get exactly what the pattern does: more than saying the first thing, this is closer to the truth.

Nouns and na-adjectives work slightly differently, because their plain form usually carries だ (先[せん]生[せい]だ, 静[しず]かだ) — and というより doesn't want that だ sitting in front of it. Drop it, and put the bare noun or na-adjective directly before the pattern instead.

```jp
彼[かれ]は先[せん]生[せい]というより友[とも]達[だち]だ。
```

*He's more a friend than a teacher.*

```jp
この部屋[へや]は静[しず]かというより暗[くら]い。
```

*This room isn't so much quiet as it is dark.*

Notice the two halves don't have to match in part of speech. 静[しず]か is a na-adjective, 暗[くら]い is an i-adjective, and というより sits between them without any trouble, because it isn't comparing grammar categories — it's comparing two descriptions of the same room.

The same freedom applies to verbs. Anything that ends in the plain dictionary form can sit in front of というより exactly as it is, with no extra piece bolted on. If you've been bracing for a special connecting form the way some patterns demand, you can relax here — the plain form you already default to is the whole story.

というより itself never changes shape. No past tense, no negative, no polite ます version living inside it. Whatever tense or politeness the sentence needs goes on the words sitting on either side of it, never on というより itself. That's one less thing to memorize than most of what you've met so far — the conjugation work all happens before というより, never to it.

## Rules and exceptions

というより always needs two descriptions of the same thing sitting in one sentence — a first guess and a better one. It has no life as a stand-alone reason the way から does; there's no reading of というより that works like because, even though both patterns attach to the same plain form.

That's also why というより never opens a conversation out of nowhere. There always has to be a first attempt sitting somewhere nearby for it to improve on — sometimes your own last sentence, sometimes something the other person just said.

This is also why というより tends to cluster with words that sit close together in meaning — 難[むずか]しい and 面[めん]倒[どう]くさい, 忙[いそが]しい and 大[たい]変[へん], つまらない and 悲[かな]しい. Pick two words that have nothing to do with each other and the sentence stops making sense, because there's no shared thing left for the second word to describe more accurately than the first.

> The word *after* というより is the one that wins. Reverse the order and you reverse which description the speaker actually stands behind — 忙[いそが]しいというより大[たい]変[へん]だ and 大[たい]変[へん]というより忙[いそが]しい are not the same claim.

```jp
今日[きょう]は忙[いそが]しいというより大[たい]変[へん]だ。
```

*Today isn't so much busy as it is rough.*

```jp
この映[えい]画[が]はつまらないというより悲[かな]しい。
```

*This movie isn't so much boring as it is sad.*

It's also easy to reach for というより when what you actually mean is instead of. English rather than can carry both jobs — a corrected description, or a chosen action instead of a different one — but というより only does the first. It never swaps one action for another; that job belongs to 代[か]わりに, which shows up again below.

A related trap: というより doesn't mean more than in the sense of quantity, the way you might compare heights or prices. It's not measuring which word is bigger; it's judging which word is truer. 忙[いそが]しいというより大[たい]変[へん]だ isn't claiming 大[たい]変[へん] outranks 忙[いそが]しい on some scale — it's saying 大[たい]変[へん] is simply the more accurate word for today.

## Casual speech

In relaxed speech, と regularly contracts to って — というのは becomes っていうのは, and というより follows the same pattern: っていうより. You'll hear native speakers drop it mid-sentence, correcting themselves or someone else out loud, the same way you might in English with or, actually.

The full というより never disappears from writing or from careful, polite speech — a work email or a formal apology keeps it intact. っていうより belongs to texting, chatting with friends, and the kind of spoken Japanese where you're thinking as you talk. Treat the choice between them the same way you'd treat any other casual contraction you've already met: register, not meaning, is what changes.

If you're ever unsure which one to reach for, default to the full というより. It's never wrong, even in a casual conversation — it just sounds a shade more careful. っていうより only sounds wrong the other way around, dropped into a formal email where it reads as too loose for the occasion.

```jp
っていうより、面[めん]倒[どう]くさいだけだよ。
```

*More accurately, it's just annoying, that's all.*

## Contrast

から states a reason — a fact the speaker is pointing to as the cause of something. というより doesn't state a reason at all; it revises a description. 難[むずか]しいから休[やす]む means because it's hard, I'm resting — no correction is happening there, just a plain cause and effect.

```jp
難[むずか]しいから、今日[きょう]は休[やす]む。
```

*Because it's difficult, I'll rest today.*

代[か]わりに is the pattern actually built for swapping — one action standing in for another, not one word standing in for another. Reach for というより when you're fixing how you described something, and 代[か]わりに when you're fixing what actually happened.

```jp
休[やす]む代[か]わりに、部屋[へや]を掃[そう]除[じ]した。
```

*Instead of resting, I cleaned the room.*

Put side by side, the difference is easy to feel: 休[やす]む代[か]わりに means resting got replaced by something else entirely — cleaning happened, not resting. If you swapped in というより there instead, you would need two descriptions of the same single event, which resting and cleaning simply are not. The pattern you pick tells the listener what kind of correction they're getting — a fact about the world, or a better choice of words.

というより never argues that the first word was wrong — only that the second one is closer. Later, として will pick up a different job entirely, handing a noun a role to stand in rather than correcting anything about it. Keep them separate in your head from the start, and you won't be tempted to reach for というより out of habit on a sentence where nothing actually needs revising.
caution_notes: というより corrects or refines a description you already put into words — it doesn't mean instead of the way 代わりに does, so don't swap the two.
Before a noun or na-adjective, drop だ — say 先生というより, never `先生だというより`.
というより can't stand alone as a reason for something; that's what から is for.
っていうより is the everyday casual contraction and fits speech, not formal writing.

items.explanation_markdown:
Picture this: your friend's family runs a small noodle shop, and today you're standing behind the counter helping out because they're short-handed. A regular customer glances over, assumes you work there, and asks a question about the menu. You want to be clear you're not staff — you're just here for the afternoon, because he's your friend, and nothing more official than that. Japanese has one small word built exactly for that clarification, and once you notice it, you'll start seeing it everywhere: on job applications, in weather reports, in the fine print under a photo caption.

```jp
私[わたし]は友[とも]達[だち]として手伝[てつだ]っています。
```

*I'm helping as a friend.*

That として is doing all the work in that sentence. It's not saying who you are in general — it's saying what role you're filling right now, in this exact situation, for this exact stretch of time. Doctor, guest, teacher, a cardboard box pressed into service as a chair: として names the hat someone or something is wearing for the moment, without making any bigger claim about them beyond that.

## How it works

Structurally, として could not be simpler: it attaches directly to a noun, with nothing in between. Noun plus として means "in the capacity of [noun]," or, in more natural English, "as [noun]." There's no conjugation to learn and no politeness level to track — として itself never changes shape no matter what comes before or after it. That's the whole conjugation story for this pattern: there isn't one.

```jp
私[わたし]は医[い]者[しゃ]として病[びょう]院[いん]で働[はたら]いています。
```

*I work at the hospital as a doctor.*

Swap out the noun and the entire situation shifts with it. Put 客[きゃく] in that slot instead of 医[い]者[しゃ], and suddenly you're not the one treating people at the hospital — you're the one being served somewhere else entirely.

```jp
今日[きょう]は客[きゃく]として来[き]ました。
```

*Today I came as a guest.*

としてisn't reserved for jobs and social roles, either. Any noun can slot into it, including an ordinary object being pressed into a purpose it wasn't originally built for. This is one of the more useful everyday uses of として, and it's easy to miss if you only ever practice it with professions.

```jp
箱[はこ]を椅[い]子[す]として使[つか]いました。
```

*I used the box as a chair.*

The box never stops being a box in any real sense — として just tells you what function it's serving in that particular moment. The same logic covers people wearing more than one hat over the course of a single day: a teacher explaining something to a class of students, or a family sharing one roof.

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]として学[がく]生[せい]に説[せつ]明[めい]しました。
```

*As the teacher, I explained it to the students.*

```jp
家[か]族[ぞく]として一[いっ]緒[しょ]に住[す]んでいます。
```

*We live together as a family.*

By now you've seen として ride along with several very different nouns, and the shape never budges:

- 医[い]者[しゃ]として — as a doctor
- 客[きゃく]として — as a guest
- 先[せん]生[せい]として — as a teacher
- 家[か]族[ぞく]として — as a family

Notice that in every one of these sentences, the noun in front of として is doing double duty. It names what the person or thing is, and として immediately narrows that down to say in what capacity that fact matters for the sentence you're building. Take away として and you're left with a bare noun sitting there with no job to do — the sentence stops making sense on its own.

## Rules and exceptions

としてonly ever follows a bare noun. Not an i-adjective, not a na-adjective, not a verb, and not a whole clause sitting there on its own — a noun, full stop. If you catch yourself reaching for something like `忙しいとして`, that's a sign you need an entirely different construction; adjectives and verbs simply don't slot into this pattern the way nouns do, and there's no version of として that patches around that gap.

> Resist the urge to add の in front of として out of habit. Some of the patterns you already know want Noun plus の sitting in front of them — として never does. `友達のとして` is not natural Japanese; it's simply 友[とも]達[だち]として, noun straight into the particle with nothing between them.

Here's the part that trips people up once they've had として for a while: it doesn't claim the role is permanent. 私[わたし]は医[い]者[しゃ]として病[びょう]院[いん]で働[はたら]いています tells you that, in this context — at the hospital, doing this specific job — the person is functioning as a doctor. It says nothing about whether medicine is their whole identity, whether they'll always be one, or what they do on the weekend. は would make a claim about identity in general, the kind of thing you'd put on a business card. として only ever talks about the capacity someone occupies for the purpose of the sentence sitting in front of you, and that capacity can change completely from one sentence to the next, even within the same conversation.

## Contrast: として vs 代[か]わりに

You've already met 代[か]わりに for "instead of" — one thing or person standing in for another. It's easy to blur the two together because both follow a noun and both, in a loose sense, involve someone occupying a position that isn't automatically theirs. But they answer different questions. として tells you what role someone is genuinely filling; 代[か]わりに tells you who or what they're replacing while that person is absent.

```jp
医[い]者[しゃ]として働[はたら]きました。
```

*I worked as a doctor.*

```jp
医[い]者[しゃ]の代[か]わりに働[はたら]きました。
```

*I worked in place of the doctor.*

Read those two side by side and the gap opens right up. The first sentence describes a doctor doing a doctor's job — nothing unusual about it at all. The second describes someone who is not the doctor stepping in because the doctor couldn't be there — maybe a nurse, maybe an intern, maybe you, on a very different kind of day. Same profession named, same verb, two completely different scenes, and として versus 代[か]わりに is the only thing telling them apart.

This is worth sitting with for a second, because the mix-up runs in a predictable direction: learners reach for として when they actually mean "filling in for," since both patterns get translated into English with some flavor of "as" or "in place of." If the sentence is about substituting for someone who's absent, you want 代[か]わりに. If it's about a role someone genuinely, presently occupies, として is the word you want, and no amount of translation-matching will save you from checking which situation you're actually describing.

For now, として is your word for naming which hat you're wearing in a given sentence — friend, doctor, guest, chair. Later on, when you want to talk about something instead of functioning as it — discussing your trip rather than acting as its guide through it — that job belongs to について, which is coming up soon.
caution_notes: として only ever follows a bare noun — never an i-adjective, a na-adjective, or a verb on its own.
Don't insert の before として; unlike some patterns you've learned, として attaches straight to the noun.
として names the role someone or something occupies for this sentence, not a permanent identity, so don't treat it like は.
として and 代わりに both follow a noun but answer different questions — として names the role occupied, 代わりに names who is being replaced — so swapping them flips the meaning.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're catching up with a friend who just got back from a trip, and you've got a dozen questions lined up — the food, the flight, whether it rained the whole time. In English you'd just say "tell me about the trip." Japanese has one small, extremely useful piece of grammar that does that exact job: について, glued directly onto whatever noun you want to ask, talk, or think about.

```jp
旅[りょ]行[こう]について話[はな]しましょう。
```

*Let's talk about the trip.*

That's the whole shape of it: **noun + について** = "about / regarding [noun]." No verb changes, no conjugation to learn — you just attach it and go. English "about" is a slippery little word that can mark a topic, an approximate amount, or a direction ("walking about the park"); について only ever does the first job, which actually makes it easier to use once you stop reaching for a one-to-one English match.

## How it works

について started life as に + ついて, from a verb that means something like "to touch on" or "to be attached to" — you don't need to memorize that, but it's why the pattern feels like it's "landing on" a topic rather than describing it from a distance. All you need in practice is the shape: it bolts straight onto a noun, with nothing in between — no の, no な, nothing.

```jp
旅[りょ]行[こう] → 旅[りょ]行[こう]について
```

*trip → about the trip*

Once it's attached, the whole について phrase works like an adverbial add-on: it tells a verb like 話[はな]す (to speak), 考[かんが]える (to think), 知[し]る (to know), or 質[しつ]問[もん]する (to ask a question) what it's aimed at.

```jp
彼[かれ]はその映[えい]画[が]について何[なに]も知[し]らない。
```

*He doesn't know anything about that movie.*

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]に日本[にほん]の歴[れき]史[し]について質[しつ]問[もん]した。
```

*I asked the teacher a question about Japanese history.*

Notice that に is still doing its normal job in that second sentence, marking who got asked — について doesn't replace any particle you already know. It just adds "on the subject of X" on top of whatever the sentence is already doing. You'll also want について for asking about a topic in the first place, with a question word standing in for the noun.

```jp
何[なに]について話[はな]していますか。
```

*What are you talking about?*

That's the natural question that a について answer replies to — someone asks 何[なに]について, and you answer with 旅[りょ]行[こう]について, 映[えい]画[が]について, whatever fits.

There's also a more formal cousin: につき. It means exactly the same thing, "regarding," but it belongs to written notices, memos, and business Japanese rather than conversation.

```jp
宿[しゅく]題[だい]の問[もん]題[だい]につき、説[せつ]明[めい]します。
```

*Regarding the homework problem, I'll explain it.*

You'll meet につき on posted signs and formal documents far more often than in speech — keep について for talking to people, and recognize につき when you're reading something official.

One more shape worth knowing: について can also sit in front of の and modify a noun, turning "about X" into "the [thing] about X." Compare a plain topic sentence with a noun phrase built the same way.

```jp
旅[りょ]行[こう]についての話[はなし]は面白[おもしろ]かった。
```

*The story about the trip was interesting.*

Here について isn't attached to a verb at all — it's attached to 話[はなし] (story) through の, describing what kind of story it was. The underlying idea never changes; only the job the whole phrase is doing in the sentence does.

## Rules and exceptions

について is not a topic marker the way は is. は tells the whole sentence "here's what we're discussing from now on"; について tells one specific verb "here's what you're aimed at." Because they're doing different jobs, you can actually stack them — について + は gives you an "as for the topic of X..." feel, useful when you're pivoting to a new subject partway through a conversation.

```jp
その問[もん]題[だい]については明日[あした]考[かんが]えます。
```

*As for that problem, I'll think about it tomorrow.*

> について needs a plain noun sitting in front of it — never a verb directly. Something like `会うについて` (trying to say "about meeting") doesn't work; you'd first need to turn the verb into a noun-shaped phrase, which is further down the road. For now, keep について glued to things, not actions.

The other trap is picking a verb that can't take a "subject matter" in the first place. について pairs naturally with verbs of talking, thinking, knowing, asking, and writing — the kind of verb that can be "about" something. It doesn't pair with verbs of motion or plain existence; "about the store" doesn't combine with 行[い]く or ある the way it combines with 話[はな]す or 考[かんが]える. If the verb can't logically have a topic, について has nothing to attach its meaning to, and native speakers will just find the sentence confusing rather than politely correcting the grammar.

It's also worth being honest that について can feel a little formal or writerly even in its plain form — in very casual chatting, people sometimes just drop the topic in with は or leave it implied by context rather than reaching for について at all. That's not a rule you need to apply yourself yet; just don't be surprised if a native speaker's casual speech has fewer について phrases than a textbook dialogue does.

Learners often reach for について when they actually mean "because," and the two have nothing to do with each other. から marks a reason — the thing that caused something — while について marks a topic — the thing being discussed. "I'm worried about the exam" sounds like it should use について, but if what you mean is "because of the exam" (the exam is the cause of the worry), that's から territory, not について. Ask yourself whether the noun is the subject matter of a conversation or the reason something happened; that question sorts the two every time.

## Contrast: について vs として

You've already met として for "as / in the role of" — same shape (noun, nothing in between), completely different job underneath. として tells you what capacity someone is acting in; について tells you what topic someone is talking about. Swap one for the other and the sentence's meaning changes, not just its tone.

```jp
彼[かの]女[じょ]は先[せん]生[せい]として教[きょう]室[しつ]で話[はな]した。
```

*She spoke in the classroom as a teacher.*

```jp
彼[かの]女[じょ]は先[せん]生[せい]について教[きょう]室[しつ]で話[はな]した。
```

*She spoke in the classroom about a teacher.*

Same words, same slot in the sentence, and the only difference — として versus について — decides whether she was doing the talking in a professional capacity, or was the one being talked about. This pair trips people up for a while because both patterns look so similar on the page; the only fix is slowing down and asking "is this noun the role, or the topic?"

Worth remembering too: と、から、代[か]わりに、というより、and 場[ば]合[あい] all attach to very different structures — plain-form clauses, not bare nouns — so について doesn't compete with them the way it competes with として. として is the one pattern close enough in shape to actually cause mix-ups, which is exactly why it's worth this much attention. If you can ask yourself "is this noun playing a role, or is it what's being discussed?" before you pick a particle, the two stop colliding.

Whenever you catch yourself reaching for "about" in Japanese, check first whether you're pointing at a topic mid-sentence (について) or naming a role someone's filling (として) — they'll keep bumping into each other until that split becomes automatic. Once that split feels settled, について itself will start showing up everywhere: in questions, in answers, in the small talk that opens almost any conversation, because "what's this about" is one of the most useful questions there is.

Down the line you'll meet によると, which sounds related but marks something else entirely: not what you're discussing, but whose word you're taking it on.
caution_notes: について needs a plain noun in front of it — it can't attach directly to a verb.
につき is the formal, written-notice version of について; use について when you're speaking.
について only pairs with verbs that can take a subject matter, like 話す or 考える — not verbs of motion or existence like 行く or ある.
として and について share the same bare-noun shape but mark different things — role versus topic — so swapping one for the other changes what the sentence means.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're deciding whether to bring an umbrella tomorrow, and you haven't looked at the sky yourself — you're going by what the newspaper said this morning. That's the whole job によると does: it hangs a claim off a source, so nobody mistakes the information for your own opinion or guess.

```jp
新[しん]聞[ぶん]によると、明日[あした]は雨[あめ]です。
```
*According to the newspaper, tomorrow it will rain.*

You didn't decide it would rain. The newspaper did. によると is the little tag that keeps that distinction visible every time you repeat something you heard, read, or were told, instead of quietly presenting it as your own conclusion.

This matters more in Japanese conversation than English speakers expect. Stating something flatly, with no source attached, can sound like you're claiming personal authority over it — "it will rain tomorrow," full stop, as if you checked yourself. によると lets you soften that into "here's what I was told," which is both more honest and, often, more polite.

It also protects you. If the newspaper turns out to be wrong, "the newspaper said so" is a very different claim from "I said so." Attaching a source up front means you're never stuck defending information you never generated in the first place — you were just the messenger, and によると makes sure everyone knows it.

## How it works

によると attaches straight onto a noun — the person, place, or medium the information came from. No の, no な, nothing wedged in between; it just glues on directly, the way a label sticks to a jar.

You already know と for a natural, automatic result: if X happens, Y follows as a matter of course. によると is built from that same と. により is a slightly formal way of saying "based on / by way of," and stacking と onto it gives you "if you go by [source], then [what follows] comes out like this." Read that way, the literal shape of the phrase and its English meaning line up almost exactly — you're not memorizing an arbitrary chunk, you're recognizing a pattern you already know wearing a more formal outfit.

```jp
ラジオによると、今日[きょう]は雪[ゆき]です。
```
*According to the radio, today it's snowing.*

The source doesn't have to be a single word. Any noun phrase can sit in front of によると, as long as it still names where the information came from rather than describing what happened.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]の話[はなし]によると、テストは来[らい]週[しゅう]です。
```
*According to what my friend said, the test is next week.*

友[とも]達[だち]の話[はなし] — "my friend's talk" — is one noun phrase, so によると attaches to the whole thing exactly the same way it attaches to 新[しん]聞[ぶん] or ラジオ. Swap in 先[せん]生[せい]の話[はなし] or 医[い]者[しゃ]の話[はなし] and nothing else about the sentence changes. A bare person also works just as well as a media source: a teacher, a doctor, anyone whose word you're relaying rather than your own.

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]によると、宿[しゅく]題[だい]は明日[あした]までです。
```
*According to the teacher, the homework is due tomorrow.*

```jp
医[い]者[しゃ]によると、病[びょう]気[き]はすぐ治[なお]ります。
```
*According to the doctor, the illness will heal soon.*

Notice that what follows によると is always a plain, complete statement — 明日[あした]は雨[あめ]です, 病[びょう]気[き]はすぐ治[なお]ります. によると doesn't reach into that statement and change its tense or its politeness level; it just frames where the statement came from. You can put a past-tense claim, a present-tense claim, or a plain guess after it, and the source phrase in front never has to match that tense. 医[い]者[しゃ]によると is present tense, but the doctor could just as easily have been describing something that already happened — the tense of the source and the tense of the claim are independent of each other.

That independence is also why によると sits so comfortably at the very front of a sentence. It's setting up context — where this information is from — before you get to the actual news, the same way "according to the newspaper" leads an English sentence rather than trailing at the end.

## Rules and exceptions

によると only takes a noun. It can't hang off a full sentence the way から can — you can't say something like `雨が降るによると` and expect it to mean "according to the fact that it's raining." If the source you want to name is an event or a whole idea rather than a person, place, or piece of media, によると usually isn't the tool for the job; you'd need to turn that idea into a noun phrase first, the way 友[とも]達[だち]の話[はなし] turns "my friend talked" into something によると can attach to.

> Because によると always marks somebody else's information, `私によると` — literally "according to me" — sounds strange when it's meant as "in my opinion." The whole phrase assumes the claim is being relayed from an outside source, not generated on the spot by the speaker. For your own view, you'd reach for a completely different pattern, not によると.

によると also has a near-twin, によれば — same meaning, same attachment rule, fully interchangeable in most sentences. によれば leans a little more formal and shows up more often in writing, announcements, and news broadcasts than in casual chat, but nobody will blink if you use either one in either setting. Some learners assume the two must split some subtle difference in meaning, the way many near-synonym pairs do — here, that's mostly not the case. Pick whichever sounds smoother to your ear once you've been exposed to enough real sentences.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]によれば、彼[かれ]は元[げん]気[き]です。
```
*According to my friend, he's doing well.*

That's the same structure as every other example so far — noun, then によれば, then the plain statement being relayed — just with the more formal-sounding half of the pair. Try reading it back with によると instead; nothing about the meaning shifts, only the register does, and only slightly.

## Contrast

から states your own reason for doing something; it's your logic, your conclusion. によると states someone else's information; you're not vouching for it, just passing it along. Swap one for the other and the sentence stops meaning what you intended, because they answer different questions — "why are you doing this?" versus "where did this claim come from?"

```jp
天[てん]気[き]が悪[わる]いから、傘[かさ]を持[も]って行[い]きます。
```
*Because the weather is bad, I'm bringing an umbrella.*

天[てん]気[き]が悪[わる]いから is something you concluded yourself, probably from looking outside or checking the sky. 新[しん]聞[ぶん]によると is a fact somebody else supplied. If you tried to say 天[てん]気[き]が悪[わる]いによると, it wouldn't parse as "because the weather is bad" — によると needs a noun sitting directly in front of it, not a whole clause, and から is doing a fundamentally different job in the first place: giving a reason, not naming a source.

について marks what's being talked about; によると marks where the talk came from. The two answer different questions and can even sit in the same conversation without stepping on each other.

```jp
天[てん]気[き]について話[はな]しました。
```
*I talked about the weather.*

天[てん]気[き]について話[はな]す just names the topic — weather — and says nothing about who told you what. That's the exact gap によると fills. Imagine reporting both pieces at once: what the conversation was about, and where the claim inside it came from. について handles the first job, によると the second, and neither one can do the other's work.

Put all of that together and by the time you're a few weeks past this lesson, the choice between によると, から, and について should feel less like a grammar rule and more like a reflex: ask yourself whether you're naming a source, giving your own reason, or flagging a topic, and the right particle chain more or less picks itself.

によると is a small, specific job: crediting a source before you hand over a claim. It's not about being formal for its own sake — it's about being accurate regarding whose information you're actually repeating. Hold onto that instinct; it comes back once we reach 限[かぎ]り, another phrase built around "as far as," except that one marks the edge of what you personally know rather than where you heard it.
caution_notes: によると always attaches directly to a noun naming the source — never to a verb or full clause.
によると relays someone else's information; for your own opinion or reasoning, use a different pattern, not 私によると.
によれば is interchangeable with によると but leans a bit more formal and written.
Don't confuse によると (where the information came from) with について (what is being discussed).

items.explanation_markdown:
You're standing on the platform, bag in one hand, coffee in the other, when the overhead speaker crackles on: 台[たい]風[ふう]のため、電[でん]車[しゃ]が遅[おく]れています。 You don't need much Japanese to catch the shape of it — a typhoon, then のため, then a delay. That のため is doing all the connective work in the sentence: it states the typhoon as the reason for the delay, and it does it in the flat, matter-of-fact voice you'd expect from a station announcement, not from a friend texting you an excuse for being late. Nobody on that platform is personally responsible for the storm, and the sentence is built to make that clear — the typhoon is simply named as the fact behind what happened.

```jp
台[たい]風[ふう]のため、電[でん]車[しゃ]が遅[おく]れています。
```

*Because of the typhoon, the trains are running late.*

That's ため in its cause sense — a formal "because of" or "due to" that turns up constantly in announcements, notices, and news, anywhere someone wants to state a reason as a plain fact rather than as their own personal excuse. It sounds formal in translation, but it isn't rare or bookish in daily life: it's the wording on the handwritten sign taped to a closed shop's door, the line in a note home from your child's school, or the sentence a doctor writes on a note excusing you from work. Anywhere someone needs to state a reason without arguing for it, ため is usually close by.

## How ため works

ため actually started life as an ordinary noun, something close to "sake" or "result" — you can almost feel the old sense of "for the sake of X" sitting underneath every sentence that uses it this way. Whatever's doing the causing sits right in front of it, and whatever happened as a result follows after the comma. The part that takes getting used to is what "right in front of it" looks like, because the shape changes depending on what kind of word is doing the causing — a noun needs different handling than an adjective, and an adjective needs different handling than a verb.

**Noun + の + ため.** This is exactly the pattern you just saw with 台[たい]風[ふう]のため. It's the same の that glues two nouns into one phrase, the way 日本[にほん]の車[くるま] means "the car of Japan" — 台[たい]風[ふう] and ため get joined the same way, with 台[たい]風[ふう] filling the role that 日本[にほん] fills in that other phrase.

```jp
風邪[かぜ]のため、学[がっ]校[こう]を休[やす]みました。
```

*I took the day off school because of a cold.*

**な-adjective + な + ため.** An adjective like 静[しず]か (quiet) can't sit directly against ため any more than a noun can — it needs the same な bridge it would use in front of any noun it's describing, the way you'd say 静[しず]かな部屋[へや] for "a quiet room."

```jp
この公[こう]園[えん]は静[しず]かなため、よく散[さん]歩[ぽ]します。
```

*Because this park is quiet, I often take walks here.*

**い-adjective, plain form, no bridge needed.** い-adjectives already end in something that can attach straight onto whatever comes next, so 忙[いそが]しい (busy) just walks right up to ため with nothing in between — no な, no の, nothing.

```jp
今[こん]週[しゅう]は忙[いそが]しいため、旅[りょ]行[こう]に行[い]けません。
```

*Because this week is busy, I can't go on the trip.*

**Verb, plain form.** Same idea again: no だ, no です, just the plain form of the verb sitting directly in front of ため.

```jp
電[でん]車[しゃ]が遅[おく]れたため、会[かい]議[ぎ]に遅[おく]れました。
```

*Because the train was late, I was late for the meeting.*

Notice that the verb there is in the past tense — 遅[おく]れた, not 遅[おく]れる. That's not an accident, and it's exactly what the next section is about.

## Rules and exceptions

ため has a second life you'll bump into constantly, and it's worth naming early so it doesn't trip you up later: when it follows a verb of deliberate action in the plain non-past form, it means "in order to" instead of "because of." 勉[べん]強[きょう]するため means "in order to study" — something you're choosing to do on purpose, not a reason that's been forced on you from outside. The cause meaning you're learning here shows up instead with adjectives, nouns, and verbs describing a state, a result, or something nobody chose — which is exactly why 遅[おく]れた, already finished and nobody's fault, reads naturally as a cause, while 勉[べん]強[きょう]する, something you're actively deciding to do, reads as a purpose instead. Once you notice this split, it stops being confusing and starts being useful: the tense and the verb type are quietly telling you which meaning you're looking at before you've even reached ため itself.

> If you're ever unsure which meaning you're looking at, ask whether the person could have chosen not to do it. A typhoon, a cold, a delayed train — nobody picks those. Studying, working — those are choices, and ため after a plain dictionary-form verb like that almost always means "in order to."

There's a second trap worth naming, and it's a purely mechanical one. Unlike から, which sits happily right after だ (学[がく]生[せい]だから, 静[しず]かだから), ため never tolerates だ in front of it, no matter how natural that might feel by analogy. This one catches people who've already gotten comfortable with から, because the instinct is to reach for だ out of habit before the noun or な-adjective settles in.

> A noun takes の and an な-adjective takes な in front of ため — never だ. `病気だため` and `静かだため` are both wrong; it has to be 病[びょう]気[き]のため and 静[しず]かなため.

One last note, this time on spelling rather than meaning: ため and ために mean exactly the same thing here and attach exactly the same way to everything above. ために is just the fuller of the two forms, and either one shows up in writing without any real shift in meaning or formality — pick whichever one sounds better to your own ear in the moment.

```jp
天[てん]気[き]が悪[わる]いために、洗[せん]濯[たく]ができません。
```

*Because the weather is bad, I can't do the laundry.*

## Contrast with から

You already have から for stating a reason, and から carries your own voice in it — it's the shape of an explanation you're personally standing behind, whether that's an excuse to a friend or a reason you're offering for something you did. ため does the same basic job on paper, but drops your voice out of the sentence entirely and just states the fact instead.

```jp
病[びょう]気[き]だから、会[かい]社[しゃ]を休[やす]みます。
```

*Because I'm sick, I'm taking the day off work.*

```jp
病[びょう]気[き]のため、会[かい]社[しゃ]を休[やす]みます。
```

*Owing to illness, I will be absent from work.*

Same illness, same absence, but a different register. The first line sounds like a text you'd send a friend — casual, personal, your own reasoning in your own words. The second sounds like the line inside the email you'd actually send your boss, or the notice pinned to a break-room board: the same facts, dressed in ため's stiffer, more distant voice. Reach for から when you're explaining yourself; reach for ため when you're just reporting the situation as a fact and letting the reader draw their own conclusions.

This is also where the noun-attachment rule from the last section earns its keep: から sits after だ (病[びょう]気[き]だから), while ため replaces that だ with の (病[びょう]気[き]のため). Once that swap is automatic, telling the two patterns apart in the wild gets a lot faster — you'll catch yourself recognizing the register a sentence is written in before you've even finished reading the reason itself.

It's worth being honest that the line between the two isn't always crisp. Spoken Japanese borrows ため for effect sometimes, and formal writing occasionally leans on から when the writer wants to sound a little more direct. Treat から versus ため as a strong tendency you can lean on, not an unbreakable law — the two patterns share the same job, and real speech shuffles the boundary around more than any textbook rule likes to admit.

So ため takes whatever's sitting in front of it — noun, な-adjective, い-adjective, or plain verb — bridges the gap with の or な wherever one's needed, and hands you a stated cause with your own voice left out of it, exactly where から would feel too casual. Hold onto that sense of something sitting outside anyone's control: it comes back before long, when 限[かぎ]り starts marking just how far a fact like that holds true.
caution_notes: Nouns and な-adjectives never take だ before ため — it has to be 病気のため and 静かなため, never 病気だため or 静かだため.

When ため follows a plain non-past verb describing something someone chose to do, like 勉強するため, it usually means 'in order to' rather than 'because of' — the cause reading shows up with adjectives, nouns, and verbs describing states or already-finished events.
ため is a formal, written-feeling connector; in casual conversation about your own personal reasons, から still sounds far more natural.
