items.explanation_markdown:
You're running fifteen minutes behind and your friend is already waiting outside the station. You don't know the exact number of minutes standing between you and them — nobody ever does when they're rushing — but "soon" isn't going to cut it either, and neither is guessing wrong and looking like you don't know your own city. Japanese has a word built exactly for that kind of honest, useful guess: くらい (its twin spelling ぐらい does the same job), tacked straight onto a number to turn it into an estimate instead of a promise.

```jp
駅[えき]まで五[ご]分[ふん]くらいかかります。
```
*It takes about five minutes to get to the station.*

Five minutes, give or take — that's the whole job くらい is doing in that sentence, and once you notice it you'll hear it everywhere: prices, wait times, ages, distances, anything a speaker isn't willing to pin down to the exact digit. But the same small word turns into something much more dramatic once you point it at a whole action instead of a number. Picture a day where the work never stopped landing on your desk.

```jp
頭[あたま]が痛[いた]くなるくらい忙[いそが]しかった。
```
*I was busy enough that my head started to hurt.*

Notice what changed: くらい isn't measuring minutes here, it's measuring how busy you were by handing the listener a consequence and saying "that's the size of it — you do the math." Same trick, happier flavor this time:

```jp
泣[な]きたいくらい嬉[うれ]しかった。
```
*I was happy enough to want to cry.*

## How it works

くらい attaches directly onto a plain form — no です, no だ, no adjustment of any kind. A number, a noun, a plain-form verb, a plain-form adjective: whatever sits right before it stays exactly as it already looks in the dictionary or the sentence you'd say to a friend. That's the one mechanical rule worth memorizing, and the rest of this lesson is really just watching that single rule play out in different scenes. If you ever catch yourself reaching for です or だ right before くらい, stop — that's a habit carried over from patterns that need a full sentence in front of them, and くらい simply isn't one of those.

With a noun, くらい gives you a rough size for a thing, and that thing doesn't even have to be a number — it can be a pointing word like これ, sizing something up against an unspoken standard the listener is expected to fill in for themselves.

```jp
これくらいの雨[あめ]なら傘[かさ]は要[い]らない。
```
*If it's only about this much rain, you don't need an umbrella.*

That sentence is doing two things at once, and the second one is worth slowing down for. Besides giving a rough size, くらい is quietly downplaying the rain — "this much" is being framed as no big deal. くらい is very good at that shrinking move, which is exactly why it shows up whenever someone is asking for the bare minimum from another person, or brushing something off as too small to worry about.

```jp
少[すこ]しくらい手伝[てつだ]ってくれてもいい。
```
*You could at least help a little.*

With a verb, the plain form goes in the exact same way — nothing about the verb itself changes, くらい just sits right after it. 泣[な]きたい (want to cry) was already sitting in its plain form on its own two sentences ago, which is why it slotted in earlier without any extra step at all — the たい ending behaves like any other plain form once it's built.

One more mechanical note, and then we're done with the machinery: くらい and ぐらい are the same word wearing two spellings. Neither one is more polite and neither is more casual — it's mostly a matter of which sounds smoother coming right off the word before it, and that's especially true after numbers, where ぐらい tends to win out.

```jp
千[せん]円[えん]ぐらいで新[あたら]しい傘[かさ]が買[か]えます。
```
*You can buy a new umbrella for about a thousand yen.*

You'll see both spellings constantly in the wild, and you can pick whichever one rolls off your tongue more easily — nobody is going to read anything into the choice, the way they might if you mixed up a formal and casual verb ending.

## Rules and exceptions

くらい always needs something sitting in front of it to size up — a number, a noun, an action, a state. It can't open a sentence and it can't stand in for the comparison by itself; there has to be a "this much" already on the table before the word can say "about that much" or "to the point of that."

> くらい can read as a little dismissive when it follows something small a person did, has, or could do. 少[すこ]しくらい手伝[てつだ]ってくれてもいい lands closer to "the least you could do is help a little" than to a neutral, polite request. If that edge isn't what you're going for, either drop くらい and ask directly, or reach for ほど instead — it carries almost the same idea without the jab.

One thing くらい genuinely doesn't do: build the "not as X as Y" negative comparison. That job belongs to ほど, not to くらい, and trying to force くらい into it is one of the more common wrong guesses learners make once they notice how much overlap the two words otherwise have. Keep the two jobs separate in your head — くらい sizes something up on its own, ほど is the one you reach for when you're stacking one thing against another and saying it falls short.

## Picking between くらい, ほど, and かなり

You already know ほど for extent — Noun or plain form + ほど, "to the extent of," including that "the more X, the more Y" shape you learned earlier. くらい and ほど overlap heavily, and in a huge number of sentences you can swap one for the other and barely move the meaning at all.

```jp
泣[な]きたいほど嬉[うれ]しかった。
```
*I was happy enough to want to cry.*

Set that next to the くらい version a few paragraphs back — same event, same intensity, same translation. The difference sitting between them is register, not meaning: くらい feels like something a friend says over coffee, ほど feels like something you'd read in a novel or hear from someone choosing their words a little more carefully. When you're not sure which one fits in casual conversation, くらい is the safer default, and it will rarely sound wrong even in situations where a stricter speaker might have preferred ほど.

かなり belongs to a different family entirely, and it's worth being clear on why so the three words stop blurring together. It's a plain degree adverb — it sits in front of an adjective or a verb and just states a level, no comparison required and no consequence needed to prove it.

```jp
かなり忙[いそが]しかった。
```
*I was quite busy.*

かなり忙[いそが]しかった tells you the level and stops right there. 頭[あたま]が痛[いた]くなるくらい忙[いそが]しかった tells you the level by proving it — here's what happened because of how busy I was, now you do the math yourself. Reach for かなり when a plain degree is all the sentence needs and you're not trying to paint a scene; reach for くらい, or its more formal cousin ほど, when you want to hand the listener evidence instead of just an adjective and let them feel the size of it themselves.

くらい is going to keep showing up every time you size one thing up against another — and once you're stacking two of those comparisons side by side instead of just leaning on one, that's exactly the situation 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で is built for.
caution_notes: くらい needs a number, noun, or plain-form verb/adjective in front of it — it can't open a sentence or stand for the comparison on its own.
くらい can sound dismissive when it follows something small someone did or offered to do, so watch your tone before using it about another person's effort.
くらい and ぐらい are just two spellings of the same word, not a polite/casual pair, so either is fine after most words.
Swapping くらい for ほど rarely changes the meaning, but ほど reads more literary — in everyday chat, くらい is the safer default.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend asks how the new restaurant near the station was, and one compliment doesn't cover it — the place was cheap, and it was good. English glues those together with "not only... but also." Japanese has its own glue for exactly this: だけでなく.

```jp
このレストランは安[やす]いだけでなく、おいしいです。
```

*This restaurant isn't only cheap — it's delicious too.*

だけでなく builds on だけ (only), a word you already use to shut other options out. Flip that shutting-out inside out with でなく (でない, "is not," wearing its て-form) and だけ stops closing a door and starts opening one: not just this — this, and something else too.

## How it works

だけでなく always needs two things: the plain form of whatever comes right before it, and something after it — usually marked with も or でも — that names the second item. Drop either half and the sentence stops going anywhere.

After a verb or an い-adjective, だけでなく attaches straight onto the plain form, no extra piece needed.

```jp
日本[にほん]語[ご]は難[むずか]しいだけでなく、面[おも]白[しろ]い。
```

*Japanese isn't only difficult — it's interesting too.*

Nouns and な-adjectives need one extra piece first: な, the same connector they use right before a noun. Say the plain sentence to yourself first (先[せん]生[せい]だ, 親[しん]切[せつ]だ), then swap だ for な before だけでなく.

```jp
彼[かれ]は先[せん]生[せい]だけでなく、医[い]者[しゃ]でもあります。
```

*He isn't only a teacher — he's also a doctor.*

```jp
彼[かれ]は親[しん]切[せつ]なだけでなく、有[ゆう]名[めい]だ。
```

*He isn't only kind — he's also famous.*

> Skip the な after a noun or な-adjective and you get `先生だだけでなく` or `親切だだけでなく` — both sound like a stutter, not a sentence. だ never survives directly in front of だけでなく.

Verbs behave exactly like い-adjectives here — plain form, straight in, no な involved.

```jp
彼[かの]女[じょ]は日本[にほん]語[ご]を話[はな]すだけでなく、英[えい]語[ご]も話[はな]す。
```

*She doesn't only speak Japanese — she speaks English too.*

## Rules and exceptions

The second half of the sentence carries half the meaning, not decoration. だけでなく promises a second item is coming, and も or でも is what actually delivers it — leave that marker off and the sentence sounds like it forgot where it was going.

> This one trips people up the first week: だけでなく feels complete on its own because the first half is already a full sentence. It never is — always finish the thought.

## Casual speech

In relaxed conversation でなく often shrinks to じゃなく, the same shift you've already seen in ではない → じゃない. Nothing about the meaning changes — it just sounds like something a friend would actually say over lunch, not something read off a menu.

```jp
高[たか]いだけじゃなく、まずい。
```

*It's not only expensive — it's bad-tasting too.*

## Contrast with ほど

You already have ほど for pushing one fact to its extreme — 死[し]ぬほど忙[いそが]しい takes a single situation and turns it up as far as it will go. だけでなく isn't turning anything up; it's setting a second, separate fact down next to the first one.

```jp
今日[きょう]は忙[いそが]しいだけでなく、宿[しゅく]題[だい]も多[おお]い。
```

*Today isn't only busy — there's a lot of homework too.*

```jp
今日[きょう]は死[し]ぬほど忙[いそが]しい。
```

*Today I'm busy to the point of dying.*

Line them up and the split is clear: the ほど sentence has one fact cranked to its limit; the だけでなく sentence has two separate facts standing side by side.

Once "not only X" feels automatic, keep に限[かぎ]らず in your peripheral vision — it does something similar but reaches wider, saying a whole category isn't limited to just one example. Until then, だけでなく is the one to reach for whenever a single compliment, or complaint, doesn't cover it.
caution_notes: Attach だけでなく directly after the plain form of a verb or い-adjective, but insert な after a noun or な-adjective first — だ never survives directly in front of だけでなく.
だけでなく almost always needs も or でも in the second half to name the added item; leaving that marker off makes the sentence sound cut off.
In casual speech でなく commonly contracts to じゃなく, matching the same shift seen in ではない → じゃない, without changing the meaning.

items.explanation_markdown:
You tell 彼[かれ] that your 会[かい]社[しゃ] has a lot of 残[ざん]業[ぎょう], half expecting some solidarity about how uniquely bad this is. He just shrugs — 銀[ぎん]行[こう] apparently has exactly the same problem, and probably every 会[かい]社[しゃ]員[いん] he knows too. That move he just made — naming the one case everyone would assume is the whole story, then saying the real picture is wider than that — is exactly what に限[かぎ]らず (*not limited to*) does, packed into a single word.

```jp
残[ざん]業[ぎょう]は会[かい]社[しゃ]に限[かぎ]らず、銀[ぎん]行[こう]でも多[おお]いです。
```

*Overtime isn't limited to companies — it's common at banks too.*

に限[かぎ]らず sits right after a noun with nothing extra needed — no の, no な, nothing to conjugate first. It flags that noun as the obvious-but-incomplete case, and whatever shows up later in the sentence, usually marked by も or でも, is the part that widens the picture. You'll run into this shape constantly in writing that's trying to describe a trend rather than one person's afternoon — company notices, articles, that kind of thing.

Notice, too, that に限[かぎ]らず still contains に — the same に you already use to mark a target or a point of comparison in dozens of other sentences. That's not an accident; the whole phrase is built on "limited to [noun]," and に marks exactly the noun the limiting would apply to, if the sentence weren't busy denying it. Once you see that, the word stops feeling like a fixed chunk to memorize and starts feeling like something you could have half-guessed.

## How it works

The whole structure boils down to **Noun + に限[かぎ]らず**. You pick the narrow case first — the one thing people would guess on their own without being told anything else — attach に限[かぎ]らず directly onto it, and then say what else belongs in the same picture. There's no extra step in between; the noun and に限[かぎ]らず sit right next to each other.

```jp
動[どう]物[ぶつ]が好[す]きなのは女[おんな]の子[こ]に限[かぎ]らず、男[おとこ]の子[こ]も好[す]きです。
```

*Liking animals isn't limited to girls — boys like them too.*

Look at the second half of that sentence: 男[おとこ]の子[こ]も好[す]きです. The も there is doing the actual work of widening things — it's saying "boys, too." に限[かぎ]らず names the narrow case (女[おんな]の子[こ]); the second half names the case being added on top of it. Take the も away and the sentence stops making its point, because nothing is left to pick up what に限[かぎ]らず set up in the first place. This is the detail that trips people up the first week — に限[かぎ]らず on its own only sets the stage; something later has to walk through the door it opened.

```jp
甘[あま]い物[もの]が好[す]きなのは学[がく]生[せい]に限[かぎ]らず、先[せん]生[せい]も好[す]きです。
```

*Liking sweets isn't limited to students — teachers like them too.*

Same skeleton every single time: narrow case + に限[かぎ]らず, then a broader case marked with も, or でも when what's being added is a place rather than a person or a thing — that's what 銀[ぎん]行[こう]でも was doing back in the first example. Whichever particle shows up, its job is always identical: confirm that the picture doesn't stop at the noun you just named.

It's worth pausing on why でも shows up for 銀[ぎん]行[こう] but plain も shows up for 男[おとこ]の子[こ] and 学[がく]生[せい] and 先[せん]生[せい]. でも is で (the particle marking a place, a means, or a context) plus も — so it's reserved for spots where you'd normally mark that noun with で anyway, like a location where something happens. 男[おとこ]の子[こ] and 学[がく]生[せい] aren't places, so they just take a bare も. Once you notice that, you're not really learning a new rule here at all — you're just applying particles you already know on top of a case that's already been set up by に限[かぎ]らず.

## Rules and exceptions

に限[かぎ]らず only ever attaches to a noun. It doesn't bolt onto an adjective or a verb directly, and it isn't built for widening a single action or a one-off event — it's built for widening a category of people, places, or things. If what you actually want to say is closer to "not only did this happen, that happened too," you need a different tool; this one is strictly for "not only this group, that group as well."

The noun in front of に限[かぎ]らず also tends to name a group or a category rather than one specific individual. 女[おんな]の子[こ], 学[がく]生[せい], 会[かい]社[しゃ]員[いん], 大人[おとな], 日本[にほん] — every noun you've seen so far names a whole class of people or places, never "that one particular 先[せん]生[せい] standing by the door." That's not a hard grammatical wall so much as a habit that falls out of what the pattern is for: you reach for に限[かぎ]らず when you're making a claim broad enough to need widening in the first place.

> に限[かぎ]らず reads like something pulled from a report or a news article — it's a formal, mostly written pattern. In everyday speech, people reach for だけでなく far more often; に限[かぎ]らず tends to show up describing a trend across a whole group, not a friend complaining to you over coffee.

```jp
忙[いそが]しいのは会[かい]社[しゃ]員[いん]に限[かぎ]らず、学[がく]生[せい]も忙[いそが]しいです。
```

*Being busy isn't limited to office workers — students are busy too.*

```jp
病[びょう]気[き]になるのは大人[おとな]に限[かぎ]らず、子[こ]供[ども]もなります。
```

*Getting sick isn't limited to adults — children get sick too.*

Both of those read a little like lines from a health pamphlet, and that's the point — に限[かぎ]らず is most comfortable making a general claim about two groups, phrased almost like a small piece of trivia, rather than narrating one specific afternoon in one specific 家[いえ]. That's also why you won't see it much in casual chat: nobody opens a text message to a friend with a sentence that sounds like a public health notice.

## Contrast

You already know だけでなく for "not only X, but also Y," and に限[かぎ]らず is reaching for the exact same target. Swap one for the other and the meaning barely moves:

```jp
動[どう]物[ぶつ]が好[す]きなのは女[おんな]の子[こ]だけでなく、男[おとこ]の子[こ]も好[す]きです。
```

*It's not just girls who like animals — boys like them too.*

That sentence says almost the same thing as the に限[かぎ]らず version a few paragraphs back, but the register isn't the same at all. だけでなく sounds like something a friend would actually say to you across a table; に限[かぎ]らず sounds like a line from a report describing a pattern across an entire population. Neither one is more "correct" than the other — they're just dressed for different rooms, and picking the wrong one for the room is the kind of small mismatch that makes otherwise fluent Japanese sound slightly off.

There's an honest bit of mess here worth naming: plenty of native speakers use に限[かぎ]らず in speech too, especially anyone used to giving presentations or writing reports for work, and plenty of written Japanese leans on だけでなく when the writer wants something a little softer. The formal-versus-casual line is real, but it's a leaning, not a locked gate — treat it as your default guess, not a rule you'll never see broken.

```jp
環[かん]境[きょう]問[もん]題[だい]は日本[にほん]に限[かぎ]らず、世[せ]界[かい]の問[もん]題[だい]です。
```

*Environmental problems aren't limited to Japan — they're a global issue.*

That's the register に限[かぎ]らず is most at home in: describing something bigger than the one example everybody reaches for first. 環[かん]境[きょう]問[もん]題[だい] stops being a story about one country the moment に限[かぎ]らず shows up in front of 日本[にほん] — the sentence is already pointing you toward 世[せ]界[かい] before its second half even arrives. だけでなく could sit in that same sentence and still be grammatical, but it would read like a casual aside instead of the opening line of a serious piece of writing.

You've now seen に限[かぎ]らず do the same job seven different ways — companies, animals, sweets, busy schedules, getting sick, and finally a whole country's worth of 環[かん]境[きょう]問[もん]題[だい] — and every single time the shape was identical: name the narrow case, attach に限[かぎ]らず, then let も or でも carry in whatever else belongs. That repetition isn't an accident of this lesson; it's the actual rhythm of how the pattern gets used in real writing, sentence after sentence, report after report.

に限[かぎ]らず tells the listener that the case you just named isn't the whole story — something wider is going on beyond it. Hold onto that same formal, report-like feel: に関[かん]して leans on the exact same register once you get there.
caution_notes: に限らず attaches only to a noun — it never sits directly after an adjective or a verb.
The sentence almost always needs a も or でも later on to name what else is included; without it, the widening never lands.
に限らず belongs to a formal, mostly written register — in casual conversation, だけでなく is far more common.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your older brother works constantly — up before six, never turns down overtime, the kind of person who answers work calls on Sunday. Your younger brother works when the mood strikes him, and it shows: shorter hours, more naps, a much lighter load on his shoulders. You want to say both of those things in the same breath, not as two flat, disconnected statements sitting next to each other with a period between them. You want the sentence itself to carry the little tug between the two brothers. That's the job of 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で — on the other hand.

```jp
兄[あに]はよく働[はたら]く一[いっ]方[ぽう]で、弟[おとうと]はあまり働[はたら]かない。
```

*My older brother works a lot; my younger brother, on the other hand, doesn't work much.*

You already have でも for "but," and だけでなく for "not only... but also." Neither quite fits here. でも would split this into two separate sentences and lose the sense that you're weighing one fact against the other inside a single thought. だけでなく would suggest the two facts pile up in the same direction, which is exactly backwards — these two facts pull apart, not together. 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で sits in the middle of one sentence and points at that gap directly.

It helps to notice what 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で is literally built from. 方[ほう] — the same 方[ほう] you already know as "direction" or "way" — turns 一[いっ]方[ぽう] into something like "one side" or "one direction." で then marks that as the ground you're standing on while you say the first half. So the phrase is quietly telling you: here's one side of this, and once you're through with it, expect the other side to follow. That mental picture — one side, then the other — is worth keeping close, because it's exactly what stops the pattern from feeling like a random grammar rule.

## How it works

一[いっ]方[ぽう]で attaches straight onto the **plain form** — the casual, dictionary-style version of a word, the one you'd use talking to a friend rather than the polite です/ます one — of whatever comes right before it. For verbs and い-adjectives, nothing changes at the seam; you just tack 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で on where a period would otherwise go.

```jp
忙[いそが]しい → 忙[いそが]しい一[いっ]方[ぽう]で
```

*busy → busy, but on the other hand...*

You already saw the verb version above with 働[はたら]く. Here's the い-adjective version in a full sentence, with a room that's great in one way and inconvenient in another:

```jp
部屋[へや]は広[ひろ]い一[いっ]方[ぽう]で、駅[えき]から遠[とお]いです。
```

*The room is spacious, but on the other hand it's far from the station.*

Notice that nothing had to change about 広[ひろ]い itself — the plain form of an い-adjective already ends the way 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で needs it to, so the two just sit next to each other.

な-adjectives — the describing words that need a な glued on right before a noun, like 上手[じょうず]な人[ひと] (a skilled person) — need that same な glued on right before 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で too. Think of 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で as behaving like a noun for grammar purposes here: whatever would normally need な before a noun needs な before this.

```jp
上手[じょうず]だ → 上手[じょうず]な一[いっ]方[ぽう]で
```

*good at it → good at it, but on the other hand...*

```jp
兄[あに]は料[りょう]理[り]が上手[じょうず]な一[いっ]方[ぽう]で、妹[いもうと]は下手[へた]です。
```

*My older brother is good at cooking, but on the other hand my younger sister is bad at it.*

Nouns follow the same な-adjective logic, except the connecting piece is usually である rather than a bare だ. This is one of the few spots where 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で leans a little more formal and essay-like than most of what you've studied so far — which fits its job. You reach for 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で when you're weighing two sides of something carefully, the way a newspaper article or a written report might, not when you're just chatting about your day.

```jp
学[がく]生[せい]である一[いっ]方[ぽう]で
```

*being a student — but on the other hand...*

This is also why 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で shows up so often around opinions and comparisons: describing a plan's upside against its downside, a person's strength against their weakness, a place's convenience against its cost. Anywhere you'd naturally hold two sides of something up next to each other, 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で is doing quiet, structural work.

## Rules and exceptions

一[いっ]方[ぽう]で only works glued into a single sentence, joining what came before it to what comes after. It can't stand at the front of a fresh sentence on its own the way でも can. Picture it as a hinge fixed in the middle of one sentence rather than a door you can open onto a new one — if you find yourself wanting to start a new sentence with it, you actually want でも instead.

The plain-form rule is strict, and this trips people up early on because everything else around a sentence like this can still be polite. Something like `忙しいです一方で` isn't a form anyone writes — keep the piece right before 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で plain, and let the very end of the whole sentence carry whatever politeness level you need.

```jp
その店[みせ]は安[やす]い一[いっ]方[ぽう]で、あまりきれいじゃない。
```

*That shop is cheap, but on the other hand it's not very clean.*

Notice あまりきれいじゃない there — the plain negative of the な-adjective きれい, not a です form. That's the shape 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で expects immediately on either side of it.

For な-adjectives and nouns, skip straight to な or である; a bare だ sitting right in front of 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で, like `上手だ一方で`, reads as a mistake rather than a shortcut, even though だ is the plain form you'd use almost everywhere else.

There's also a quieter rule about meaning, not grammar: the two halves need some real tension between them for 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で to earn its keep. Swapping in two facts that don't actually pull against each other — being busy, say, and liking cats — just reads oddly, because there's no gap left for 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で to point at. The pattern needs friction to work with, the same way a pair of scales needs something on both sides before it means anything. If two clauses don't have that friction, plain て or し usually does a better, plainer job of just listing facts side by side.

> One more trap worth naming: 一[いっ]方[ぽう]だ — the same word, minus で — means something completely different. It attaches to a verb of change and says that thing just keeps happening on its own, no second clause needed, as in `忙しくなる一方だ` ("it just keeps getting busier and busier"). Same three kanji, unrelated job. If there's no second half being weighed against the first, you're looking at that other pattern, not this one.

## Contrast

You've already met だけでなく — not only... but also — for stacking two facts that agree with each other and point the same way. 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で is what you reach for the moment the two facts stop agreeing.

```jp
姉[あね]は真面目[まじめ]なだけでなく、優[やさ]しいです。
```

*My older sister isn't just serious — she's kind too.*

```jp
姉[あね]は真面目[まじめ]な一[いっ]方[ぽう]で、厳[きび]しいです。
```

*My older sister is serious, but on the other hand she's strict.*

Swap one connector for the other in that pair and the whole relationship between the two clauses flips. だけでなく tells you the second fact piles onto the first in the same direction, rounding out a positive picture. 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で tells you it pulls the other way, adding an edge to the picture instead. Same two adjectives about the same person, opposite shape of sentence — and opposite feeling by the end of it.

Both connectors share that same slightly formal, considered feel compared to something like でも, which is worth remembering as a pair: reach for だけでなく when you're building a case that stacks up, and reach for 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で the moment that case needs a "but, at the same time" running through the middle of it.

Hold onto this instinct for weighing two sides of something against each other. It's exactly what you'll need soon, when にとって lets you weigh a fact against someone's particular point of view rather than against another fact, and one side of a comparison starts depending on who's doing the looking. For now, though, the two-sided sentence itself is the whole trick — get comfortable weighing one plain-form clause against another, and the rest of this family of connectors will feel a lot less like separate rules and more like variations on the same move.
caution_notes: 一方で attaches only to the plain form — a polite です/ます form right before it, like 忙しいです一方で, is not something native speakers write.
一方で joins two clauses inside one sentence; it can't open a fresh sentence on its own the way でも does.
For na-adjectives and nouns, use な or である before 一方で — a bare だ sitting there, like 上手だ一方で, reads as a mistake.
一方だ without で is a different, unrelated pattern meaning a trend just keeps going, not a two-sided comparison.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend won't stop raving about a movie you found unbearably boring. Neither of you is lying about anything — you're just rating the same two hours from two completely different seats. English handles this with a clunky little preposition swap ("interesting to you," "boring to me"), and it's easy to miss that Japanese has a dedicated tool for exactly this job: にとって, roughly "for [someone]" or "as far as [someone] is concerned."

```jp
この映[えい]画[が]は君[きみ]にとって面[おも]白[しろ]い。
```

*This movie is interesting to you.*

```jp
でも、僕[ぼく]にとってはつまらない。
```

*But it's boring to me.*

Same movie, opposite verdicts, zero contradiction — because each sentence names whose eyes are doing the judging before it hands down a verdict. Once you can say that out loud instead of just arguing past each other, a whole category of disagreements stops sounding like fights and starts sounding like two accurate reports filed from two different desks.

This is also just useful small talk. "What's expensive for a student isn't expensive for a company employee," "what's difficult for a beginner isn't difficult for a teacher" — にとって is the connective tissue in half the opinions people actually trade in daily conversation, precisely because most opinions worth stating are opinions from somewhere.

## How it works

にとって attaches straight onto a noun — a person, a group, even something more abstract — and whatever fact or opinion follows is understood to be true specifically from that noun's side, not as some universal claim about the world. There's no conjugation to memorize here: Noun + にとって, and you're done building the frame.

```jp
私[わたし]にとって、日本[にほん]語[ご]の勉[べん]強[きょう]は大[たい]変[へん]だ。
```

*Studying Japanese is tough for me.*

Notice what that sentence is *not* saying. It isn't claiming that studying Japanese is objectively brutal for every learner on Earth — it's a report from one specific desk, 私[わたし]にとって, mine. That distinction matters more than it looks like it should, because it's the difference between an opinion and a claim you'd have to defend for everyone.

The noun in front doesn't have to be a single person, either. Families, classes, whole rooms of people work exactly the same way, no special form required:

```jp
家[か]族[ぞく]にとって、その話[はなし]は嬉[うれ]しかった。
```

*That news made the whole family happy.*

Scale that noun all the way up and it still works the same way — society, a whole country, an entire industry can all sit in front of にとって without any special handling, because the pattern was never about the size of the group. It only cares that there's a noun there, and that everything after it is being judged relative to that noun rather than to nobody in particular.

And what comes after にとって doesn't have to be about feelings at all. Plain difficulty, ease, cost, convenience — anything that's judged relative to somebody's situation fits here just as naturally:

```jp
この仕[し]事[ごと]は彼[かれ]にとって簡[かん]単[たん]だ。
```

*This job is easy for him.*

If you're curious where the shape comes from: とって is a form of 取[と]る, "to take" or "to pick something up." Picture literally picking the whole claim up and handing it over to someone — にとって is Japanese's way of saying "hand this over to that person and see how it looks from where they're standing." You don't need to unpack the etymology every time you use it; it's just a chunk you learn to reach for as one piece, but the picture is a handy one to keep in your back pocket the first few times it feels unfamiliar.

## Rules and exceptions

にとって only clips onto nouns. It can't follow a verb or a plain adjective directly, because there's simply no noun there for it to grab onto. A learner reaching for something like "for it to be difficult" and writing `難しいにとって` has skipped the noun にとって actually needs — you'd have to turn the whole idea into a noun first, and that's a different lesson for a different day.

> Don't reach for にとって when you actually mean は. にとって names whose judgment a statement belongs to; は just names what the sentence is about. 母[はは]にとって難[むずか]しい says the thing under discussion is hard *for* your mother. Swap in は instead and 母[はは]は難[むずか]しい accidentally claims your mother herself is the difficult one.

That mix-up shows up constantly in the first few weeks, because both particles are perfectly happy sitting right after a person's name. The test that actually works: are you describing the person, or are you describing something else *from* that person's side? Only the second case wants にとって. This one trips almost everyone up at least once — that's completely normal, and it stops happening once you've caught yourself doing it a couple of times.

There's a second edge worth knowing about: にとって is for judgments and evaluations, not for reporting plain actions. It answers "how does this look from someone's side," not "what does someone do." Something like `彼にとって学校に行く`, meant as a plain statement that he goes to school, doesn't work — there's no judgment being handed to anyone there, just an action, and にとって has nothing to attach its meaning to. Keep にとって for the "easy," "hard," "convenient," "wonderful" kind of statement, and leave plain actions to describe themselves.

## Casual speech

In fast, spoken Japanese, にとっては shortens the same way plenty of ては phrases do — the ては part collapses down to ちゃ, the same shift you'd see in something like 食[た]べては becoming 食[た]べちゃ.

```jp
にとっては → にとっちゃ
```

*for [someone] → for [someone] (casual, spoken)*

```jp
僕[ぼく]にとっちゃ、この宿[しゅく]題[だい]は簡[かん]単[たん]だ。
```

*This homework's easy for me.*

Keep にとっちゃ for talking, not writing. A text to a friend is fine; a written answer on an exam or a formal message is not — the shortened form reads as sloppy the second it's on paper instead of in someone's mouth.

You'll hear にとっちゃ most from people complaining, joking, or just talking fast among friends — it has that slightly clipped, dropped-shoulders energy casual contractions tend to carry in general. Recognizing it matters more than producing it at first; plenty of learners understand にとっちゃ in a conversation long before they'd reach for it themselves, and that's a perfectly fine order to learn it in.

## Contrast

にとって pairs especially naturally with だけでなく and 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で, because opinions that split by person are exactly the kind of material those two patterns were built to hold together.

```jp
この問[もん]題[だい]は学[がく]生[せい]だけでなく、先[せん]生[せい]にとっても難[むずか]しい。
```

*This problem is hard not only for the students, but for the teacher too.*

だけでなく is doing the "not only... but also" stacking here; にとって is telling you who sits on each end of that stack. Put the two together and you get one clean sentence instead of two separate complaints filed back to back.

```jp
私[わたし]にとって旅[りょ]行[こう]は楽[たの]しい一[いっ]方[ぽう]で、彼[かれ]にとっては大[たい]変[へん]だ。
```

*Travel is fun for me, while for him it's exhausting.*

一[いっ]方[ぽう]で was already built for holding two contrasting facts side by side without picking a winner. にとって is what tells you those two facts belong to two different people rather than being one confused claim about the same trip. Together they say "same trip, opposite experience" without wasting a single word proving it.

Neither pairing is required, of course — plenty of にとって sentences stand on their own just fine, one noun, one judgment, done. But once you notice how often real opinions come with an unspoken "...but not for everyone," reaching for だけでなく or 一[いっ]方[ぽう]で to say that other half out loud starts to feel less like decoration and more like finishing the thought you were already having.

## Closing thought

Whenever an opinion only makes sense once you know who's holding it, にとって is the word that says so out loud instead of leaving it implied. Later on you'll meet に関[かん]して for handing over a topic more formally rather than giving a personal read on it — a cousin worth remembering once pinning opinions to people starts feeling automatic.
caution_notes: にとって attaches only to a noun, never directly to a verb or plain adjective, so an idea like 'for it to be difficult' needs to become a noun before にとって can attach to it.
にとって and は are not interchangeable: にとって says whose judgment a statement belongs to, while は only marks the topic, so swapping one for the other changes who or what the sentence is actually about.
にとって is for judgments and evaluations relative to someone, not for reporting a plain action that person takes.
にとっては casually contracts to にとっちゃ in speech; keep the full form in writing and formal speech.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're in a 会[かい]議[ぎ] at your 会[かい]社[しゃ], and the 部[ぶ]長[ちょう] wants to hear about the economy — not chat around it, but explain it directly. That's the job に関[かん]して does: it points straight at a topic and says, this is what we're talking about now.

## How it works

に関[かん]して attaches straight onto a noun — no な, no の, nothing in between. It means "regarding" or "concerning," and it's the pattern you reach for when you're about to zero in on one topic and talk about it directly.

```jp
経[けい]済[ざい]に関[かん]して、説[せつ]明[めい]します。
```

*I'll explain regarding the economy.*

Notice the noun (経[けい]済[ざい]) comes first, に関[かん]して follows it immediately, and then the rest of the sentence does its normal work — です/ます endings, whatever verb you need.

There's a second shape worth knowing: に関[かん]する. Swap in に関[かん]する when you want to describe a following noun instead of finishing a whole sentence with it. に関[かん]する sits between two nouns like an adjective — "problems regarding X," "a book regarding X."

```jp
経[けい]済[ざい]に関[かん]する問[もん]題[だい]があります。
```

*There are problems regarding the economy.*

Same two ingredients — a noun plus に関[かん]して or に関[かん]する — just pointed at a sentence versus pointed at another noun.

## Rules and exceptions

に関[かん]して is formal. Business meetings, presentations, written reports, essays — that's its natural habitat, exactly the kind of situation your 部[ぶ]長[ちょう] just put you in.

```jp
会[かい]議[ぎ]で、部[ぶ]長[ちょう]は文[ぶん]化[か]に関[かん]して質[しつ]問[もん]した。
```

*At the meeting, the department head asked a question about culture.*

> に関[かん]して needs an actual topic to hold onto — a noun you can point at and say "this one." It doesn't work for physical nearness (a chair next to a door) or for marking who benefits from something. Those jobs belong to other words entirely.

に関[かん]して can also take は right after it — 経[けい]済[ざい]に関[かん]しては — when you want to single that topic out against some other one, something like "as for the economy, though...". You'll see this a lot once you start reading anything formal.

```jp
環[かん]境[きょう]に関[かん]して、色[いろ]々[いろ]な意[い]見[けん]があります。
```

*There are various opinions regarding the environment.*

## Casual speech

Here's the honest part: nobody says に関[かん]して to a friend over coffee. It's a formality tell — the moment you use it in casual talk, you sound like you're giving a press conference. In actual daily conversation, people just drop it and let the topic sit on its own, often marked with は or も.

```jp
環[かん]境[きょう]も大[たい]変[へん]だ。
```

*The environment's rough too.*

Same idea, "regarding the environment," just stripped down to almost nothing. You'll meet another casual way of pointing at a topic soon, when って shows up — hold onto that thought.

## Contrast

に関[かん]して and にとって look like cousins — both noun + に + something — and that similarity trips people up. But they do different jobs. に関[かん]して says *this is what I'm talking about*. にとって says *this is whose eyes I'm looking through*, a perspective, not a topic.

```jp
私[わたし]にとって経[けい]済[ざい]は難[むずか]しいです。
```

*For me, the economy is difficult.*

```jp
経[けい]済[ざい]に関[かん]して、専[せん]門[もん]家[か]に聞[き]きます。
```

*Regarding the economy, I'll ask a specialist.*

Swap them and the sentence breaks: `私に関して経済は難しいです` reads as something closer to "regarding me, the economy is difficult" — not what you meant at all. If you can rephrase your sentence as "from X's perspective," reach for にとって. If you can rephrase it as "on the subject of X," reach for に関[かん]して.

に関[かん]して gives you a clean, professional way to point straight at a topic — the meeting-room version of "so, about the economy." Keep an ear out for って later; it does something related in a much more casual register.
caution_notes: に関して is formal and reads as stiff or press-conference-like in casual conversation, where people usually just drop it.
に関して needs a real topic noun; it can't be used for physical nearness or for marking who something is done for.
Don't confuse に関して (the topic being discussed) with にとって (whose perspective) — swapping them changes the meaning of the sentence.
Use に関する, not に関して, when the phrase describes a following noun rather than ending a clause.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend is describing someone from work, and by the end of it you're just shaking your head: "そういう話[はなし]は聞[き]きたくない。" You didn't ask for every detail, and you don't need it — the moment you heard the shape of the story, you already knew you didn't want to hear the rest. そういう does exactly that job for you: it points at a whole category of thing — talk, people, weather, food, whatever — without naming a single specific example.

```jp
そういう話[はなし]は聞[き]きたくない。
```

*I don't want to hear that kind of talk.*

そういう means roughly "that kind of," and it comes with two close cousins that split the same job by distance. こういう means "this kind of" — something right in front of you, or something you're about to describe yourself. ああいう means "that kind of" too, but for something far from both you and the person you're talking to, the same distant feeling あれ carries when you point at something across the room instead of something in your hand. So this isn't three unrelated words to memorize; it's one job (naming a category instead of a specific thing) done at three distances, the same way これ・それ・あれ split "this/that/that over there."

Why bother with a category word at all, instead of just describing the thing directly? Because most of the time you don't actually want to relitigate the details. Your friend's story wasn't really about one coworker — it was about a whole familiar type of story, the kind you've heard a dozen times with different names swapped in. そういう lets you skip straight to that judgment without pretending you need to hear it again.

## How it works

All three attach directly in front of a noun — no gap, no particle, nothing between them and the word they're modifying. Whatever sits right after the blank is the thing being sorted into a category, and そういう itself tells you nothing on its own; it's entirely about what follows it.

```jp
こういう天[てん]気[き]は苦[にが]手[て]だ。
```

*I'm no good with this kind of weather.*

```jp
ああいう人[ひと]には会[あ]いたくない。
```

*I don't want to meet that kind of person.*

Notice the shape of the word itself, because it explains a lot of what comes next: そういう ends in う, not い. That matters more than it looks like it should. Words that end in い — 高[たか]い, 面[おも]白[しろ]い — are i-adjectives, adjectives that inflect on their own the way an English verb does, and plenty of them can end a sentence all by themselves (this is delicious → おいしい。). そういう never does that. It has exactly one form, forever, and that one form exists only to sit in front of a noun.

```jp
彼[かれ]はそういう人[ひと]だ。
```

*He's that kind of person.*

Look closely at what's actually being described in that sentence: it isn't そういう, it's 彼[かれ], described through 人[ひと]. そういう just supplies the category — it tells you what kind of 人[ひと] you're dealing with, then gets out of the way. Try to drop the noun and let そういう carry the sentence by itself, and it stops meaning anything at all.

> `そういうだ` isn't a sentence on its own. そういう has no meaning without a noun sitting directly after it — you need something like そういう人[ひと]だ or そういうものだ, never そういう standing alone.

## Rules and exceptions

The noun after そういう・こういう・ああいう doesn't have to be a concrete word like 話[はなし] or 人[ひと]. Very often it's a placeholder noun instead — こと (a matter, an abstract thing that happened or was said) or もの (a thing, used more for the nature or essence of something). You reach for these when you're categorizing an idea rather than an object you could point at.

```jp
あの人[ひと]はそういうことを言[い]う人[ひと]ではない。
```

*He's not the kind of person who says that sort of thing.*

Here そういうこと isn't naming a specific sentence someone said — it's naming the *category* of thing that gets said, the same way "that kind of talk" works in English without quoting anyone directly. This is one of the most common jobs そういう does in real conversation: summing up an entire remark, complaint, or situation as "that sort of thing" instead of repeating it.

You'll also run into そういうの constantly in casual speech — の here is the nominalizer, a little word that turns a whole description into a thing you can talk about, so そういうの means something like "that kind of thing/one" used loosely for anything from an object to a whole situation. It's shorter and more casual than そういうもの, and you'll hear it far more often in conversation than in writing.

One more sharp edge, and it's an easy one to trip on because it looks so close: こんな, そんな, and あんな — words you already know as "this/that kind of" — cover similar ground, but they don't behave the same way grammatically. They're shaped like na-adjectives, so they can end a sentence on their own (そんなだ works as a loose comment, "it's just like that") and they can modify a verb directly (そんなに食[た]べないで, "don't eat that much"). そういう can't do either of those things — it only ever sits directly in front of a noun. When you're not sure which to reach for and a noun follows right away, そういう is the safer, more neutral-sounding choice; こんな/そんな/あんな tend to carry more of the speaker's feeling about the thing.

This trips learners twice, usually in opposite directions. Some people, once they learn そんな, try to stretch it in front of every noun the way they'd use そういう — that mostly works, but it quietly adds an emotional color (surprise, complaint, admiration) that plain そういう doesn't carry. Others learn そういう first and then try to use it to end a sentence the way そんなだ does, which simply doesn't work; there's no version of そういう that stands alone. Keep the two families separate in your head by function rather than by translation: そういう describes and categorizes, そんな reacts.

## Contrast

You already have に関[かん]して for bringing up a topic — その書[しょ]類[るい]に関[かん]して, "regarding that document." On the surface it looks like it's doing something similar to そういう, since both can follow a demonstrative and both can precede or set up a noun phrase. They aren't interchangeable, though, and the difference matters.

```jp
そういう書[しょ]類[るい] → その書[しょ]類[るい]に関[かん]して
```

*that kind of document → regarding that document*

そういう labels the noun as belonging to a category — a type of document, not one specific piece of paper. に関[かん]して doesn't sort anything into a category at all; it just marks a topic, "on the subject of this." Swap one for the other and the sentence stops meaning what you wanted. そういう書[しょ]類[るい]にはよく問[もん]題[だい]がある is a general comment about documents of that type — this kind of paperwork tends to have problems. その書[しょ]類[るい]に関[かん]して質[しつ]問[もん]がある is about one particular document already sitting in front of you — you have a question about this exact piece of paper, not about its category.

```jp
こういう話[はなし]は前[まえ]からあった。
```

*This kind of story has been around for a while.*

That last one is a small, useful habit: こういう話[はなし]は前[まえ]からあった doesn't claim anything about one specific story you just heard — it's a comment on the whole category, the observation that stories shaped like this one keep coming up. That's the real payoff of そういう・こういう・ああいう: they let you talk about a pattern you've noticed without having to pin down or repeat a single example of it.

That's the whole shape of it: そういう・こういう・ああいう sort things into a category by distance, they never stand alone, and they only ever point forward at a noun. Hold onto that habit of pointing at something without naming it — it's exactly the instinct って will ask of you soon, when you start quoting other people's words the same loose way.
caution_notes: そういう, こういう, and ああいう never stand alone at the end of a sentence — they always need a noun (or こと / もの) directly after them.
Don't confuse そういう with こんな / そんな / あんな — those can end a sentence or modify a verb, but そういう can only sit in front of a noun.
に関して marks the topic being discussed, not a category — swapping it for そういう changes what the sentence is actually about.
ああいう points at something distant from both speaker and listener, the same distance あれ covers — don't reach for it when こういう or そういう fits better.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend is scrolling through a work chat, phone tilted so you can see, and taps a message before saying:

```jp
これって難[むずか]しい？
```

*Is this thing hard?*

She's not asking you to define "hard" in the abstract — she's holding up the exact thing on the screen and asking about it, right now, in the middle of a conversation that's already happening. That's the job って does. It's a single syllable that lets you grab whatever's sitting between you two — a thing, a rumor, something someone just said — and comment on it without breaking your stride. You'll hear it constantly once you start listening for it, in two related but distinct jobs.

## How it works

The first job, and the one most textbooks introduce first, is reporting what someone said or thinks, casually. In neutral or formal Japanese, you'd use と before 言[い]う (to say) or 思[おも]う (to think) — 忙[いそが]しいと言[い]う, "to say [someone]'s busy." In casual speech, って steps into that exact と slot:

```jp
兄[あに]が忙[いそが]しいって言[い]ってた。
```

*My older brother said he's busy.*

言[い]う hasn't gone anywhere — it's still doing the reporting, shrunk down to 言[い]ってた (was saying). All that changed is what comes before it. と sounds like you're citing something; って sounds like you're just passing it along mid-conversation, the way you'd mention something a friend told you an hour ago. Line the two up and the swap is obvious:

```jp
学[がっ]校[こう]を休[やす]むと言[い]った → 学[がっ]校[こう]を休[やす]むって言[い]った。
```

*He said he'd skip school. → same thing, said the way you'd actually say it to a friend.*

Once you've got that swap down, you can drop 言[い]った entirely and let って carry the whole "I heard / they said" feeling on its own — 忙[いそが]しいって with nothing after it still reads as "they said he's busy," because in conversation the missing 言[い]ってた is obvious from context. That compression is most of what makes casual reported speech sound casual: not extra words, but fewer of them.

The second job doesn't report anything at all. って can also pick up whatever's already on the table — something you or the other person just mentioned — and mark it as what you're now talking about, the way は usually would. Swap は for って and the sentence stops sounding like a statement out of nowhere and starts sounding like a reaction to something:

```jp
それって面[おも]白[しろ]い？
```

*Is that thing interesting?*

Nobody said anything in that sentence, and nobody's being quoted. それって just means "that thing you brought up" — って is doing は's job, only with the specific flavor of "you mentioned this, and now I'm asking about it." Both uses attach the exact same way, to the exact same plain forms; only the sentence around them tells you which job って is doing.

## Rules and exceptions

って is casual through and through. There's no formal register it belongs in — talking to a teacher, a doctor, or your boss, you'd reach for と言[い]う or と思[おも]う (or their polite equivalents) instead. Dropping って into a sentence you're saying to someone you'd normally speak politely to will land as oddly familiar, the way slipping into slang mid-presentation would in English.

> Quoting and topic-picking can look identical on paper. 忙[いそが]しいって on its own could mean "they said [someone]'s busy" (with 言[い]ってた simply omitted) or "about being busy, though —" depending on what was said right before it. There's no grammatical flag that tells you which; you're relying on context the same way a native speaker does.

For verbs and い-adjectives, って attaches straight onto the plain form with nothing in between — 忙[いそが]しいって, 休[やす]むって. Nouns and な-adjectives are a little different: when you're specifically reporting speech, they often pick up an extra だ right before って (便[べん]利[り]だって, "they say it's convenient"), matching the だ that would sit in front of と言[い]う in the neutral version (便[べん]利[り]だと言[い]う). The topic-picking job, on the other hand, never adds that だ — it just goes straight onto the noun or な-adjective, because there's nothing being quoted to begin with.

## Casual speech

って already is the casual form of と — that's the whole reason it exists — but it keeps contracting further the more casual the conversation gets. 忙[いそが]しいって言[い]ってた can shrink to just 忙[いそが]しいって, with 言[い]ってた left implied; that shorter version shows up constantly in texting, where every extra word costs you a beat.

```jp
これは面[おも]白[しろ]いです。
これって面[おも]白[しろ]いよね。
```

*This is interesting. / This is interesting, right?*

The first line is what you'd write on a form or say to someone you've just met. The second is what you'd actually say to a friend sitting next to you, looking at the same screen — casual, a little softer, inviting agreement rather than just stating a fact.

## Contrast

にとって, which you've already met, also lets you frame a sentence around a particular person, but it's doing close to the opposite of って's topic-picking job. にとって nails down whose perspective a sentence belongs to — "for me," "for him" — while って's topic-marking use doesn't specify anyone's viewpoint at all; it just grabs a topic and leaves the question open for whoever's listening.

```jp
これは私[わたし]にとって難[むずか]しい。
あれって難[むずか]しい？
```

*This is difficult for me. / Is that thing over there hard?*

The first sentence tells you exactly whose difficulty this is — mine, specifically, maybe not yours. The second doesn't claim anyone's viewpoint at all; it's just two people looking at the same thing, one of them asking the other what they think.

って comes back soon in ったら and ってば, once it stops quietly picking up topics and starts calling someone out by name — hold onto the shape of it, because you'll recognize it immediately.
caution_notes: って is purely casual — swap back to と言う / と思う, or their polite forms, with teachers, bosses, or anyone you'd normally speak politely to.
The same って sentence can be reporting someone's words or casually picking up a topic — only the conversation around it tells you which, so don't expect a grammatical flag to disambiguate.
Nouns and な-adjectives often take an extra だ before って when reporting speech (便利だって), but that だ never appears when って is just picking up a topic.

items.explanation_markdown:
Picture this: you've called your brother's name three times from across the room, and he hasn't so much as glanced up from whatever he's doing. You're not asking him a question anymore, and you're not stating a neutral fact about him either. You're doing something that sits in between — flagging him down, mixing his name with a little "seriously, come on" energy — and that specific move is exactly what ったら and ってば exist for.

They attach to a noun (almost always a person, often just their name) or to something you've already said once, and they add one thing on top of it: a flash of exasperation. Not anger exactly — more like the feeling of repeating yourself to someone who really should already know better by now.

```jp
兄[あに]ったら、話[はなし]を聞[き]いてない。
```
*My brother, seriously, isn't listening to what I'm saying.*

Nothing else changed in that sentence. 兄[あに] (older brother) is still just 兄[あに], 話[はなし] is still just 話[はなし]. The only new piece is ったら sitting right after the person's name, and it's doing all the emotional work by itself.

## How it works

The simplest use: attach ったら or ってば straight onto a noun that names a person, and you get something like "hey, [person], honestly" — an exasperated call-out, not a question and not a neutral report.

```jp
彼[かれ]ったら、いつも宿[しゅく]題[だい]を忘[わす]れる。
```
*Him, honestly, he always forgets his homework.*

No particle sits between 彼[かれ] and ったら. That's the whole shape: noun, then the pattern, then whatever complaint follows. You could swap in 友[とも]達[だち], 兄[あに], 先[せん]生[せい], or any person's name and the structure wouldn't move at all.

ったら and ってば are close enough in this job that you'll hear the same speaker reach for either one in the same breath, but they lean in slightly different directions. ったら tends to open a complaint, pulling attention onto a person and what they're doing (or not doing). ってば tends to close one, landing after you've already said the actual content once and you're restating it because the first attempt didn't land.

```jp
分[わ]かったってば。
```
*I said I get it.*

分[わ]かった is just the plain past of 分[わ]かる — "I understood," "I got it" — nothing new added to the words themselves. ってば tacked on the end tells the listener this isn't the first time you've said it, and you're a little tired of saying it again.

That's the second job of the pattern, and it's worth keeping separate from the first: instead of attaching to a bare noun, ってば (almost never ったら here) attaches to the end of a whole plain-form sentence — something you're re-delivering, not introducing for the first time. No です, no ます, no politeness layer of any kind; the entire point of adding ってば to something is to drop the formality and let a bit of impatience show through.

Because the noun-attachment job and the whole-sentence job look so different on the page, it helps to ask yourself one question when you see ったら or ってば: is this sitting right after a bare person, or right after a full plain-form claim? The answer tells you which of the two jobs you're looking at.

Both jobs share the same underlying feeling, even though the grammar looks different. Whether you're calling out a person's name or repeating your own sentence, you're pointing at a gap between what should have happened and what actually happened — someone should be listening and isn't, or someone should have heard you the first time and apparently didn't. Once you notice that gap, the two uses stop feeling like two separate rules and start feeling like one instinct with two attachment points.

## Rules and exceptions

> This ったら is not the conditional ったら you may run into elsewhere, the one that means "if" or "when" and attaches after a verb to set up a condition. Same sound, a completely different job — here it never builds a condition. It sits on a bare noun for address, or on something already said, and adds attitude, nothing more.

Because the whole pattern is built to shed formality, it has no polite form. Bolting です or ます onto a sentence and then adding ってば would read as contradictory — you'd be dressing the sentence up formally and venting about it in the same breath, and native speakers just don't do that.

```jp
要[い]らないってば。
```
*I said I don't need it.*

要[い]らない is already the plain, blunt form of "don't need it." That bluntness is part of the point: ったら・ってば live entirely in the register where you'd also hear だ instead of です, and plain verb forms instead of ます forms.

The exasperation also needs something real behind it — a person who isn't listening, a fact you've already stated once. Say ってば after a sentence nobody has heard yet, and it just sounds strange, because there's nothing to actually be tired of repeating.

```jp
猫[ねこ]がまた花[はな]を壊[こわ]したってば。
```
*I said the cat broke the flower again.*

That また (again) is doing quiet extra work here — it signals this is not the cat's first offense, which is exactly the kind of backstory that makes ってば land naturally instead of sounding random or out of nowhere.

One more sharp edge: this pattern almost never opens a conversation cold. You reach for ったら・ってば in the middle of an exchange, after some listening or ignoring has already happened. A first sentence to a stranger would never carry either one — there's no shared history yet for the exasperation to attach to.

This is also, honestly, a spoken pattern first and a written one second. You will hear it constantly in casual conversation and in dialogue written to sound like real speech, but it rarely shows up in anything formal — a report, a notice, an email to someone you don't know well. If you're ever unsure whether a piece of writing is casual enough for ったら・ってば, a good rule of thumb is to check whether だ or です is doing the work elsewhere in the same paragraph; だ means you're in the right register, です means you're not.

## Contrast

You've already met って for casually reporting or quoting something — 兄[あに]が来[く]るって, "I heard my brother's coming," said flat, with no feeling attached one way or the other.

```jp
兄[あに]が来[く]るって。
```
*I heard my brother's coming.*

ったら・ってば take that same casual register and add friction. Swap って for ってば on a sentence about a person's habit, and you stop reporting information and start venting about it.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]ってば、また遅[ち]刻[こく]した。
```
*My friend, honestly, was late again.*

Same friend, same fact — late again — but ってば turns a report into a complaint. That's the whole difference between the two patterns: って carries information without judging it; ったら・ってば carry the same kind of information while making it obvious you have feelings about it.

It's worth sitting with how small the actual change is — one word swapped, everything else identical — because that's usually how the sharpest grammar distinctions in Japanese work. The words themselves barely move; the attitude sitting underneath them does all the shifting.

It also helps to notice what って and ったら・ってば have in common, since that's what makes the swap so easy to make by accident. Both drop straight onto plain-form content with no extra particle, both belong to the same casual register, and both are things you'd say to someone you already know well. The only thing that changes is whether you're neutrally passing something along or letting the listener know it's bothering you.

A little bit of frustration is healthy vocabulary to be able to reach for. Hold onto it, because とか is coming up soon for something much calmer — casually listing things side by side, no edge involved at all.
caution_notes: ったら・ってば only appear in casual speech and never combine with です or ます — the whole pattern exists to drop formality, not keep it.
This ったら is unrelated to the conditional ったら (if/when) — don't reach for it when you mean "when I get home, I'll call."
The pattern needs something real behind it — a person not listening, a claim already made once — or it just sounds like noise rather than a genuine complaint.

items.explanation_markdown:
You've been texting a friend about a weekend trip, and they still haven't given you a straight yes or no. You aren't asking them the question again — you already asked it once — you just need one sentence you can say to someone else about the situation: "I don't know if they're coming." Asking outright a second time would be pushy, and just reporting "they didn't answer" loses the actual content of what's bothering you: whether they'll show up. That's the exact shape かどうか is built for: packing a whole yes-or-no question inside a bigger sentence, so it can sit there as information instead of as a question you're firing at someone.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]が来[く]るかどうか分[わ]からない。
```

*I don't know whether my friend is coming or not.*

Break it down. 来[く]る sits in plain form — the dictionary form, the one a verb is listed under — and かどうか glues straight onto the end of it. か is the same question particle you already use to turn a statement into a question; どうか adds a sense of "either way, one way or the other." Together they build a self-contained embedded question — not something you're asking out loud, but a whole yes-or-no question sitting inside the sentence, doing the job a noun would do. 分[わ]からない is just sitting downstream of it, reacting to that packaged question the way it would react to any ordinary noun: you don't know it.

## How it works

Any plain-form verb takes かどうか directly, present or past, with nothing extra glued in between. You'll usually find it sitting right in front of a small family of verbs about knowledge and checking — 分[わ]かる (to understand or know), 知[し]る (to know), 教[おし]える (to tell someone), 聞[き]く (to ask or listen). Think of かどうか as the question itself, packaged up, and those verbs as what you're doing with it: you know it, you don't know it, you're asking someone else to answer it, or you're telling somebody the result.

This is different from just tacking か onto the end of a sentence to ask a question outright. か on its own, standing alone at the end, is a real spoken question aimed at whoever's listening — it wants an answer right now. かどうか never asks anybody anything directly; it just names the question as a topic, the same way a noun names a thing, so the rest of the sentence can talk about it. That's the whole trick behind calling this "embedded" — the question gets folded into a bigger sentence instead of standing on its own.

```jp
明日[あした]雨[あめ]が降[ふ]るかどうか分[わ]からない。
```

*I don't know whether it will rain tomorrow or not.*

い-adjectives behave the same way — plain form straight onto かどうか, nothing to remember beyond that. い-adjectives never had a だ to begin with, so there's nothing to trip over here; the habit of just tacking かどうか onto whatever plain form you already have works cleanly.

```jp
彼[かれ]が忙[いそが]しいかどうか教[おし]えてください。
```

*Please tell me whether he is busy or not.*

Nouns and な-adjectives are where people trip. Their plain form technically ends in だ — 学[がく]生[せい]だ, 元[げん]気[き]だ — but that だ disappears the moment かどうか shows up. You say 元[げん]気[き]かどうか, never `元気だかどうか`. かどうか already carries its own weight; it doesn't need だ standing in front of it to sound complete. It helps to remember that だ's whole job is to close a sentence off, to say "and that's a fact." かどうか is doing the opposite — holding the sentence open, refusing to close it off one way or the other — so a word whose entire purpose is closure just doesn't belong there anymore.

```jp
彼[かれ]が元[げん]気[き]かどうか知[し]りたい。
```

*I want to know whether he is doing well or not.*

```jp
彼[かれ]が学[がく]生[せい]かどうか分[わ]からない。
```

*I don't know whether he is a student or not.*

かどうか is just as comfortable sitting on a past-tense plain form, for when the thing you're uncertain about has already happened, or already been decided, and you simply haven't heard the result yet. The uncertainty isn't about whether the event happened — it did, one way or the other — it's about which way it went, and that you haven't been told.

```jp
試[し]験[けん]に合[ごう]格[かく]したかどうか、まだ分[わ]からない。
```

*I still don't know whether I passed the exam or not.*

Timing matters here in a way that's easy to gloss over. 合[ごう]格[かく]するかどうか would put the exam result itself still up in the air — you haven't taken it yet, or the results simply aren't decided. 合[ごう]格[かく]したかどうか, past tense, means the result already exists somewhere; you're only missing the news of it. Same pattern, same かどうか, but the tense on the verb in front of it tells the listener exactly where the uncertainty actually lives.

## Rules and exceptions

かどうか only handles yes-or-no uncertainty — situations where the honest answer is "yes" or "no," even if you don't currently know which. The moment a question word like 誰[だれ] or 何[なに] enters the sentence, かどうか breaks, because that word is already doing the work of asking a question on its own; どうか has nothing left to add. Drop the どうか and keep plain か.

> `誰が来るかどうか` doesn't work — 誰[だれ] already turns the sentence into a question by itself.

```jp
誰[だれ]が来[く]るか分[わ]からない。
```

*I don't know who is coming.*

The same logic covers いつ, どこ, どの, and every other question word on your list — none of them ever combine with どうか. It's worth sitting with why: どうか is really asking "one way, or the other way?" That only makes sense when there are exactly two ways to land, yes or no. 誰[だれ] opens up a whole crowd of possible answers, not two, so どうか simply has nothing to attach its "either way" to.

かどうか is also neutral about politeness on its own — it doesn't make a sentence more or less formal by itself. Whatever comes after it carries the register: 分[わ]からない is plain and casual, 分[わ]かりません would be the polite version of the exact same sentence, and かどうか sits unchanged in front of either one.

## Contrast: かどうか vs って

You've met って as a casual way to quote or bring up something someone said. It's tempting to blur it with かどうか, since both sit right after a plain-form verb, but they're doing opposite jobs. って hands over someone else's words as settled fact — as far as the report goes, that's that. かどうか is the opposite: it flags that nothing is settled yet, that you genuinely don't know which way things will go.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]は来[く]るって言[い]っていた。
```

*My friend said they were coming.*

```jp
でも、友[とも]達[だち]が本[ほん]当[とう]に来[く]るかどうか分[わ]からない。
```

*But I still don't know whether my friend is really coming or not.*

Notice what changed between those two lines: nothing said out loud contradicts what your friend told you. かどうか isn't calling them a liar — it's just honest about the gap between what was said and what you actually know. This is the kind of mess that's genuinely part of speaking Japanese honestly: people report things with って constantly, and かどうか is exactly the tool for admitting, right afterward, that a report isn't the same thing as a fact you've confirmed yourself. Native speakers lean on both in the same breath all the time, precisely because plans fall through and words don't always match what happens.

Whenever a sentence needs to hold an unanswered yes-or-no question inside it — the thing you don't know, the thing you're asking about, the thing you're checking on — plain form plus かどうか is the tool. Hold onto that lone か sitting at the front of it; you'll run into it again, doing a much smaller job, inside か何[なに]か.
caution_notes: Never add だ before かどうか after a noun or な-adjective — it's 元気かどうか, not 元気だかどうか.
かどうか only works for yes-or-no uncertainty; a question word like 誰 or 何 pairs with plain か instead, never with かどうか.
Match the tense to what you actually mean — 合格したかどうか asks about an outcome that already happened, while 合格するかどうか asks about something still undecided.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're texting a friend on a slow Saturday afternoon: 映[えい]画[が]か何[なに]か見[み]ない？ — want to watch a movie or something? You don't actually have a title in mind, and you're not going to research one before you hit send. Maybe nothing good is showing, maybe you just want an excuse to hang out and a movie is the easiest thing to name first. か何[なに]か lets you throw out one example — 映[えい]画[が], a movie — while openly admitting you don't care whether it ends up being that exact thing. Say it plainly, without か何[なに]か, and you've made a specific plan you now have to follow through on. Add か何[なに]か, and you've made an offer that's easy for both of you to bend.

## How it works

か何[なに]か attaches straight onto a noun: **Noun + か何[なに]か**. Nothing conjugates and nothing changes shape — you're not adding a verb ending or picking a form, you're just dropping two small words right after whatever thing you're using as your example.

```jp
映[えい]画[が]か何[なに]か見[み]ない？
```

*Want to watch a movie or something?*

The か here isn't the yes/no question particle you already know from patterns like かどうか — that か turns a whole clause into "whether." This か is a different, older job: the same か that means "or" when you're choosing between two things (A か B). Pair it with 何[なに]か, "something," and か何[なに]か reads as "or something" tacked straight onto whatever noun came before it. Put the two together right after a noun and you get "[that noun] or something like it" — a real suggestion, wrapped in a shrug. It sounds casual because it basically is casual; you'll hear it constantly among friends and rarely in a formal announcement.

Whatever particle the sentence actually needs — を, が, に, and so on — goes *after* か何[なに]か as a whole unit, not stuck onto the bare noun first. か何[なに]か behaves like the noun grew two extra syllables; the rest of the sentence treats it as one piece.

```jp
コーヒーか何[なに]か飲[の]みますか。
```

*Would you like coffee or something?*

Here か何[なに]か sits between コーヒー and 飲[の]みます, doing the job a plain object marker を would otherwise do. Once か何[なに]か is in the sentence, you drop を entirely — a bare noun plus を plus か何[なに]か is not something anyone says, even though you might expect the object marker to still be needed somewhere. か何[なに]か already tells the listener what role コーヒー is playing.

You can also put か何[なに]か in front of ある, when you're asking whether something — anything in a loose category — happens to be around, rather than hunting for one named item.

```jp
机[つくえ]の上[うえ]に紙[かみ]か何[なに]かありますか。
```

*Is there paper or something on the desk?*

Whoever answers isn't expected to produce paper specifically. A notebook, an envelope, the back of a receipt — anything writable would satisfy the question. That's the whole point of naming 紙[かみ] here: it's a stand-in for "a thing like this," not a strict requirement, and a good answer might hand over something that isn't paper at all.

## Rules and exceptions

か何[なに]か only works when the noun in front of it could plausibly be swapped for something similar without breaking the sentence. That's the real test, and it's worth running before you use か何[なに]か on anything. In 映[えい]画[が]か何[なに]か見[み]ない？, swap 映[えい]画[が] for 音[おん]楽[がく] (music) or 本[ほん] (a book) and the invitation still basically works — some easy, low-effort thing to do together. That's what makes 映[えい]画[が] a legitimate "example, not the point" noun. If swapping the noun would change what you're actually asking for, か何[なに]か is the wrong tool.

> Don't reach for か何[なに]か when you genuinely mean one specific, known thing. `友達か何か` reads like you're unsure whether the person is actually your friend — almost never what you mean. Say 友[とも]達[だち] alone and drop か何[なに]か entirely; vagueness about a fact, rather than about an example, is not what this pattern is for.

か何[なに]か is built for objects, food, and activities — everyday, replaceable items — not for people's identities or specific locations. That's part of why native speakers wince at trying to bolt it onto 誰[だれ] (who) or どこ (where): naming a vague place or a vague person is a different kind of vagueness than naming a vague *thing*, and か何[なに]か isn't the tool for it. You'll eventually meet other words built for those jobs; for now, keep か何[なに]か parked on ordinary nouns.

It also helps to notice what か何[なに]か is not doing: it isn't hedging because the speaker is unsure of the facts, and it isn't being polite for politeness's sake. It's a deliberate choice to leave a detail open because the detail genuinely doesn't matter yet. That's a small distinction, but it explains why か何[なに]か shows up so often in casual invitations and offers, and so rarely in anything that reads like a report or a form — nobody fills out an application with "book or something" as an answer.

か何[なに]か can also soften a whole request, so it doesn't come across as a demand, even when what you're describing is generous.

```jp
弟[おとうと]に本[ほん]か何[なに]か買[か]ってあげよう。
```

*I'll buy my younger brother a book or something.*

You haven't picked the book yet — you might not even end up buying a book at all, just something in that general spirit, maybe a game or a magazine. That vagueness is doing real work here: it signals you're being generous and easygoing about the choice, not that you're indecisive or don't care about the gift. Naming one concrete noun instead — 本[ほん]を買[か]ってあげよう, no か何[なに]か — sounds like the decision is already final.

## Contrast: か何[なに]か vs そういう・こういう

You already have そういう and こういう for "that kind of" and "this kind of" — both point at a category the listener can already picture, because it came up in conversation, because they said it, or because it's obvious from context. か何[なに]か is not that. It doesn't lean on anything already shared between speaker and listener; it introduces the category itself, right there in the sentence.

```jp
そういう話[はなし]は好[す]きじゃない。
```

*I don't like that kind of talk.*

そういう話[はなし] only works if you and the listener both already know which kind of 話[はなし] is meant — something specific was just said or implied a moment ago. か何[なに]か does the opposite job: it introduces a brand-new example that hasn't come up before, and tells the listener up front not to take it too literally.

```jp
忙[いそが]しいから、甘[あま]いものか何[なに]か食[た]べたい。
```

*I'm busy, so I want to eat something sweet or whatever.*

Try swapping in そういうもの here and the sentence falls apart — there's no "that kind of thing" already on the table for そういう to point back to; nobody has mentioned sweets yet. か何[なに]か doesn't need a category the conversation already agreed on; it invents one on the spot, right where it's used, which is exactly why it works so well for first mentions and offhand suggestions.

Put the two side by side and the split is simple: そういう・こういう point backward, at something already named; か何[なに]か points forward, at something you're naming for the very first time and don't intend to pin down. Mixing them up doesn't usually produce nonsense — it just produces a sentence that assumes shared context nobody actually has, which is a strange thing to do to a listener who's hearing an idea for the first time.

## Closing thought

か何[なに]か buys you room to suggest something without committing to it — the noun you name is a placeholder, not a decision, and everyone in the conversation understands that instantly.

```jp
公[こう]園[えん]で音[おん]楽[がく]か何[なに]か聞[き]きたい。
```

*I want to listen to music or something in the park.*

Once you're ready to string several loose examples together instead of offering just one, you'll meet とか — "things like this, things like that" — which does for a whole list what か何[なに]か does for a single, disposable guess.
caution_notes: Don't use か何か when you mean one specific, known thing — 友達か何か sounds like you doubt the person even is your friend.
Once か何か is in the sentence, drop the object marker を — a bare noun plus を plus か何か is never said together.
か何か is for replaceable objects, foods, and activities, not for vague people or vague places.
