items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend texts you: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]何[なに]する？ (What are you doing this weekend?) You haven't actually decided anything yet — maybe a movie, maybe some shopping, maybe you'll just see how you feel Saturday morning. Naming one single plan would be a lie; you don't have one. Naming nothing feels evasive, like you're dodging the question. What you want is a loose, no-commitment answer: a couple of examples that sketch the shape of your weekend without pinning down exactly what happens. That's the job とか does, and once you have it, this kind of half-decided answer stops feeling awkward to give — you're not lying about your plans, you're just being honest that they aren't plans yet.

```jp
週[しゅう]末[まつ]は映[えい]画[が]とか買[か]い物[もの]とかしたいです。
```

*I want to do things like watch a movie or go shopping this weekend.*

とか rides along right after a noun and says, in effect, *this, or something like it*. Say it once and you've named one example from a bigger, unnamed set. Say it twice and you've named two, with the same understanding: there might be more you're just not bothering to list. Neither example is "the plan" — they're both stand-ins for a whole category of things you might feel like doing.

## How it works

Structurally, とか is about as simple as N4 grammar gets: Noun + とか, and if you're naming a second example, Noun + とか again. It attaches straight to the noun — no だ, no です, no conjugation to worry about — and then the rest of the sentence carries its own politeness level as normal, completely independent of とか itself. Whatever verb or adjective follows behaves exactly as it would if とか weren't there at all.

There's no fixed ceiling on how many nouns you can chain this way. Three or four, each followed by its own とか, works by the same rule as two — though past two or three, a list starts to feel less like a casual toss-off and more like you're reciting a full itinerary, which undercuts the whole point of reaching for とか in the first place.

```jp
映[えい]画[が]とか買[か]い物[もの]したいです。
```

*I want to do stuff like watch a movie, maybe go shopping.*

You can drop the second とか once the listener already gets the idea, the way this sentence does — 買[か]い物[もの] just sits there as a plain second item, and nobody blinks. The full doubled shape is the default you reach for, especially the first time you introduce a list, but it isn't mandatory once the pattern is established in the conversation.

> A single noun + とか is already a complete, valid listing on its own — it doesn't need a partner. It just means "this, and other things in the same category," with the rest left comfortably unsaid.

```jp
週[しゅう]末[まつ]はテレビとか見[み]ます。
```

*This weekend I'll watch stuff like TV, among other things.*

Notice テレビとか never gets a second とか here — there's no second named example, just an implied "and whatever else." That's the hedge doing its job with a single item, and it's a shape learners tend to under-use, reaching for a full two-noun list even when one example plus とか already says everything they mean.

Because とか attaches to a noun rather than a whole sentence, the resulting noun-plus-とか group behaves exactly like any other noun afterward. It can take が as a subject, を as an object, は as a topic — whatever the sentence needs, the same way any plain noun would.

```jp
果物[くだもの]とか野[や]菜[さい]とかが体[からだ]にいいです。
```

*Things like fruit and vegetables are good for your body.*

果物[くだもの]とか野[や]菜[さい]とか as a whole becomes the subject here, then が marks it as usual. The listener understands you don't mean only those two foods — you mean the whole neighborhood of healthy things they stand in for. Try swapping が for を and the same logic carries straight over: 果物[くだもの]とか野[や]菜[さい]とかを食[た]べます would mean eating things in that same loose category, not just those two items on a plate.

## Rules and exceptions

とか is unmistakably casual. It's the register of texting a friend or chatting over lunch, not the register of a report, a job interview, or answering a doctor precisely about what hurts.

> In careful or formal speech, とか's vagueness reads as sloppy rather than friendly. If you actually need to be exact — a doctor asking what symptom you have, a boss asking what's on today's agenda — name the thing plainly and leave とか out entirely.

The other common trap is mixing up とか with か何[なに]か, which you already know. か何[なに]か gestures at one item you can't quite name or don't care to specify — "a movie or something." とか, on the other hand, lays out real, concrete examples of a category, even while leaving the exact edges of that category open. The two aren't interchangeable, even though both sound hedgy and both feel casual.

```jp
明日[あした]は映[えい]画[が]か何[なに]か見[み]ませんか。
```

*Want to watch a movie or something tomorrow?*

```jp
明日[あした]は映[えい]画[が]とかテレビとか見[み]ませんか。
```

*Want to watch stuff like a movie or TV tomorrow?*

The first sentence is one blurry idea — you haven't even decided it's a movie, could be anything. The second hands over two concrete examples standing in for a bigger, unnamed set of options. Same invitation, same politeness level, very different amount of information given to the listener. If someone answers the second question with "どっち？" (which one?), that's a fair response — you handed them two real options to choose between, not one vague placeholder.

One more thing worth knowing: とか is built for nouns, not for handing off someone else's exact words. If you're quoting what a friend said, casually, that's って's job, not とか's — don't reach for とか just because both patterns feel relaxed and conversational. They solve different problems that happen to share the same casual register.

In speech, a noun plus とか can even be the whole answer by itself. Asked 何[なに]が食[た]べたい？ (What do you feel like eating?), you can just say 肉[にく]とか。(Something like meat, I guess.) and trail off — the noun-plus-とか group already carries a complete thought, so the rest of the sentence is genuinely optional in casual talk, not just shortened.

## Contrast

You've also met そういう for pointing back at "that kind of" thing once a category already exists in the conversation. とか is how you build that category out loud in the first place, by naming a few of its members; そういう is how you refer back to the whole category once it's already on the table. One creates, the other recalls.

```jp
そういう料[りょう]理[り]が好[す]きです。
```

*I like that kind of cooking.*

```jp
寿[す]司[し]とかラーメンとか、そういう料[りょう]理[り]が好[す]きです。
```

*I like that kind of food — sushi, ramen, things along those lines.*

Name the examples with とか first, then wrap them up with そういう, and you've done in one breath what would otherwise take a whole extra sentence: given a couple of concrete anchors, then pointed at the entire category they represent. Learners who skip straight to そういう without ever having named anything leave the listener wondering what category they even mean — そういう has nothing to point back at yet.

The two patterns also differ in how heavy they feel. とか is light — you can toss out one or two examples mid-sentence without slowing down. そういう carries a little more weight; it asks the listener to hold an entire category in mind at once, which is exactly why it works best after とか has already done the work of sketching that category out with real examples.

とか's whole job is staying loose — a couple of named examples standing in for a category you don't feel like spelling out completely. Hold onto that habit of trailing off after a short list; it's exactly the kind of half-settled sentence that ところが later loves to interrupt, flipping something you thought was decided into something unexpected. For now, the win is smaller and more immediate: you can finally answer 週[しゅう]末[まつ]何[なに]する？ honestly, without pretending you've already decided.
caution_notes: とか is casual — swap it out (or drop it) in formal writing and careful speech, since its vagueness reads as sloppy rather than friendly there.
A single noun plus とか already implies "and other things like it" — you don't need a second とか to make that reading valid, even though pairing two examples is the more common shape.
Don't confuse とか with か何か: とか lists real, specific examples of a category, while か何か gestures at one item you can't or won't name.
とか attaches to nouns for listing, not to someone else's exact words — reach for って when you're casually quoting what somebody said.

items.explanation_markdown:
You are three weeks into a new job, and a friend asks how it's going. The honest answer isn't one thing — the pay is genuinely good, but you're barely home before nine most nights. English reaches for "but" and moves on without marking the shape of that sentence any further. Japanese has a word built specifically for this kind of honesty: 反[はん]面[めん], literally "the opposite (反[はん]) side (面[めん])" — the flip side of the same coin, not two unrelated facts you happen to be listing together.

```jp
彼[かの]女[じょ]の新[あたら]しい仕[し]事[ごと]は給[きゅう]料[りょう]がいい反[はん]面[めん]、休[きゅう]暇[か]が短[みじか]い。
```

*Her new job pays well, but the flip side is that vacation is short.*

That's the whole idea: state one fact, attach 反[はん]面[めん], then state the fact sitting on the other side of it. Both halves describe the same subject — the job — so 反[はん]面[めん] isn't just noting that two things differ, it's pointing at a trade-off baked into one thing. Once you notice the shape, you'll hear it everywhere: good but, easy but, fast but — always two true things about one situation, pulling in different directions.

## How it works

After a verb or an i-adjective, 反[はん]面[めん] attaches straight onto the plain form. No extra piece, no particle in between — you just say the fact, then 反[はん]面[めん], then the other fact.

```jp
この店[みせ]の料[りょう]理[り]はおいしい反[はん]面[めん]、値[ね]段[だん]が高[たか]い。
```

*This restaurant's food is delicious, but on the other hand the price is high.*

Negative plain forms work exactly the same way. 反[はん]面[めん] doesn't care whether the fact attaching to it is positive or negative — only that it's a complete plain-form clause it can hook onto.

```jp
彼[かの]女[じょ]はお酒[さけ]を飲[の]まない反[はん]面[めん]、よく食[た]べる。
```

*She doesn't drink alcohol, but on the other hand she eats a lot.*

Na-adjectives are the one place the shape changes a little: you need な between the adjective and 反[はん]面[めん], the exact same な you already use before any noun with a na-adjective.

```jp
この町[まち]は便[べん]利[り]な反[はん]面[めん]、人[ひと]が多[おお]い。
```

*This town is convenient, but on the other hand there are a lot of people.*

Potential verbs — the "can do X" forms like 話[はな]せる or 書[か]ける — are just verbs as far as 反[はん]面[めん] is concerned, so they attach the same way any plain verb does.

```jp
彼[かれ]は日本[にほん]語[ご]を話[はな]せる反[はん]面[めん]、書[か]くのが苦[にが]手[て]だ。
```

*He can speak Japanese, but on the other hand he's bad at writing.*

You'll also run into 反[はん]面[めん] opening a fresh sentence as その反[はん]面[めん], pointing back at something already said instead of attaching to the clause right before it. The logic is identical — it's the same flip-side idea, just given a full sentence break instead of a comma. Treat それ-style openings as the same pattern wearing a different collar; nothing about what 反[はん]面[めん] is doing changes.

## Rules and exceptions

反[はん]面[めん] only works when both halves are true about the same subject or topic at the same time. It isn't a general-purpose "but" for any two facts you happen to be putting next to each other — it specifically flags that one thing has two sides.

```jp
兄[あに]は頭[あたま]がいい反[はん]面[めん]、あまり勉[べん]強[きょう]しない。
```

*My older brother is smart, but on the other hand he barely studies.*

That sentence holds together because both facts belong to one person's one situation — smart, and yet barely studying. If the two halves described different people, or two events with no real connection, 反[はん]面[めん] stops making sense and you'd reach for でも or しかし instead.

> Don't drop the な after a na-adjective. `便利反面` reads as broken — you need `便利な反面`, the same rule that governs every na-adjective standing in front of a noun.

反[はん]面[めん] also leans formal and written. You'll see it constantly in essays, news writing, and careful spoken explanations where someone is laying out a considered trade-off. In a fast, casual conversation between friends, けど or でも usually carries the same contrast with far less weight behind it — reach for 反[はん]面[めん] when the point is that this really is a built-in trade-off, worth stating plainly, not just a passing however.

One more thing worth being honest about: native speakers don't use 反[はん]面[めん] for every small difference. If the gap between the two facts is minor or unremarkable, plain だが or でも does the job without making the contrast sound like a big deal. Save 反[はん]面[めん] for the moments where the two sides genuinely feel like they belong to one thing and pull against each other.

## Contrast

You already know とか for stringing together loose, similar-feeling examples — things that belong to roughly the same category, without any claim about how they relate to each other.

```jp
彼[かれ]は忙[いそが]しいとか大[たい]変[へん]とか言[い]っている。
```

*He keeps saying things like "I'm busy" and "it's rough."*

とか doesn't care whether the items it lists agree with each other — 忙[いそが]しい and 大[たい]変[へん] are just two flavors of the same complaint, tossed out loosely, no structure implied beyond "here are some examples." 反[はん]面[めん] does close to the opposite job: it takes two facts that pull against each other and insists they both belong to one subject.

```jp
彼[かれ]の仕[し]事[ごと]は忙[いそが]しい反[はん]面[めん]、楽[たの]しい。
```

*His job is busy, but on the flip side, it's fun.*

Swap 反[はん]面[めん] for とか in that sentence and the meaning falls apart. 忙[いそが]しいとか楽[たの]しいとか言[い]っている would just mean he vaguely mentions being busy and having fun sometimes, with no claim that the two sit in tension. 反[はん]面[めん] is doing real work in the original: busy and fun, both true, pulling in different directions, about the same job.

Hold onto that feeling of two things pulling against each other inside one fact — you'll meet it again soon in ところが, for when the turn is less of a built-in trade-off and more of a flat-out surprise.
caution_notes: 反面 needs な after a na-adjective (便利な反面) but attaches directly to the plain form after verbs and i-adjectives — dropping the な is a common mistake.
Both halves joined by 反面 must describe the same subject or topic; if you're contrasting two different people or unrelated situations, でも or しかし fits better, not 反面.
反面 leans formal and written — in fast casual conversation, けど or でも usually carries the same contrast with less weight.
Save 反面 for a genuine, notable trade-off; for a minor or unremarkable difference, plain だが or でも is the more natural choice.

items.explanation_markdown:
You bought a new pair of shoes. They were on sale, the color was exactly what you wanted, and you walked out of the store feeling like you'd won. Less than a week later, the sole peels off the left one while you're crossing the street.

```jp
新[あたら]しい靴[くつ]を買[か]った。とても安[やす]かった。
ところが、すぐに壊[こわ]れた。
```
*I bought new shoes. They were very cheap.*
*However, they broke right away.*

That third line is where ところが earns its keep. The first two sentences built up an expectation — new shoes, a good price, nothing to complain about — and then ところが yanks the story somewhere you didn't see coming. That's the whole job of this word: it marks the exact point where a situation you thought you understood turns out to have a catch.

It's tempting to translate ところが as a plain "but," and most dictionaries will hand you exactly that gloss. It isn't wrong, but it undersells what's happening. "But" can join two facts that were never expected to line up in the first place — "the shoes were cheap, but I don't really like the color" is a mild, low-stakes "but." ところが is reserved for the moment the story actively double-crosses you. If nobody would raise an eyebrow at your sentence, ところが is probably too strong a word for it.

## How it works

ところが sits at the front of its own sentence, right after the full stop of the sentence before it. Nothing about that first sentence changes shape to make room for it — no special ending, no attaching to a verb stem, no plain-form requirement the way something like かどうか demands. You finish your first sentence normally, in whatever form you'd already use — plain or polite, past or present — then start a fresh sentence with ところが, drop a comma, and say what actually happened.

```jp
新[あたら]しいレストランに行[い]った。
ところが、値[ね]段[だん]がとても高[たか]かった。
```
*I went to a new restaurant.*
*However, the price was very expensive.*

The shape is always: Sentence. + ところが、+ Sentence. Because ところが is doing all the connecting work by itself, it never needs help from another word — you won't see it stacked onto something else in the same slot. It stands alone, and it always opens the sentence that carries the surprise, never the one that sets it up.

It also doesn't care what kind of sentence it's attaching to. The first half can end in a verb, an adjective, or a noun-plus-copula, in plain speech or polite speech, and ところが sits down after it exactly the same way every time. Compare that to something like かどうか, which only accepts a plain-form verb or adjective right before it and rejects です outright — ところが has no such restriction, because it isn't attaching to anything at all. It's standing at the start of a brand-new sentence, looking back at the one that just ended.

## Rules and exceptions

ところが wants something that actually happened — a real event you're reporting on, usually a first half in the past tense that turned out to be a setup for a second half nobody predicted. It isn't built for hedging about the future or floating a plan that might fall through; it's for telling someone what did happen, and how it didn't go the way the first sentence implied.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]を駅[えき]で待[ま]った。
ところが、友[とも]達[だち]は来[こ]なかった。
```
*I waited for my friend at the station.*
*However, my friend didn't come.*

> Use ところが on two facts that were never actually in tension with each other and it reads like a plot twist that never arrives — the listener braces for a reversal and gets a shrug instead. Save it for a moment where something genuinely goes sideways; if nothing sideways happened, a plain connecting word does the job better.

Real speech is a little messier than that rule makes it sound. You'll hear ところが used in narration, news reports, and casual storytelling even when the "surprise" is fairly mild — more of a scene-turn than a shock. Don't fight that texture too hard while you're still getting a feel for it; leaning toward genuine reversal is the safer habit to build first, and the softer, everyday uses will come naturally once the core sense is solid.

This one is worth sitting with, because you already have the instinct for it in English — you say "but then" or "except" in exactly this spot without thinking. The only new muscle is remembering that in Japanese, that pivot word starts its own sentence instead of getting stitched onto the end of the one before it.

There's also a habit worth building around who ところが is allowed to surprise. It almost always describes something happening to the speaker, or something the speaker is reporting on as an outside observer — not a plan the speaker themselves is still deciding on. If you haven't lived through the twist yet, or you're only guessing that something might go wrong, ところが is the wrong tool; you'd want a different, more tentative way of talking about it. ところが speaks with the confidence of someone describing something that's already over and done.

## Contrast: ところが vs. 反[はん]面[めん]

You've already met 反[はん]面[めん] for holding two sides of the same thing up against each other — a "while at the same time" kind of contrast. It's built for describing standing qualities, not for narrating an event that overturned what you expected.

```jp
兄[あに]は厳[きび]しい反[はん]面[めん]、優[やさ]しい。
```
*My older brother is strict, while also being kind.*

That sentence is a portrait: two traits that sit side by side in the same person, all the time, with nothing surprising about either one. ところが needs something different — a timeline, a before and an after, something that was true and then, unexpectedly, stopped being true.

It helps to notice that 反[はん]面[めん] sentences usually still make sense if you flip the order — "strict while also kind" and "kind while also strict" describe the same person either way. Try that with ところが and it breaks immediately: "always strict, however today kind" tells a specific story in a specific direction, and reversing it — "kind today, however always strict" — describes someone completely different. That directionality is the real fingerprint of ところが. It isn't just joining two ideas; it's insisting that the second one landed as a surprise given the first.

```jp
兄[あに]はいつも厳[きび]しい。
ところが、今日[きょう]は優[やさ]しかった。
```
*My older brother is always strict.*
*However, today he was kind.*

Same brother, the same two qualities even, but now there's a story: always strict, until today, when he wasn't. Try swapping in 反[はん]面[めん] here and the sentence falls apart — 反[はん]面[めん] doesn't know what to do with "today" breaking a pattern; all it knows how to do is hold two sides of one unchanging picture at once.

That's the test you can run in your head. If the honest next question is "and then what happened?" and the answer overturns the first half, reach for ところが. If you're just describing two sides of the same coin with no event involved, 反[はん]面[めん] is the better tool.

Neither of them is right or wrong in some absolute sense — they're answering different questions. 反[はん]面[めん] answers "what is this thing like?" ところが answers "what happened, and how did it not go the way it looked like it would?" Once you can hear that difference, mixing them up gets a lot harder to do by accident.

Hold onto that distinction — それでも lives in the same neighborhood, for the moments later on when the surprise doesn't end the story, it just makes whatever comes next harder to pull off.
caution_notes: ところが needs a genuine turn of events; using it to link two facts that were never in tension just sounds like a false alarm.
Nothing about the first sentence changes form for ところが — it simply opens the next sentence on its own, followed by a comma.
ところが reports something that already happened, so don't reach for it to hedge about a future plan or an unconfirmed guess.
反面 holds two qualities of one thing at the same time; ところが needs a before-and-after where the first part gets overturned, so the two aren't interchangeable.

items.explanation_markdown:
Picture your older brother waking up with a fever. He should stay in bed today — that's the obvious move. Instead he gets dressed and walks out the door to work like nothing happened. English has a whole family of words for that shrug — still, anyway, regardless — but Japanese has one word built for exactly this move: それでも.

```jp
兄[あに]は熱[ねつ]があった。それでも仕[し]事[ごと]に行[い]った。
```

*My older brother had a fever. Even so, he went to work.*

That's the whole shape of it. State what happened. Put a period down. Drop それでも in as its own little sentence-opener. State what happened next — something the first sentence should have stopped, and didn't.

That gap between what should happen and what actually does is the whole point of the word. それでも doesn't soften the obstacle, apologize for it, or explain it away — it just names the obstacle, closes the sentence on it, and lets the next sentence walk straight through it anyway.

## How it works

それでも always sits between two separate ideas: **Sentence. + それでも + Sentence.** The first sentence lays out a fact that creates resistance — bad weather, an injury, a lack of sleep, anything that would normally get in the way of what comes next. The second sentence reports that the resistance didn't work.

```jp
雨[あめ]が降[ふ]っていた。それでも兄[あに]は散[さん]歩[ぽ]した。
```

*It was raining. Even so, my brother went for a walk.*

Notice that それでも doesn't attach to anything — it isn't glued onto a verb stem the way a conjugated ending would be, so there's nothing here to conjugate. Past tense, present tense, casual or polite, it stays それでも no matter what came before it. Its only job is standing at the front of the second sentence and pointing back at the first one.

That's also why it never changes shape for politeness. The sentences around it might be polite or plain, but それでも itself is neither — it's just a connector, not a verb or an adjective, so there's no です or ます form of it to reach for.

It also doesn't shrink in casual speech the way some polite words do — わからない becoming わかんない, or では becoming じゃ. それでも already sounds plain and complete on its own, so there's nothing left to trim, and you'll hear it exactly this way whether the conversation is formal or between old friends.

You'll also see it show up mid-sentence, right after a clause joined with が, instead of after a fresh period. It's still doing the same job — the が just means the writer chose to keep both halves in one breath instead of splitting them into two sentences.

```jp
兄[あに]は薬[くすり]を飲[の]んだが、それでも熱[ねつ]は下[さ]がらなかった。
```

*My brother took his medicine, but even then his fever didn't go down.*

Either way — full stop or が — the test is the same: can you point at the sentence right before それでも and name the thing it should have blocked? If yes, you're using it correctly.

Both versions show up constantly in ordinary storytelling — someone recapping their weekend, a coworker explaining why they're late, a doctor summarizing a patient's stubborn symptoms. Anywhere someone reports "this happened, and then, against expectation, this also happened," それでも is doing quiet work in the background.

## Rules and exceptions

それでも needs the first sentence to carry real weight. It has to describe an obstacle a listener would nod along to — "yes, that should have been a problem." Drop in something trivial and それでも starts to sound like you're announcing a fight that never happened.

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]は説[せつ]明[めい]を三[さん]回[かい]した。それでも私[わたし]は意[い]味[み]が分[わ]からなかった。
```

*The teacher explained it three times. Even so, I didn't understand the meaning.*

Three explanations is genuine effort — the kind of thing that should have produced understanding. それでも earns its keep here because the outcome really does fight against the setup.

Compare that to a setup with barely any weight — one quick reminder, say, instead of three full explanations. それでも would feel like overkill there, as if you were bracing the listener for a much bigger fight than the sentence actually describes. The word carries its own sense of scale, so save it for obstacles that are genuinely heavy.

> それでも always looks backward at something already stated. It can't reach forward into a hypothetical — a sentence like "if the exam turns out to be hard, I'll study anyway" isn't a job for それでも. It wants a sentence that already happened or is already true, not a guess about a future that hasn't landed yet.

The obstacle also doesn't have to be one blunt fact — a whole earlier situation can serve as the setup, as long as a reader can point back and name what it was.

```jp
説[せつ]明[めい]は難[むずか]しかった。それでも学[がく]生[せい]は頑張[がんば]って勉[べん]強[きょう]した。
```

*The explanation was difficult. Even so, the student kept at their studying.*

This is also why それでも rarely opens a conversation cold. Someone hearing it for the first time needs the earlier sentence to be sitting right there — spoken out loud a moment ago, or written just above. Start a chat with それでも and nobody knows what "even so" is supposed to be answering.

## Contrast

Here's a piece of trivia that makes それでも easier to hold onto: it's literally それ (that) plus でも (even) — "even that" worn down into "even so." Which means you already knew half of this word. でも on its own means but/however, and それでも just points that でも squarely at the sentence sitting right in front of it.

Swap それでも for a bare でも and you lose that pointing-back feeling. でも can open a sentence out of nowhere, contrasting two things that were never really in tension to begin with.

```jp
天[てん]気[き]は悪[わる]かった。でも、公[こう]園[えん]はきれいだった。
天[てん]気[き]は悪[わる]かった。それでも私[わたし]たちは公[こう]園[えん]を歩[ある]いた。
```

*The weather was bad. But the park was pretty.*
*The weather was bad. Even so, we walked through the park.*

The first pair is just two facts sitting side by side — bad weather, pretty park, no real friction between them. The second pair says the bad weather should have kept everyone indoors, and it didn't; that resistance is the part only それでも carries.

ところが is the other neighbor worth separating out, and it's an easy pair to mix up because both sit after a full stop and both introduce something a little unwelcome. The difference is in what kind of "unwelcome": ところが reports a genuine twist, a result nobody was steering toward. それでも reports a course that held steady on purpose, against pressure everyone could already see coming.

```jp
薬[くすり]を飲[の]んだ。ところが熱[ねつ]は上[あ]がった。
薬[くすり]を飲[の]んだ。それでも熱[ねつ]は下[さ]がらなかった。
```

*I took the medicine. However, my fever went up unexpectedly.*
*I took the medicine. Even so, my fever didn't go down.*

The fever spiking is the twist ところが is built for — nobody expected the medicine to backfire. The fever holding steady is the opposite of a twist: everyone half-expected the obstacle to win, and それでも is just confirming that it did. If you can rewrite a それでも sentence as "and, unsurprisingly, the obstacle won anyway," you've got the right word.

反[はん]面[めん] is worth one more line, mostly so you don't confuse the shapes. 反[はん]面[めん] welds directly onto a plain-form clause inside a single sentence, describing two sides of the same subject at once — it never needs a full stop before it the way それでも does. Once you're watching for that period, the two stop looking anything alike.

That's the whole pattern: name the obstacle, then let それでも announce that it lost. It's a small word to carry that much weight — one clause of setup, one word of pivot, one clause of payoff — but that's exactly why it reads as calm instead of dramatic. It isn't fighting the obstacle; it's just reporting, flatly, that the obstacle didn't get its way.

Hold onto the ところが comparison — once そこで shows up, you'll see it pick up right where それでも leaves off, moving the story from "and yet, nothing changed" to "so here's what I did about it."
caution_notes: それでも always needs a real, already-stated obstacle in the sentence before it — used on something trivial, it can sound like you're overreacting.
それでも can't point at a hypothetical; the sentence before it has to describe something that already happened or is already true, not a future guess.
それでも rarely opens a conversation on its own — without an earlier sentence naming the obstacle, listeners won't know what it's answering.

items.explanation_markdown:
You left the house and the sky opened up on you halfway to the station. You didn't just stand there getting soaked — you did something about it. In Japanese, the sentence that reports what you decided to do next often opens with そこで, a word that works like "so, at that point" — it's the hinge between a situation you found yourself in and the deliberate move you made in response.

そこで doesn't just mean "and then." It carries a small implication: something happened, you registered it, and you acted. That makes it different from a plain time-sequence word like そして (and then) — そして just lines events up in order, while そこで insists that the second event happened *because of* the first one, as a response someone chose to make. Keep that piece in mind; it's the whole engine of the pattern.

## How そこで works

The shape is simple: one full sentence describing a situation, a period, then そこで, a comma, and a second full sentence describing the action taken because of that situation. そこで always opens the second sentence — it never sits in the middle of one sentence joined by a comma the way から can. You're always looking at two separate sentences, and そこで is the word standing at the start line of the second one, pointing back at the first.

```jp
雨[あめ]が降[ふ]った。
そこで、近[ちか]くの喫[きっ]茶[さ]店[てん]に入[はい]った。
```
*It rained.*
*So I went into a nearby coffee shop.*

The first sentence just reports what happened — no judgment, no plan yet. The second sentence is where the story turns: you noticed the rain, and そこで marks the exact point where noticing became doing. Drop そこで and the two sentences just sit next to each other with no signal that one caused the other; the connection has to be guessed from context instead of stated.

```jp
宿[しゅく]題[だい]の意[い]味[み]が分[わ]からなかった。
そこで、先[せん]生[せい]に聞[き]いた。
```
*I didn't understand what the homework meant.*
*So I asked the teacher.*

Here's the part that matters most about そこで, and it's the one rule everything else in this lesson hangs off of: the second sentence has to be an action — something the speaker actively did — not another fact or feeling. `宿題の意味が分からなかった。そこで、少し不安だった。` (I didn't understand the homework. So I felt a little anxious.) technically parses as a sentence, but it reads strangely, because feeling anxious isn't a response you chose the way asking a question is. A feeling just happens to you; そこで wants something you *did*. Keep the sentence after そこで doing something, not just being something, and the pattern will always sound natural.

That constraint is also what tells you そこで apart from a simple list of events. If you can't answer "what did the speaker decide to do about it?" with the second sentence, そこで is probably the wrong connector for that pair.

そこで can also chain forward. Once a second sentence has been set up with そこで, the story is free to keep going in plain past tense — 宿[しゅく]題[だい]の意[い]味[み]が分[わ]からなかった。そこで、先[せん]生[せい]に聞[き]いた。分[わ]かった。 (I didn't understand the homework. So I asked the teacher. I understood.) — without needing another そこで to hold the third sentence in place. The connector only has to fire once, at the pivot from situation to response; everything after that just continues the story in order.

## Rules and exceptions

そこで is a narration word. It shows up naturally when you're explaining a sequence of events — telling a story, writing a report, walking someone through what happened after the fact — and it sounds a little formal or writerly for quick back-and-forth chat. If a friend asks "why did you do that?" a plain だから answer fits the moment better than reaching for そこで, which reads more like the voice of someone recounting the whole episode from a bit of distance.

```jp
頭[あたま]が痛[いた]かった。
そこで、薬[くすり]を飲[の]んだ。
```
*My head hurt.*
*So I took some medicine.*

That sentence works equally well spoken or written, but notice the shape: a state (頭[あたま]が痛[いた]かった) followed by a clear, chosen action (薬[くすり]を飲[の]んだ). Swap the order — put the action first and the state second — and そこで stops making sense, because by definition it's always pointing backward at whatever came right before it.

This is also why そこで never attaches directly to a noun or an adjective the way か何[なに]か or とか do. It only ever opens a full sentence, because its whole job is to summarize "given the situation just described" in one word before handing off to the response. There's no shorter form and no version that tucks into the middle of a clause.

> そこで is spelled and pronounced exactly like そこ (there) plus the particle で (at / by means of). When そこ is pointing back at a place already mentioned, and で is just marking where something happens, you get the same two syllables meaning something completely different.

```jp
公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]った。
そこで、友[とも]達[だち]を待[ま]っていた。
```
*I went to the park.*
*There, I waited for my friend.*

Read that second sentence out loud and it looks identical to the connector. The difference is entirely about what came before it: 公[こう]園[えん] (park) was just introduced, so そこ has something concrete to point at, and で is simply saying where the waiting happened. If the previous sentence names no place at all, there's nothing for そこ to refer to, and the reading collapses back into the connector — there's no situation-and-response pair to explain otherwise. When you're unsure which reading you're looking at, ask whether a place was just named in the sentence before it; if yes, check the locative reading first, because that's the one a bare grammar gloss won't warn you about.

## Contrast: そこで vs ところが vs それでも

You already know ところが and それでも, and they share そこで's job of opening a sentence that responds to the one before it — but they pull in the opposite direction. そこで says the second sentence follows naturally from the first: situation, then response, the kind of link you'd expect. ところが says the second sentence breaks the first one's expectation instead.

```jp
空[そら]は明[あか]るかった。
ところが、雨[あめ]が降[ふ]った。
```
*The sky was bright.*
*However, it rained.*

Swap ところが for そこで in that pair and the sentence stops making sense — nobody responds to a bright sky by making it rain; there's no decision being reported, just an unwelcome surprise. それでも works in the same contrastive direction as ところが, but it points back at the whole situation rather than one surprising fact: "even given everything I just told you, this still happened." Neither ところが nor それでも ever announces a chosen action the way そこで does — they announce a twist, not a decision, and that's the fastest way to tell the three apart once you've got a candidate sentence in front of you.

So the quick test: if the second sentence is something the speaker decided to do because of the first, reach for そこで. If it's something that happened anyway, against what you'd expect, ところが or それでも is doing the work instead. Once you've asked "is this a decision or a twist?", the right connector usually picks itself.

It helps to line the three up side by side in your head. そこで: situation, then chosen response — smooth, expected. ところが: situation, then a single fact that undercuts it — sharp, sudden. それでも: situation, then persistence in spite of it — the situation doesn't get resolved, it just gets pushed through. All three open a new sentence and all three look backward, but only one of them is ever reporting a decision.

Hold onto that shape — you'll meet a close cousin soon, そのため, which points even more directly at the reason behind the second sentence rather than the moment of deciding to act on it.
caution_notes: そこで looks and sounds exactly like そこ (there) plus the particle で, so check whether the previous sentence just named a place before reading it as the connector.
The sentence after そこで needs to be a real action the speaker chose to take, not just another fact or feeling — pairing it with a state instead of a decision reads oddly.
そこで belongs to narration and explanation, so it can sound stiff as a quick spoken answer to a casual "why did you do that?"

items.explanation_markdown:
Your train stalls on the tracks for twenty minutes, and by the time you reach the office, everyone is already sitting down for the meeting. When a coworker asks what happened, you don't need to retell the whole story of the delay — you can report it like a headline: cause, then effect, one sentence pointing straight at the next.

```jp
電[でん]車[しゃ]が遅[おく]れた。
そのため、会[かい]議[ぎ]に遅[ち]刻[こく]した。
```
*The train was delayed.*
*Because of that, I was late to the meeting.*

そのため sits at the start of the second sentence and points straight back at the one before it — that first sentence is the cause, and everything after そのため is simply what came of it. It's already a fused word, built from その (that) plus a piece meaning "for the sake of," so it never splits apart, conjugates, or changes shape no matter what surrounds it.

Notice, too, what そのため is quietly leaving out. It never says whether the delay was expected, whether you're annoyed about it, or whether being late was a big deal — it just states the link between the two facts and moves on. That flatness is the whole point: it's a connector for reporting outcomes, not for narrating feelings about them.

## How it works

そのため always follows a full, complete sentence — plain or polite, past or present — and opens the next one, usually with a comma right after it. You're not attaching it to a verb stem or a noun the way most particles work; it just sits there on its own, functioning as what you could call a **consequence connector** — a little word whose only job is to link "this happened" to "and because of it, so did this." There's no verb form to memorize and no particle to swap in or out. All of its work is done by where it sits, not by how it bends.

Because そのため needs a complete, finished sentence in front of it, you'll never see it wedged directly onto a noun the way か何[なに]か or とか attach to one. The cause has to close itself off as its own full thought first, period and all, before そのため can point back at it.

- Always follows a full sentence, never a bare noun or verb stem.
- Keeps exactly the same shape whether the sentences around it are casual or polite.
- States a plain, factual consequence — not something anyone decided to do.
- Needs the cause already spoken or written — it never opens a new topic out of nowhere.

```jp
風邪[かぜ]をひいた。
そのため、学[がっ]校[こう]を休[やす]んだ。
```
*I caught a cold.*
*Because of that, I stayed home from school.*

The politeness of the surrounding sentences never touches そのため itself. Watch what happens when the whole exchange gets dressed up:

```jp
財[さい]布[ふ]をなくしました。
そのため、お金[かね]がありませんでした。
```
*I lost my wallet.*
*Because of that, I didn't have any money.*

Compare that to the cold example above — same connector, same job, even though one conversation is casual and the other is polite. そのため doesn't conjugate, doesn't take a particle of its own, and doesn't care what tense or politeness level the sentences around it are in. It's the one constant in an otherwise shifting sentence.

## Rules and exceptions

そのため needs a real sentence stating a cause sitting right in front of it. You can't open cold with そのため and expect the listener to guess what "that" refers to — the cause has to already be on the table, whether it's the sentence directly before or something explained a little earlier in the same conversation. It also carries a slightly formal register — a way of describing how casual or dressed-up something sounds — so you'll run into it constantly in news reports, workplace emails, and explanations, more than in relaxed chat about your weekend.

> Watch out for `そのために` — same characters, one extra に, a completely different job. That version means "in order to" or "for the sake of that," pointing forward at a goal you're working toward, not backward at a cause you're reporting. そのため looks back at what already happened; そのために looks forward at what you're trying to make happen.

There's no casual, shrunk-down version of そのため the way です contracts to じゃ in speech. It's already about as plain and portable as a connector gets, so you'll meet it in nearly the same shape everywhere you read or hear it — spoken news, a coworker's email, or a friend explaining why they're late, though a friend is just as likely to reach for something looser instead.

You'll also hear そのため used out loud, not just on the page. A speaker giving a status update in a meeting, or a train announcement explaining a delay, both lean on it — it's the sound of someone laying out a cause and then telling you plainly what followed, without dressing the second sentence up as their own opinion or reaction. That's part of why it feels a step more formal than something like だから: it's built for reporting, not for reacting.

## Contrast: そのため vs そこで vs だから

You already have そこで for "so, in response to that" — but the two pull in different directions. そこで frames what comes next as something a person decided to do about the situation. そのため frames it as a plain consequence, whether or not anyone decided anything at all.

```jp
そこで、傘[かさ]を買[か]った。
そのため、服[ふく]が濡[ぬ]れた。
```
*So I went and bought an umbrella.*
*Because of that, my clothes got wet.*

Same rainy afternoon, told two ways. Buying the umbrella is a choice made **in response** to the rain — that's そこで's territory. Getting rained on before reaching the store isn't a choice at all, just a plain result, and that's exactly what そのため reports.

There's a third connector worth placing next to these two: だから, the casual "so" you already reach for with friends. Picture someone who wasn't feeling well and just went to bed early.

```jp
だから、休[やす]んだ。
そのため、休[やす]んだ。
```
*So I rested.*
*Because of that, I rested.*

Both sentences describe the exact same choice, but they'd land in different rooms. だから is what you'd actually say out loud to a friend — quick, casual, unremarkable. そのため is what you'd write in a note explaining an absence, or what a narrator might say summing up a scene — a little more distant, a little more report-like. Swapping one for the other doesn't change the facts, only how formal the retelling sounds. Picture a text to a friend using だから, and a message to a teacher explaining the same absence using そのため — same event, two different rooms.

If a sentence describes someone actively doing something about a situation, そこで usually reads more naturally. If it describes what simply resulted — good news or bad, chosen or not — and you want that neutral, slightly written tone, reach for そのため instead of forcing an active-sounding connector onto a passive fact.

The shape you just practiced — a full sentence, そのため, another full sentence — comes back almost immediately with すると, which uses the same two-sentence structure to walk through what happened next in a sequence rather than what one sentence caused. For now, keep そのため on hand for the plain, factual "and because of that" link, and let だから and そこで carry the sentences where someone is actually speaking casually or choosing what to do next.
caution_notes: そのため only works when the sentence right before it (or clearly established just before) states a cause — don't open with it out of nowhere.
そのため itself never conjugates or changes with politeness level; only the sentences around it do.
Don't confuse そのため with the look-alike そのために, which points forward at a goal instead of back at a cause.
そのため reads as a neutral, almost report-style connector; for a livelier, more casual retelling, だから or そこで usually fits better.

items.explanation_markdown:
You open the window to let some air in, and the second your hand touches the frame you notice it — rain, coming down steady, and you had no idea it had even started. In Japanese, the connector that carries you from the first action straight into the surprise that followed it is すると.

```jp
窓[まど]を開[あ]けた。すると雨[あめ]が降[ふ]っていた。
```

*I opened the window. Then it was raining.*

すると sits at the very front of the second sentence, right after a full stop. It never changes shape — no conjugation, no politeness form, nothing to memorize beyond the word itself. That's the whole mechanic: one complete sentence, a period, すると, another complete sentence. The first sentence is the trigger — something you did, or something that was simply true — and the すると sentence reports what showed up right afterward, almost like you're narrating a scene as it unfolds in front of you.

## How it works

The first sentence can be in plain past tense, describing a single thing that actually happened once. That's the most common shape you'll meet: you did something, and すると hands you straight into what you found.

```jp
家[いえ]に帰[かえ]った。すると猫[ねこ]が机[つくえ]の上[うえ]で寝[ね]ていた。
```

*I went home. Then the cat was sleeping on the desk.*

```jp
猫[ねこ]の名[な]前[まえ]を呼[よ]んだ。すると猫[ねこ]が起[お]きた。
```

*I called the cat's name. Then the cat woke up.*

Notice who's doing what in each half. You call the cat's name — that's your action. The cat waking up is not your action; it's what happened as a direct, practically automatic consequence of yours. That's the feel すると carries: the second half is something you observed or discovered, not something you decided to do.

There's a second use of the same word, and it's easy to miss the first time you meet it. If the first sentence is in plain non-past form instead of past, すると describes a pattern that holds every time, not a one-off event.

```jp
毎[まい]朝[あさ]、電[でん]気[き]をつける。すると猫[ねこ]が起[お]きる。
```

*Every morning I turn on the light. Then the cat wakes up.*

Same connector, same two-sentence shape — the only thing that shifted is the tense of the first half, from つけた (turned on, once) to つける (turn on, every time). That tense shift is what tells the listener whether you're recounting a specific morning or describing a routine.

## Rules and exceptions

The part that trips people up is what すると is *not* allowed to introduce. The second sentence has to be something that happens on its own — a fact, a discovery, someone or something else's reaction. It cannot be your own decision about what to do next.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]を呼[よ]んだ。すると友[とも]達[だち]が来[き]た。
```

*I called my friend. Then my friend came.*

That works because "my friend came" is their action, reported as a consequence — not a plan you're announcing. Compare that to something like `友達を呼んだ。すると友達と話しましょう。` — trying to use すると to lead into your own proposal ("let's talk") is wrong. The moment the second half is a request, an invitation, an order, or a statement of intent, すると can't carry it; that job belongs to a different connector entirely.

> すると almost always reports something that has already happened or that reliably happens — treat it as a narrator's word, not a planner's word. If you catch yourself about to write a volitional form (〜ましょう, 〜よう) or a request after すると, stop and pick another connector.

The other trap is reaching for すると when the second sentence actually contradicts what you'd expect from the first. すると is neutral — mildly surprising at most, never a reversal. A genuine reversal needs a different word, which is exactly what the contrast section below is for.

## Contrast

You've already met そこで, for when the second sentence is a deliberate response you chose to make, and ところが, for when the second sentence contradicts what the first one set up. Line all three up against the same opening sentence and the differences become obvious.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]を呼[よ]んだ。そこで友[とも]達[だち]と話[はな]した。
```

*I called my friend. So I talked with my friend.*

Here the second half is something you decided to do next, on purpose — that's そこで's territory. Swap in すると and it reads as though the talking just happened to you, which isn't the sense you want when you're describing your own choice.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]を呼[よ]んだ。ところが友[とも]達[だち]は来[こ]なかった。
```

*I called my friend. However, my friend didn't come.*

Here the second half undercuts the first — you called, and yet nothing came of it. That gap between expectation and reality is what ところが is built for, and it's exactly the gap すると refuses to carry. すると's version of this scene simply has the friend showing up, no surprise, no letdown — the plainest possible next beat in the story.

So the three sit in a row: すると narrates the next thing that happened, そこで narrates the next thing you chose to do, ところが narrates the next thing that shouldn't have happened but did.

Worth holding onto for later: 反[はん]対[たい]に flips a situation the opposite way rather than simply continuing it forward, which is a slightly different move than any of these three — more on that when we get there.

For now, the shape to remember is small: one finished sentence, すると, one more sentence reporting what followed. Read a few lines of any story written in Japanese and you'll start noticing it everywhere — it's one of the plainest ways native writers move a scene forward one beat at a time.
caution_notes: すると cannot introduce your own deliberate next move — use そこで when the second half is a choice you made rather than something you noticed happen.
Never follow すると with a request, invitation, or volitional form (〜ましょう, 〜よう); it only narrates what happened or what reliably happens, never what you intend to do.
If the second sentence contradicts what the first one set up, that's ところが's job, not すると's.

items.explanation_markdown:
Picture texting a friend about Saturday's get-together: "Is everyone coming?" Almost everyone — one person can't make it. You want to say "everyone except Ken," and Japanese has a clean, single word for that job: 以[い]外[がい] (igai), meaning "except" or "other than." It attaches directly onto whichever noun you're pulling out of the group, so you never have to build a whole clause around it.

```jp
私[わたし]以[い]外[がい]はみんな来[き]ます。
```
*Everyone except me is coming.*

Notice what happened there: 以[い]外[がい] sits right after 私[わたし] (me) — no verb, no connector, just a person and then the word that says "not counting this one." That's the entire shape of the pattern: **Noun + 以[い]外[がい]**.

## How it works

以[い]外[がい] always follows a noun — whatever you're carving out of a larger group. Once it's attached, everything else in the sentence is understood to apply to the rest of that group, not to the noun sitting in front of 以[い]外[がい].

If what you want to exclude is an action rather than a thing, you can't hand 以[い]外[がい] a bare verb — it needs a noun first, so you build one with こと (a little word that turns a whole verb phrase into a thing you can talk about):

```jp
泳[およ]ぐ → 泳[およ]ぐこと
```
*to swim → swimming (the thing itself)*

```jp
泳[およ]ぐこと以[い]外[がい]、スポーツが苦[にが]手[て]です。
```
*Other than swimming, I'm bad at sports.*

Two shapes show up constantly, and they're really just 以[い]外[がい] riding on a particle you already know:

- **以[い]外[がい]に** — leans toward "besides / in addition to." Common with a positive verb ("besides X, also Y") and just as common with a negative one ("nothing besides X").
- **以[い]外[がい]は** — leans toward "as for everything except X," setting X up as the one exception to whatever comes next.

```jp
音[おん]楽[がく]以[い]外[がい]に趣[しゅ]味[み]がありません。
```
*I don't have a hobby besides music.*

```jp
日本[にほん]語[ご]以[い]外[がい]に英[えい]語[ご]も話[はな]せます。
```
*Besides Japanese, I can also speak English.*

```jp
土[ど]曜[よう]日[び]以[い]外[がい]は毎[まい]日[にち]勉[べん]強[きょう]します。
```
*I study every day except Saturday.*

に and は aren't doing anything new here — they're the same particles you've used since week one. に leans toward "additionally," は leans toward "as for the rest of the group." Neither one changes what 以[い]外[がい] itself means; they just tint the sentence around it.

## Rules and exceptions

The one rule that trips people up: 以[い]外[がい] wants a noun immediately in front of it. In English, "except" can follow almost any kind of phrase, but Japanese draws a harder line. A bare plain-form verb can't feed straight into 以[い]外[がい].

> Don't write `泳ぐ以外` on its own to mean "other than swimming." A verb needs to be turned into a noun first — usually with こと — before 以[い]外[がい] can attach: 泳[およ]ぐこと以[い]外[がい].

以[い]外[がい] pairs naturally with a negative predicate to mean "only this one." That's not really a separate rule — it's just what "not X except Y" collapses to once you say it out loud:

```jp
彼[かれ]以[い]外[がい]は誰[だれ]も知[し]りません。
```
*No one knows except him.*

Read literally, that's "as for other than him, nobody knows" — which lands as "only he knows." Once you notice that shape, 以[い]外[がい] plus a negative keeps showing up wherever the real meaning is "only."

> 以[い]外[がい] marks what's outside the group — it says nothing about how big the group itself is.

```jp
魚[さかな]以[い]外[がい]は好[す]きです。
```
*I like everything except fish.*

That sentence tells you fish is out. It doesn't tell you whether "everything" means two dishes or twenty — 以[い]外[がい] draws the boundary, not the headcount.

以[い]外[がい] doesn't care about politeness level either. It sits comfortably in plain speech and in です・ます sentences without changing shape, so you don't need a separate casual version to learn — the word itself never bends. In a quick spoken answer, people will sometimes drop the は or に and let bare 以[い]外[がい] carry the whole thought as a fragment — someone asks what you don't eat, and 魚[さかな]以[い]外[がい]。 is a complete answer on its own.

## Contrast

Everything else you've learned so far — 反[はん]面[めん], ところが, それでも, そこで, そのため, すると — links two full sentences together. 以[い]外[がい] works differently: it's a small word riding directly on a noun, not a bridge between clauses. You can't swap it in for one of those connectors and expect the sentence to hold together; they're built for different jobs.

Where they do overlap is in mood, and それでも is the closest one to check yourself against. それでも says "even given that, X still happened" — it concedes something and pushes past it:

```jp
頭[あたま]が痛[いた]かった。
それでも仕[し]事[ごと]に行[い]った。
```
*I had a headache.*
*Even so, I went to work.*

以[い]外[がい] doesn't concede anything; it just draws a line around one item and says "not this one." If you ever reach for それでも to mean "except for this," that's the moment to reach for 以[い]外[がい] instead — それでも answers "what happened anyway?" while 以[い]外[がい] answers "what's left out?"

以[い]外[がい] also isn't the same word as 他[ほか] (ほか), even though both get translated as "other." 他[ほか] is a plain noun — "another one" — that can stand on its own and take its own particles, like a subject or an object. 以[い]外[がい] never stands alone; it only exists attached to the noun it's excluding.

This is worth holding onto beyond today: 以[い]外[がい] belongs to a small family of patterns that bolt straight onto a noun instead of linking two sentences. You'll meet another member of that family soon in 以[い]来[らい], which uses the same "Noun +" shape to mean "ever since."
caution_notes: 以外 needs a noun right in front of it — a bare plain-form verb has to become a noun with こと first, as in 泳ぐこと以外.
以外 only marks what's left out of the group; it says nothing about how large the rest of the group is.
以外 plus a negative predicate usually means 'only this one,' not a double exclusion, so read 彼以外は誰も知りません as 'only he knows.'

items.explanation_markdown:
Picture this: you moved to Tokyo three years ago, and someone at a party asks how long you've been in Japan. You could just give a number, but what you actually want to say is "ever since I got here, I've been living in this city" — one clause that ties the moment you arrived to everything that has been true since. That job belongs to 以[い]来[らい] (いらい), literally "since."

## How it works

以[い]来[らい] attaches directly to a noun that names a point in time, or to the te-form of a verb (the -て form — the connecting shape you already use for "and" and for requests). Either way, it marks the moment something started, and everything after it in the sentence describes what has stayed true from that moment up to right now.

With a verb, you first build the te-form, then add 以[い]来[らい] right after it.

```jp
来[く]る → 来[き]て
```

*to come → having come*

```jp
日本[にほん]に来[き]て以[い]来[らい]、毎[まい]日[にち]忙[いそが]しいです。
```

*Ever since I came to Japan, I've been busy every day.*

Look at the shape: [action in te-form] + 以[い]来[らい] + [ongoing state]. The second half is never a one-time event — it's something that has kept being true since the te-form clause happened. That's the whole engine of 以[い]来[らい]: a starting line, then an unbroken stretch of time after it, right up to the present.

The same mechanic works for する-verbs, where the te-form is 〜して.

```jp
卒[そつ]業[ぎょう]する → 卒[そつ]業[ぎょう]して
```

*to graduate → having graduated*

```jp
卒[そつ]業[ぎょう]して以[い]来[らい]、先[せん]生[せい]に会[あ]っていません。
```

*I haven't seen my teacher since I graduated.*

With a noun, you skip the te-form entirely and attach 以[い]来[らい] straight to the time word — no verb needed at all.

```jp
先[せん]月[げつ]以[い]来[らい]、病[びょう]気[き]です。
```

*I've been sick since last month.*

That's the whole mechanic, in two shapes: noun + 以[い]来[らい], or verb-te-form + 以[い]来[らい], always followed by something ongoing.

## Rules and exceptions

以[い]来[らい] is built for change that sticks. If nothing has been continuously true since the starting point, 以[い]来[らい] is the wrong tool — it doesn't just mean "at some point after X," it means "from X, unbroken, until right now."

```jp
結[けっ]婚[こん]して以[い]来[らい]、毎[まい]日[にち]料[りょう]理[り]をしています。
```

*Ever since I got married, I've been cooking every day.*

> Only the て-form works here — a plain past tense like `来た以来` is not something you'll hear native speakers use. If you can build the て-form, you can use 以[い]来[らい]; if you're reaching for 〜た, stop and switch back to 〜て.

The other trap is scale. 以[い]来[らい] wants a starting point big enough to carry a stretch of time after it — a life event, a season, a named date — not a five-minute gap. Nobody reaches for 以[い]来[らい] over something that small; that's what plain て-form clauses without 以[い]来[らい] are for.

```jp
子[こ]供[ども]が生[う]まれて以[い]来[らい]、あまり寝[ね]ていません。
```

*Ever since our child was born, I haven't slept much.*

This one trips people the first week, because English "since" covers both jobs — the one-off "since Tuesday I've been at my desk" and the reason-giving "since you're here, help me" — and only the first of those is 以[い]来[らい]'s job. The second is a completely different word, and mixing them up is a very natural mistake to make early on.

## Contrast

You already know 以[い]外[がい] (except / other than), and it's an easy one to misread at a glance — both words start with 以[い], and both feel like they're marking some kind of boundary. But 以[い]外[がい] draws a line around what's excluded from a group; it has nothing to do with time at all.

```jp
日本[にほん]語[ご]以[い]外[がい]は分[わ]かりません。
```

*I don't understand anything except Japanese.*

そのため is a different kind of neighbor: it links a cause to its result — that happened, so this happened — while 以[い]来[らい] links a starting point to everything that has followed it. そのため cares about *why* something happened; 以[い]来[らい] cares about *since when* something has been true.

```jp
病[びょう]気[き]になりました。そのため、会[かい]社[しゃ]を休[やす]みました。
```

*I got sick. Because of that, I took the day off work.*

Swap 以[い]来[らい] in for そのため there and the sentence stops making sense — "sick, and 以[い]来[らい] I took the day off" throws away the cause-and-effect link that そのため was carrying, and replaces it with a claim about an ongoing state that was never there.

以[い]来[らい] opens a sentence by naming when an ongoing state began. Hold onto that starting-point feeling — it comes back when you meet 反[はん]対[たい]に, which flips a situation around instead of anchoring it in time.
caution_notes: 以来 needs a te-form verb or a time noun in front of it — a plain past tense like 来た以来 is not a form native speakers use, so use 来て以来 instead.
以来 marks an unbroken ongoing state that continues to the present, not a single one-off event somewhere in the past.
以来 and 以外 look alike but are unrelated — 以外 marks exclusion from a group, not a point in time.
以来 fits a starting point big enough to carry a stretch of time after it, like a life event or a named date, not a five-minute gap.

items.explanation_markdown:
You tell a friend the forecast said sun today, then you step outside straight into rain. That gap — between what you expected and what actually happened — needs its own word in Japanese, and that word is 反[はん]対[たい]に (はんたいに), "on the contrary" or "conversely." It doesn't soften bad news, and it doesn't add a reason for anything. It just flags a flat reversal: you thought one thing, reality delivered the opposite.

You'll hear 反[はん]対[たい]に just as often in conversation as you'll see it in writing — it's not a stiff, bookish word. Someone recapping their day, correcting a guess you made, or comparing two people's reactions will reach for it naturally, the same way you'd reach for "on the contrary" in English without thinking twice.

## How it works

反[はん]対[たい]に is built from the noun 反[はん]対[たい] (the opposite, or opposition) plus the particle に — the same に that turns a lot of nouns into adverbs, the way 元[げん]気[き] becomes 元[げん]気[き]に or 自[じ]由[ゆう] becomes 自[じ]由[ゆう]に. Once you see that seam, the meaning falls out naturally: 反[はん]対[たい] is "the opposite thing," so 反[はん]対[たい]に is "in the opposite way."

```jp
反[はん]対[たい] → 反[はん]対[たい]に
```

The structure is simple: 反[はん]対[たい]に sits in front of the statement that carries the reversal. Everything before it sets up an expectation — a guess, a plan, a prediction — and everything after 反[はん]対[たい]に knocks that expectation down.

```jp
今日[きょう]は暑[あつ]いと思[おも]った。
反[はん]対[たい]に、とても寒[さむ]かった。
```
*I thought today would be hot.*
*On the contrary, it was very cold.*

You'll almost always see a comma right after 反[はん]対[たい]に in writing. It isn't required by any rule, but it marks the small pause before the reversal lands, and nearly everyone writes it that way. 反[はん]対[たい]に also shows up mid-sentence, right after a contrasting が or けど, doing the exact same job without starting a new sentence:

```jp
彼[かれ]は忙[いそが]しいと言[い]ったが、反[はん]対[たい]に暇[ひま]だった。
```
*He said he was busy, but on the contrary he was free.*

Here's the part that trips people up the first week: 反[はん]対[たい]に never conjugates. It isn't an adjective bending through forms, and it isn't a verb taking a tense. It sits frozen, exactly as you see it, whether the sentence around it is past, present, polite, or plain — only the sentence *following* 反[はん]対[たい]に carries tense and politeness.

That frozen shape is also what separates 反[はん]対[たい]に from the bare noun 反[はん]対[たい], which does show up on its own and means "opposed" or "against" — someone's stance, not a reversal of an expectation.

```jp
彼[かの]女[じょ]はその話[はなし]に反[はん]対[たい]だ。
```
*She is against that story.*

That sentence never sets up something to flip; it just states a position. 反[はん]対[たい]に only earns its place when the sentence has a "you'd think X, but actually Y" shape underneath it — no setup, no job for 反[はん]対[たい]に to do.

You'll also spot plain 反[はん]対[たい] sitting in front of a noun with の, as in 反[はん]対[たい]の意[い]見[けん] (the opposing opinion). That's still the ordinary noun doing ordinary noun-modification work — describing which opinion, not flipping a whole sentence — so don't let the shared kanji fool you into treating it like 反[はん]対[たい]に.

There's also a difference in *scope* worth noticing. 反[はん]対[たい]に reaches across the whole clause that follows it, not just the next word. In 反[はん]対[たい]に、とても寒[さむ]かった above, the reversal covers "it was very cold" as a complete idea — not just 寒[さむ]かった in isolation. That's part of why it can't glue onto a single adjective or verb the way a suffix would; it needs a full statement on the other side to reverse.

## Rules and exceptions

反[はん]対[たい]に needs two sides to work: the assumption, stated or implied, and the reversal it introduces. Drop the setup entirely and 反[はん]対[たい]に reads like a connector with nothing to connect — a reversal of nothing in particular.

> Don't reach for 反[はん]対[たい]に just because two facts happen to differ. It marks a genuine flip — heat turning to cold, "easy" turning into "hard" — not a second, unrelated detail tacked onto the first sentence.

This is also why 反[はん]対[たい]に almost never opens a conversation cold. It leans on something already said or already assumed — a forecast, a rumor, a first impression — and answers it. Say it with nothing behind it and a listener will wait for the part they missed, the expectation you're supposedly correcting.

A common beginner slip is trying to fuse 反[はん]対[たい]に directly onto the word before it, as if it were a suffix, something like `暑い反対に`. That's not how it behaves: 反[はん]対[たい]に always stands alone at the head of its own clause, never glued onto the adjective or verb next to it.

```jp
テストは簡[かん]単[たん]だと思[おも]ったが、反[はん]対[たい]にとても難[むずか]しかった。
```
*I thought the test would be easy, but on the contrary it was very difficult.*

Notice that the two halves genuinely oppose each other — 簡[かん]単[たん] and 難[むずか]しい are opposite qualities, not just two facts that happen to sit in the same sentence. That's the test worth running before you commit to 反[はん]対[たい]に: can you state the flipped expectation as a clean opposite? If not, a plain でも or しかし usually fits the sentence better.

It also helps to know what 反[はん]対[たい]に is *not* doing. It never explains a cause the way そのため does — そのため links a reason to its result ("it rained, so the game was cancelled"), while 反[はん]対[たい]に never tells you why anything happened. It only reports that the outcome ended up facing the other direction from what you expected. Reach for 反[はん]対[たい]に when you want to correct an assumption, not when you want to justify an outcome.

## Contrast: 反[はん]対[たい]に vs それでも

You already know それでも for "even so" — it keeps an action going despite an obstacle, without changing what actually happened. 反[はん]対[たい]に is a different animal entirely: it says the actual result flipped to the other side, not that something pushed through in spite of it.

```jp
雨[あめ]が降[ふ]っていた。
それでも、彼[かれ]は散[さん]歩[ぽ]した。
```
*It was raining.*
*Even so, he went for a walk.*

Here the rain never stopped, and the walk happened anyway — それでも just reports that the plan survived the obstacle. Now compare a scenario where the obstacle itself turns out to be the wrong guess:

```jp
雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ると思[おも]った。
反[はん]対[たい]に、いい天[てん]気[き]になった。
```
*I thought it would rain.*
*On the contrary, it turned into good weather.*

No walk, no obstacle overcome — the rain simply never happened, and something else took its place. That's the test to run in your head: if the expected thing still occurred and something pushed through it anyway, reach for それでも. If the expected thing just didn't happen, and its opposite did instead, reach for 反[はん]対[たい]に.

Swap the two connectors in either sentence above and you'd be describing a different day entirely. それでも in the second sentence would claim the rain came and someone still got good weather out of it, which makes no sense — the two facts can't coexist. That's the giveaway that these aren't stylistic alternatives; they're built for opposite jobs.

Predictions are wrong all the time — the weather, someone's mood, how a test goes. Now you have the word for saying so plainly, no hedging and no soft landing, just 反[はん]対[たい]に and the truth.

One habit worth building now: before you write 反[はん]対[たい]に, say the expectation out loud first, even silently. If you can't finish the sentence "I thought ___" before it, there's nothing for 反[はん]対[たい]に to reverse, and the sentence probably wants でも, しかし, or それでも instead. That one-second check is the whole rule, and it holds up in every example in this lesson.
caution_notes: 反対に needs a stated or implied expectation before it — without one, it has nothing to reverse and reads like an empty connector.
Don't confuse 反対に with bare 反対, which just states someone's opposition (話に反対だ) rather than reversing an expectation.
反対に never conjugates and never fuses onto the word before it — avoid a form like 暑い反対に.
反対に flips an outcome; it doesn't explain a cause, so don't use it where そのため (reason → result) is what you actually mean.

items.explanation_markdown:
You just moved apartments, and your friend spent the whole weekend hauling boxes, assembling furniture, and hanging your curtains while you mostly stood around handing them things. When they thank *you* for the help, you need to correct the record — fast, and with feeling. Plain Japanese has a word for exactly this job: こそ.

```jp
あなたこそ頑[がん]張[ば]りました。
```

*You're the one who really worked hard.*

こそ attaches to a noun and turns a flat statement into a pointed one. あなたは頑[がん]張[ば]りました just reports a fact — you worked hard, end of sentence. Swap は for こそ and the sentence stops being neutral: it singles あなた out, as if there were other candidates for the credit and you're ruling every one of them out but this person. That's the whole job of こそ — precisely this noun, not some other one.

## How it works

The pattern is simple: **Noun + こそ**. こそ takes the seat that は (or が, or を) would otherwise occupy — you don't stack it on top of them. It works on people, things, times, anywhere a noun can sit at the front of a sentence.

```jp
彼[かれ]こそ本[ほん]当[とう]の友[とも]達[だち]です。
```

*He is a true friend, if anyone is.*

Here 彼[かれ] isn't just being described — the sentence is answering an unspoken "who is actually a true friend?" and 彼[かれ] is the answer, full stop. That's the flavor こそ always carries: an implied lineup of candidates, with the noun before こそ walking away as the clear winner.

こそ also shows up glued onto から, and this combination is common enough to know cold: からこそ means "precisely *because*," pointing at a reason and insisting it's the real one.

```jp
忙[いそが]しいからこそ、休[やす]みたい。
```

*Precisely because I'm busy, I want to rest.*

Without こそ, 忙[いそが]しいから休[やす]みたい just states cause and effect. Add こそ and you're pushing back on an assumption — maybe someone expects that being busy means you *can't* rest, and you're insisting the opposite: busy is exactly *why* you need the break.

## Rules and exceptions

- こそ replaces は, が, and を on the noun it attaches to. You will never see `私はこそ` or `友達をこそ` — pick one or the other.
- こそ needs something to push against. It reads oddly on a sentence with no implied contrast or correction floating in the background — save it for moments where you're singling one thing out *from* others, not just stating a plain fact.
- こそ is register-neutral. It doesn't make a sentence more or less polite; です/ます still does that work on its own.

```jp
彼[かの]女[じょ]こそ真面目[まじめ]です。
```

*She is the one who's genuinely diligent.*

> Watch the difference between こそ and simply raising your voice on は in English. こそ isn't stress or volume — it's a grammatical word doing the singling-out, so it shows up in writing exactly the same way it does in speech.

## Contrast

Put は and こそ side by side and the gap is easy to feel.

```jp
今日[きょう]は忙[いそが]しいです。
```

*Today is busy.*

```jp
今日[きょう]こそ忙[いそが]しいです。
```

*Today, of all days, is busy.*

The は version is a plain report — nothing special about today. The こそ version implies other days weren't like this, or that today was supposed to be the easy one, and instead it turned out to be the busy one. Same words, same です ending, completely different weight.

That's really all こそ does — it doesn't change tense, it doesn't change politeness, it just points a finger. Later on you'll meet さえ, which points a finger in the opposite direction: it flags an extreme example ("even this") rather than the definite winner こそ picks out. For now, when you want to insist on one noun over every alternative, こそ is the tool.

```jp
私[わたし]こそありがとう。
```

*No, thank *you*.*
caution_notes: こそ replaces は, が, and を on the noun it attaches to — never stack it on top of those particles.
からこそ means "precisely because," not "even though" — it doubles down on a reason rather than conceding it.
こそ reads oddly without an implied contrast; use it only when you're singling one noun out from real or assumed alternatives.
こそ does not affect politeness — です/ます still control formality on their own.
