items.explanation_markdown:
You had one of those days. Meetings stacked on meetings, the train was late twice, and by the time you got home you realized you never sat down to eat. Not "skipped a snack" busy — *forgot breakfast existed* busy. That's the feeling さえ is built for: it doesn't just say something didn't happen, it says something so basic that its absence proves how bad things really were.

さえ attaches to a noun and means **even** — but not the casual "even" you'd use for a mild surprise. It marks the single most basic, most expected item on a list and says: not even *that* one. Everything harder than it is implied to have failed too. English does something similar when you say "I didn't even open my email today" — you're not really talking about email, you're using it as proof of how little else got done.

That's the intuition to hold onto: さえ isn't primarily about the noun it's attached to. It's a comment on everything else, delivered through the one item small enough to make the point unmissable. Pick the wrong item and the sentence stops working — "even the CEO showed up" only lands as extreme if the CEO is genuinely the person least likely to show; swap in someone who shows up every week and the whole sentence falls flat. さえ is honest that way: it only works when the noun really is the low bar.

## How it works

さえ sits right after the noun it's marking, and here's the part that trips people up: it *replaces* the particles that would normally mark subject or object — は, が, を all get pushed out. さえ takes their spot instead. There's no version where you keep the old particle and add さえ next to it; the noun only gets one marker, and さえ wins that slot.

```jp
私[わたし]は忙[いそが]しくて朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べる時[じ]間[かん]さえなかった。
```

*I was so busy I didn't even have time to eat breakfast.*

Notice 時[じ]間[かん] (じかん — the word for time) has no を or が in front of it. さえ took that slot. The sentence isn't just "I didn't have time" — it's naming *time to eat breakfast* specifically as the most basic thing you'd expect to have, and saying you didn't even have that. Everything you'd normally need more time for — the actual work, the actual errands — is left for the listener to imagine as even further out of reach.

```jp
彼[かれ]は漢[かん]字[じ]さえ知[し]らない。
```

*He doesn't even know kanji.*

Same shape: 漢[かん]字[じ] (かんじ) is the noun, さえ replaces what would have been を after 知[し]る (しる — to know), and the whole sentence reads as "kanji is the baseline you'd expect him to have, and he's below it." If you were describing someone's Japanese level and wanted to make clear it's close to zero, this is the sentence that does it in five words instead of a paragraph.

There's also a stronger version: さえも. It's the exact same job, just louder — you reach for it when even さえ feels too mild for how extreme the example is.

```jp
彼[かの]女[じょ]はお金[かね]さえも持[も]っていない。
```

*She doesn't even have money.*

Money not existing is already a strong claim about how bad things are; さえも underlines it. In practice さえ and さえも are interchangeable in most sentences — さえも just leans harder on the surprise, the way stressing the word "even" with your voice does in English. Neither one is more correct than the other; it's a volume knob, not a grammar switch. If you're not sure which to pick, plain さえ is the safer default — さえも is the one you reach for on purpose, when the plain version already feels too weak for the moment.

## Rules and exceptions

The particle-replacing behavior only applies to は, が, and を — the ones whose entire job is marking subject or object and carry no meaning of their own. Particles that carry their own meaning, like に (at/to) or で (at/by), don't get evicted; さえ stacks on top of them instead (にさえ, でさえ). You won't need those combinations yet, but it's worth knowing さえ doesn't erase every particle it meets — only the three that were just pointing at the noun anyway, with nothing else to say.

> さえ needs a noun to attach to. If what you actually want to mark is an entire *action* — "he didn't even try" rather than "he didn't even have money" — you're reaching for a different tool than the one covered here; don't force さえ onto a verb directly.

This is one of those places where the textbook rule is clean but the temptation to bend it is real — English "even" attaches to almost anything, verbs included, so the instinct to do the same in Japanese is strong. Resist it here; keep さえ anchored to a noun and build the sentence around that noun instead of trying to translate word for word.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]は私[わたし]の名[な]前[まえ]さえ忘[わす]れた。
```

*My friend even forgot my name.*

This is the shape learners get wrong first: they leave は or を sitting next to さえ out of habit — something like `友達は私の名前をさえ忘れた`. That を doesn't belong there. さえ already did its job of marking the noun; stacking the old particle back on top of it is redundant and reads as a mistake, not extra emphasis. The fix is simple once you see it: whichever particle さえ is replacing, just drop it and let さえ stand alone.

```jp
そのテストは簡[かん]単[たん]で、子[こ]供[ども]さえ分[わ]かった。
```

*That test was easy; even a child understood it.*

Here さえ is doing something slightly different — instead of marking an absence, it's marking the low end of a scale of ability. A child is the last person you'd expect to understand something, so if even they did, the test really was easy. Same particle, same logic, flipped from negative to positive: さえ doesn't care whether the sentence is "didn't happen" or "did happen," only that the noun it's attached to is the least likely candidate for whatever the verb describes. That's genuinely the whole rule — once you can name the "least likely candidate" in a scenario, さえ tells you exactly where to put it, and the rest of the sentence takes care of itself.

## Contrast

You already know こそ for emphasis — it singles out one item and says *this one, specifically, for sure*. さえ and こそ can look like cousins because they both replace は/が/を on a noun, but they're pointing in opposite directions. こそ picks the item you're *most* confident about; さえ picks the item you'd *least* expect to fail.

```jp
今日[きょう]こそ宿[しゅく]題[だい]をします。
```

*Today, of all days, I will do my homework.*

こそ here is a promise: out of every day you could pick, today is the one it's actually going to happen. It's confident, forward-looking, almost stubborn — "today, unlike every other day, I mean it." Compare that to what さえ does with the same day and the same homework, just a different outcome:

```jp
今日[きょう]は忙[いそが]しくて、宿[しゅく]題[だい]さえしなかった。
```

*Today I was so busy that I didn't even do my homework.*

Swap こそ for さえ in that first sentence and the meaning flips completely — from "today is the day I finally will" to "today wasn't even good enough for the bare minimum." Same slot, same particle family, opposite emotional weather. If you mix them up, you don't get a small nuance shift; you get the sentence claiming the opposite of what happened, so it's worth pausing for a beat before you pick one.

```jp
今[こん]週[しゅう]は忙[いそが]しくて、電[でん]話[わ]さえかけなかった。
```

*This week I was so busy that I didn't even make a phone call.*

That's the pattern doing its actual job: naming the smallest, easiest thing on the list and showing that even it didn't happen. It's a small particle carrying a lot of weight — one word standing in for a whole week you'd rather not describe in detail.

Hold onto that shape — once you meet さえ〜ば later, you'll see this same noun-marking さえ start pulling double duty inside a conditional, but that's a lesson for another day.
caution_notes: さえ replaces は, が, and を on the noun it marks — never stack the old particle back on top of it.
さえ attaches to a noun, not directly to a verb; it can't be used to mark an entire action on its own.
さえ and さえも are interchangeable in most sentences — さえも simply lands harder on the surprise.
さえ and こそ both replace は/が/を on a noun, but こそ marks confidence in the best case while さえ marks failure at the easiest case — swapping one for the other flips the meaning.

items.explanation_markdown:
You want to convince your friend that money is honestly the only thing standing between them and the trip they keep talking about — not the time off, not the planning, not their nerve, just the money. Every other excuse they've floated this week gets waved away; this is the one that actually blocks the door. In Japanese you reach for さえ〜ば, the pattern that names that one single thing and shrugs off everything else.

```jp
お金[かね]さえあれば、旅[りょ]行[こう]できます。
```
*If you just had the money, you could travel.*

That さえ is the same word you already met on its own, doing extreme-example work — *子[こ]供[ども]さえ知[し]っている* ("even a child knows"). Paired with a ば-form verb, though, it stops pointing at an extreme case and starts drawing a line: meet this one condition, and everything downstream of it is fine. Nothing else in the sentence gets to argue. It's a stronger, narrower claim than a plain "if" — a plain ば-conditional just describes one path among several; さえ〜ば insists there's only one path that matters.

## How it works

さえ attaches directly after a noun, and the verb after it takes its ば-form — the same ば you already use for ordinary "if" sentences, just with さえ wedged in front to say "as long as *just* this."

```jp
頑[がん]張[ば]る → 頑[がん]張[ば]れば
```

Swap in さえ before that ば-form and the meaning tightens from a general "if you try hard" to "as long as you *just* try hard — nothing more is needed." Nothing about the ば itself changes; さえ is simply riding in front of a conditional form you can already build on your own.

When the condition itself is an action rather than "if only I had this noun," さえ moves onto the verb's masu-stem, right before すれば. This is the shape you'll see most often in real speech, because most conditions people actually name are things to *do*, not things to *own* — study, rest, wait, try. Learners tend to reach for the noun pattern first because it's the one that gets taught first, but the verb pattern is doing more of the daily work once you start listening for it.

```jp
毎[まい]日[にち]勉[べん]強[きょう]さえすれば、試[し]験[けん]に合[ごう]格[かく]できます。
```
*As long as you just study every day, you'll pass the exam.*

Notice what the sentence is quietly refusing to say: it isn't claiming studying is easy, or that nothing else matters in life. It's claiming that, of everything that could go into passing this exam, daily study is the one piece that's load-bearing. Take that piece away and the rest collapses; keep it, and the rest doesn't need to be perfect. That's the real intuition behind さえ〜ば — it's less about the size of the requirement and more about which requirement is the last one standing between you and the outcome.

```jp
少[すこ]し休[やす]みさえすれば、元[げん]気[き]になります。
```
*As long as you just rest a little, you'll feel better.*

Same shape again — 休[やす]み is the masu-stem of 休[やす]む, so さえ sits between the stem and すれば exactly the way it did with 勉[べん]強[きょう]. Once you've drilled that one seam, さえ〜ば stops feeling like a new pattern and starts feeling like a small attachment you bolt onto ば-conditionals you already know. The stem itself never changes shape for さえ — you're not conjugating anything new, just inserting a particle into a slot that was always there.

## Rules and exceptions

The condition さえ marks has to be singular and real. Stacking a second さえ into the same clause to cover two conditions doesn't add them together — it just reads as a sentence that lost track of what it was arguing. Pick the one fact that's actually doing the work and say only that. If a situation genuinely has two independent requirements, さえ〜ば is the wrong tool; you'd need a plain list of conditions instead, without さえ narrowing either one.

> さえ〜ば and plain さえ look identical at a glance, but drop the ば and you've silently switched patterns. `お金さえある` with nothing after it just states "even money exists" — an extreme example, not a minimum requirement. The ば is what turns さえ from "even" into "as long as."

さえ〜ば also leans on the condition still being open. It works for things that could still go your way — study time still ahead of you, money you could still get. If the exam already happened and your friend already failed it, `勉強さえすれば良かった` reaching back at a closed door needs a different, past-tense shape than the plain さえ〜ば you're learning here; for now, keep さえ〜ば pointed at conditions that haven't been decided yet.

One more sharp edge: さえ〜ば doesn't promise the result is *guaranteed*, only that the named condition is *sufficient* in the speaker's mind. Someone else might disagree that money alone gets your friend on a plane — さえ〜ば is a claim about what the speaker believes is enough, not an objective law of the universe.

Politeness isn't a problem here either way: さえ〜ば sits comfortably in both casual conversation and formal speech, and nothing about it contracts or softens the way some other patterns do. You'll hear it from a teacher explaining an exam requirement just as readily as from a friend complaining about money, with the same shape both times.

## Contrast

You already know plain さえ for extreme examples — "even X," no ば, no minimum bar, just a case so far out that if it applies, everything milder must apply too.

```jp
子[こ]供[ども]さえ分[わ]かります。
```
*Even a child understands.*

```jp
時[じ]間[かん]さえあれば、大[だい]丈[じょう]夫[ぶ]です。
```
*As long as I just have time, I'll be fine.*

Line one says a child clears a low bar — proof that something is easy enough for anyone. Line two says time is the *only* bar left standing — proof that everything else is already handled and this single thing is what's missing. Same word, opposite job: one measures how extreme an example is, the other measures how little is actually required.

It helps to notice what each sentence is silently comparing against. Plain さえ is always measuring against a scale of difficulty — a child is near the easy end, so if even they can do it, anyone further up the scale can too. さえ〜ば isn't measuring difficulty at all; it's measuring completeness, checking off the last item on a short list of requirements.

```jp
辞[じ]書[しょ]さえあれば、言[こと]葉[ば]が分[わ]かります。
```
*As long as I just have a dictionary, I'll understand the words.*

Swap さえ〜ば for plain さえ in that last sentence and you'd get something closer to "even a dictionary — [and yet I still don't understand the words]," an entirely different, mildly frustrated sentence. The ば is doing almost all of the meaning here, which is worth sitting with the first few times you write one of these. When you're not sure which reading a sentence you hear is going for, listen for what comes after さえ: a ば-form verb means "as long as," anything else — a period, another particle, silence — means "even."

## Closing thought

Once you can hear さえ〜ば as "name the one thing, and only that thing," a lot of everyday bargaining in Japanese — with teachers, with friends, with yourself — starts making more sense. It's the pattern people reach for when they want to cut a messy situation down to a single, negotiable variable. Hold onto that narrowing instinct: you'll meet a stricter, more formal cousin of it soon in のみ.
caution_notes: さえ〜ば and plain さえ (the "even" sibling you already know) share the same word, but only the version paired with a ば-form verb draws a minimum-requirement line — drop the ば and you're back to a plain extreme example.
さえ attaches to a noun directly, but to a verb's masu-stem (not the dictionary form) when the condition is an action, right before すれば.
さえ〜ば only works while the condition is still open to happen — it doesn't reach back to fix something that's already been decided.
Stacking a second さえ into one clause doesn't combine two conditions; keep the sentence pointed at exactly one thing.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're standing in the lobby of a friend's company, waiting while they finish a call. A small sign by the elevator catches your eye: 社[しゃ]員[いん]のみ使[つか]えます. You can guess most of it — 社[しゃ]員[いん] is the staff, 使[つか]えます is "can use" — but that middle word, のみ, is doing something specific. It's not decoration. It's telling you, flatly, that this elevator has exactly one group of people who are allowed near it, and you are not one of them.

You could read the same sign a dozen different ways in casual speech — "just staff," "staff and nobody else," "sorry, employees only" — but whoever printed that sign didn't reach for any of those. They reached for one tight, formal word that does the whole job by itself.

## How it works

のみ means "only" or "nothing but," and it attaches straight onto a noun — no particle, no conjugation, nothing in between. Noun + のみ, and that noun becomes the one and only thing the sentence is willing to allow.

```jp
会[かい]社[しゃ]の入[いり]口[ぐち]は社[しゃ]員[いん]のみ使[つか]えます。
```

*Only employees can use the company entrance.*

Notice that のみ sits right where a particle like は or が might otherwise go, and the verb follows normally after it. You don't need to add anything to make the sentence work — のみ already carries the restriction on its own. Nothing before it, nothing after it, just the noun and the verb doing their normal jobs around it.

のみ also sits comfortably right before です, closing out a sentence the same way a regular noun would.

```jp
このレストランは現[げん]金[きん]のみです。
```

*This restaurant is cash only.*

Read that one out loud and you can hear why it works so well as signage: it's short, it's blunt, and there's no room to misread it. です is doing the same job it always does — wrapping up the sentence — and のみ has already done the work of narrowing "payment" down to one single option before です even gets there.

That's the shape you'll see most often: a rule, a policy, a sign — something written down, meant to be read rather than said out loud. A workplace posts a notice, a store prints a sign, an exam proctor hands out a printed instruction sheet, and every one of them reaches for のみ instead of anything looser.

```jp
試[し]験[けん]の間[あいだ]は日本[にほん]語[ご]のみ話[はな]せます。
```

*During the exam, only Japanese may be spoken.*

Same pattern each time: take the one noun that's allowed, drop のみ right after it, and let the rest of the sentence — a verb, です, whatever you need — carry on exactly as it would without のみ there at all. The grammar around it never has to change shape to make room.

## Rules and exceptions

のみ is formal, written-register Japanese — it belongs to the same world as printed rules and official announcements, not to a conversation between friends. You'll meet it constantly in signs, contracts, and business writing, and almost never hear it in someone's casual speech about their own day.

> Don't reach for のみ when you're just chatting. Saying `これのみ食べた` to a friend about your lunch sounds like you're reading from a memo, not describing a sandwich.

That stiffness is the whole point of the word, not a flaw in it. A company doesn't want its entrance policy to sound warm and conversational — it wants it to sound like a rule, and のみ carries exactly that weight. Once you can hear that formality, you'll start noticing のみ everywhere: on ticket machines, in contracts, on the fine print under a store's opening hours.

This lesson only covers のみ attached directly to a noun, which is by far the form you'll need most at this level. It can also attach after other things in more advanced writing, but treat that as a different problem for a different day — for now, noun first, のみ right after it, nothing in between. Resist the urge to bolt it onto a verb the way you might with some other patterns; at this stage, keep it a noun's word.

## Contrast

You already know 以[い]外[がい] for "except" — it pulls one thing *out* of a group and leaves the rest standing. のみ does the opposite: it throws everything out except the one thing it names.

```jp
日[にち]曜[よう]日[び]以[い]外[がい]は毎[まい]日[にち]仕[し]事[ごと]です。
```

*Every day except Sunday is work.*

```jp
日[にち]曜[よう]日[び]のみ休[やす]みます。
```

*I only rest on Sunday.*

Same subject, same week, completely different shape of sentence. 以[い]外[がい] tells you what's left after removing one day from the group; のみ tells you that one day is all there is, full stop. Swap one for the other in either sentence and the meaning flips almost entirely — worth sitting with that pair until the difference feels automatic.

さえ makes a different kind of point. It picks an extreme example to prove how easy or how surprising something is — "even a beginner could do this." のみ never argues that way; it just draws a hard line around who's allowed in, with no interest in surprising you.

```jp
この仕[し]事[ごと]は大人[おとな]のみできます。
```

*Only adults can do this job.*

```jp
この仕[し]事[ごと]は子[こ]供[ども]さえできます。
```

*Even children can do this job.*

Same job, same verb, and the two sentences say almost opposite things about how demanding the work is. 大人[おとな]のみ makes it sound like it takes real skill, something only a narrow group can manage; 子[こ]供[ども]さえ makes it sound so simple that even the least likely candidate can pull it off.

Sign-language のみ and this さえ trick don't fight for the same space — you'll usually know which one you need from the tone of what you're writing, not from the vocabulary itself. If you're posting a rule, reach for のみ. If you're making a point about how easy or surprising something is, reach for さえ instead.

That elevator sign wasn't being rude. It was just doing what のみ always does — naming one group and closing the door on everyone else, briefly and without apology. Hold onto that flat, no-exceptions feel; you'll want it again once we get to ほかない, where "there's no choice but to" carries the same refusal to budge.
caution_notes: のみ is formal, written-register Japanese — using it in ordinary conversation sounds like you're reading from a notice board.
This lesson's のみ attaches directly after a noun with nothing in between; don't insert a particle before it.
のみ and 以外 point in opposite directions: 以外 removes one thing from a group, while のみ keeps nothing but that one thing.
Don't confuse のみ with さえ: さえ reaches for an extreme example to make a point, it doesn't wall off who's allowed to do something.

items.explanation_markdown:
It's past midnight and you're standing outside the station. The gate is shut, the trains have stopped for the night, and the one taxi that passed didn't slow down. Your phone is dead, so calling anyone is out. Home is a long way off on foot, but there is genuinely nothing else left to try. The Japanese sentence that fits this exact feeling is short:

```jp
歩[ある]いて帰[かえ]るほかない。
```
*I have no choice but to walk home.*

ほかない takes a situation where every other option has been stripped away and names the one that remains. It isn't a preference and it isn't advice. It's the last door still open, and you're walking through it only because the rest are locked.

## How it works

The build is about as plain as N4 grammar gets. Take a verb in its plain **dictionary form** (the shape you'd look up in a dictionary — 行[い]く, 待[ま]つ, 帰[かえ]る) and attach ほかない straight onto the end. Nothing changes shape, nothing conjugates.

```jp
行[い]く → 行[い]くほかない
```
*go → have no choice but to go*

The ほか in there is the ordinary noun meaning "other", the one you already know from 他[ほか]の人[ひと], "other people". The ない on the end is just the negative of ある, "to exist". Put literally, the phrase says "(doing this) — there is no other". No other road, no other move. Once that literal picture is in your head, the meaning stops needing to be memorised.

Here is the station scene filled out a little more:

```jp
電[でん]車[しゃ]が止[と]まったから、駅[えき]で待[ま]つほかない。
```
*Since the trains have stopped, I have no choice but to wait at the station.*

And a weekend version — the kind of Sunday where the plan quietly falls apart:

```jp
今日[きょう]は雨[あめ]だから、家[いえ]にいるほかない。
```
*It's raining today, so I have no choice but to stay home.*

For a polite context — speaking with a teacher or a customer, or writing a formal email — swap ない for ありません. The meaning is identical; only the register moves up.

```jp
彼[かれ]に謝[あやま]るほかありません。
```
*I have no choice but to apologize to him.*

Those two endings, ほかない and ほかありません, are the entire toolkit you need here. There is no past-tense or negated version to learn for this course.

## Rules and exceptions

The attachment point is strict: a **plain dictionary-form verb**, and nothing else. Not the past, not the negative, not the polite ます-stem, and not a noun or a na-adjective standing on its own.

- `行ったほかない` — wrong; the past tense doesn't belong here
- `行きますほかない` — wrong; no polite stem in front of it
- `学生ほかない` — wrong; ほかない doesn't clip onto a bare noun like this

If what you want is "there's no choice but *this thing*" with a noun, you need a different construction. ほかない is built for actions, not objects.

> ほかない is not emotionally neutral. It carries a clear undertone of *this is not what I wanted*. If the outcome actually suits you, or you're choosing it freely, ほかない will sound strangely bleak. Keep it for the forced hand.

Because the reason for the trap usually matters, ほかない very often follows a から or ので clause, or a なら. The clause before explains why the other options are gone; the pattern delivers what that leaves you with.

```jp
誰[だれ]も来[こ]ないなら、一人[ひとり]でするほかない。
```
*If no one comes, I'll have no choice but to do it alone.*

## Register and small variations

This is a formal pattern with a written feel. You'll meet it in newspaper opinion pieces, in reports, in a manager passing on a decision that's already been made. Between friends, Japanese speakers usually pick something lighter, so don't sprinkle ほかない through casual conversation.

You may also see は slipped in for weight: ほかはない. It's the same pattern with a little more stress on the "no other" part — nothing new, just a form to recognise.

When the situation is about redoing something from scratch, the pattern still simply clips onto the dictionary form:

```jp
もう一[いち]度[ど]やり直[なお]すほかない。
```
*There's nothing for it but to start over once more.*

## Up against のみ

The closest thing you've already learned is のみ, the formal "only". Both narrow the field to a single item, so they can feel swappable — until you actually swap them and watch the meaning tilt.

のみ is a flat statement of fact: *this and nothing else*, with no feeling attached. It sits on a noun.

```jp
待[ま]つのみだ。
```
*There is only waiting.*

ほかない sits on a verb and adds the resignation: *every other option is gone, so this one is forced on me*.

```jp
待[ま]つほかない。
```
*There's no choice but to wait.*

"There is only waiting" can be calm, even disciplined — an athlete steadying themselves before a result. "There's no choice but to wait" is someone who wanted to act and can't. Same corner, different feeling. Want the bare fact? Use のみ. Want the trapped feeling? Use ほかない.

## The one-line version

ほかない = plain dictionary verb + "and there is no other move" — the single option left standing once the rest have been ruled out. When we reach 上[うえ]で later, you'll see the other side of this: settling on a course *after* weighing everything, instead of being handed only one.
caution_notes: Attach ほかない only to a plain dictionary-form verb, never to a past, negative, or polite stem, and never to a bare noun or na-adjective.
Use only ほかない or the polite ほかありません; this course has no past or negated version of the ending.
ほかない carries a note of reluctance, so avoid it for an option you actually want or choose freely.
The pattern is formal and written-leaning, so reach for something lighter in casual conversation.

items.explanation_markdown:
You check the weather app, and the little train icon has gone red. A storm rolled through overnight, and the line into the city is dead. Someone asks why you are late, and you need to name the thing that caused the shutdown — not a person who decided it, but an event that forced it.

```jp
台[たい]風[ふう]によって、電[でん]車[しゃ]が止[と]まった。
```

*The trains stopped because of the typhoon.*

That is によって. You take a noun — here 台[たい]風[ふう] — and attach によって straight onto it to say 'because of this', 'by means of this', or 'through this'. It points at the thing sitting behind an outcome.

## How it works

The structure is as plain as it looks: a noun, then によって. Nothing sits between them — no の, no な, no です. If you can name it as a noun, you can feed it in.

によって does four related jobs, and they all grow from a single idea: the noun is the source or the pivot of whatever follows.

**Cause.** An event or a force produces a result. This is the 'because of' reading, and you meet it constantly in news, announcements, and any moment you want to sound a little formal about a cause.

```jp
地[じ]震[しん]によって、たくさんの家[いえ]が壊[こわ]れた。
```

*The earthquake destroyed many houses.*

In stiffer writing — signs, reports, official notices — によって tightens to により. It is the same word clipped short, not a new one: same meaning, drier tone, nothing else changes.

```jp
台[たい]風[ふう]によって → 台[たい]風[ふう]により
```

*'Because of the typhoon', then the same phrase in its formal form.*

**Means or method.** The noun is the tool or the process that gets something done. Here によって sits close to で ('with', 'using'), but it frames the noun as a whole procedure — a negotiation, a vote, a piece of research — rather than a single object in someone's hand.

```jp
会[かい]議[ぎ]によって、新[あたら]しい予[よ]定[てい]が決[き]まった。
```

*The new schedule was settled through the meeting.*

**The doer in a passive sentence.** When a sentence is passive and you want to name who actually performed the action, によって marks that person. The reason is bookish: older Japanese built its passives this way, and formal modern writing kept the habit. You see it most with verbs of making and writing.

```jp
彼[かの]女[じょ]は祖[そ]母[ぼ]によって育[そだ]てられた。
```

*She was raised by her grandmother.*

```jp
この歌[うた]は有[ゆう]名[めい]な人[ひと]によって作[つく]られた。
```

*This song was made by a famous person.*

**'Depending on'.** The noun is a variable, and the rest of the sentence shifts as that variable shifts. This is the reading people miss, because English often leaves the second half implied. Japanese does not — the sentence has to end on something that moves, a word like 変[か]わる.

```jp
人[ひと]によって意[い]見[けん]が変[か]わる。
```

*Opinions vary from one person to the next.*

## Rules and exceptions

The noun attaches bare. Learners fresh from drilling noun-modifying の sometimes write `地震のによって` — cut that の. It is always 地[じ]震[しん]によって.

For the passive 'by', ordinary speech usually just uses に. If your teacher praises you, in conversation that is 先[せん]生[せい]に褒[ほ]められた, not 先[せん]生[せい]によって褒[ほ]められた. Save によって for formal writing, or for verbs of creation like 作[つく]る and 書[か]く, where a plain に can read as a location rather than a person.

> により is not a casual option. It belongs to written and spoken formality: reports, ceremonies, the station announcement itself. Drop it into a chat with a friend and you sound like you are reading aloud from a manual.

```jp
地[じ]震[しん]により、たくさんの人[ひと]が困[こま]った。
```

*The earthquake left many people in difficulty.*

One more trap: によって in the 'depending on' sense needs a real outcome clause. 'Depending on the person' is not a finished thought in Japanese any more than in English — you have to say what actually changes.

## Contrast

The closest thing you already know in this register is のみ, the formal 'only'. のみ and により surface in the same places — notices, forms, official writing — and both sound wrong across a dinner table. Their jobs differ: のみ narrows the field to a single option, while により points at a cause or a means.

```jp
この問[もん]題[だい]は会[かい]議[ぎ]により無[な]くなった。
```

*This problem went away through a meeting.*

```jp
この店[みせ]は現[げん]金[きん]のみ使[つか]える。
```

*This shop takes cash only.*

Swap the two and the sentences break: `会議のみ無くなった` would say 'only the meeting disappeared', and `現金により使える` would say 'usable by means of cash', which is not what a sign wants to tell you. A quick check: if the English slot takes 'only', you want のみ; if it takes 'because of' or 'by', you want により.

## One line to keep

によって hooks onto a noun to name the cause, the method, or the doer behind an outcome — により when the register is formal. Later you meet 上[うえ]で, another buttoned-up connector, where the noun is a step you finish before moving on rather than the force driving the result.
caution_notes: Attach によって straight to the noun — write 地震によって, never 地震のによって.
により is only the formal, written contraction of によって; keep it out of casual conversation.
For 'by' in an everyday passive, plain に is normal (先生に褒められた); によって suits formal writing and creation verbs like 作る and 書く.
In the 'depending on' sense, によって still needs an outcome clause that actually changes, such as one ending in 変わる.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're lacing up your shoes to run to the convenience store before it closes. Your sister leans out of the kitchen: the fridge is empty, can you grab milk? You're already going out the door. You don't want to make the trip twice, and Japanese has one word for exactly this 'since I'm heading there anyway' move: ついでに.

```jp
コンビニに行[い]くついでに、牛[ぎゅう]乳[にゅう]を買[か]ってくる。
```

*While I'm going to the convenience store, I'll pick up some milk.*

The main mission is the convenience store. The milk is a rider — something small you fold into a trip you were making regardless. That is the whole feel of ついでに: one primary action, and a second, lighter action that gets a free ride on it. The two are not equal partners, and that imbalance is the point.

## How it works

ついでに attaches in two ways, depending on what sits in front of it.

**Dictionary-form verb + ついでに.** The verb names the trip or task you're already committed to. Attach ついでに straight onto the plain dictionary form — nothing comes between them.

```jp
駅[えき]まで歩[ある]くついでに、手[て]紙[がみ]を出[だ]す。
```

*While I'm walking to the station, I'll mail the letter.*

Walking to the station is happening no matter what. Mailing the letter is the passenger. Watch the order: the action you were already doing comes first, then ついでに, then the add-on. A comma after ついでに is normal and helps the reader feel the seam.

**Noun + の + ついでに.** When the occasion is naturally a noun — shopping, a walk, a work trip — join it with の.

```jp
買[か]い物[もの]のついでに、図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で本[ほん]を返[かえ]す。
```

*While I'm out shopping, I'll return the books at the library.*

Here 買[か]い物[もの] is the trip and returning the library books is the extra stop. する-verbs give you a choice: you can treat 掃[そう]除[じ] as a bare noun (掃[そう]除[じ]のついでに) or use the full verb (掃[そう]除[じ]するついでに). Both are fine and mean the same thing.

```jp
台[だい]所[どころ]を掃[そう]除[じ]するついでに、冷[れい]蔵[ぞう]庫[こ]も洗[あら]う。
```

*While I'm cleaning the kitchen, I'll wash out the fridge too.*

The も on 冷[れい]蔵[ぞう]庫[こ] is doing quiet work — it says 'this one as well, on top of the kitchen.' ついでに and も are natural partners, because the pattern is fundamentally about adding one more thing.

## Rules and exceptions

**The add-on has to be the smaller thing.** ついでに only sounds right when the second action is minor next to the first. If the second action is really your main goal, a listener will be puzzled.

```jp
会[かい]社[しゃ]から帰[かえ]るついでに、スーパーで野[や]菜[さい]を買[か]う。
```

*On my way home from work, I'll buy vegetables at the supermarket.*

Going home is the big fixed event; buying vegetables is slipped inside it. Flip the weights — if the shopping were the real reason you left — and ついでに becomes the wrong tool.

**Same person on both halves.** ついでに is not 'two people doing things at the same moment.' Whoever makes the trip is the one who does the extra task.

**Both actions share one occasion.** You can't use ついでに to staple together two errands from different days or separate trips. It is one outing, one stretch of being out, with an opportunity taken inside it.

> After a verb, ついでに clamps directly onto the dictionary form. Learners who just met the noun pattern sometimes carry the の across and write `行くのついでに` — that extra の is wrong. Only nouns take の.

One honest note: in relaxed speech you'll sometimes hear the の dropped after a noun as well, as in `買い物ついでに`. It is casual and common, but の is the standard choice and the one to write.

## Contrast

Your recent particles — こそ, さえ, のみ — all *narrow* or *spotlight*. のみ in particular means 'only this, nothing else.'

```jp
今日[きょう]は郵[ゆう]便[びん]局[きょく]のみ行[い]く。
```

*Today I'll go only to the post office.*

ついでに pulls the opposite way. It doesn't trim the list down to one; it adds a second thing onto the single trip you were already taking.

```jp
郵[ゆう]便[びん]局[きょく]に行[い]くついでに、銀[ぎん]行[こう]にもお金[かね]を出[だ]す。
```

*While I'm at the post office, I'll also take out money at the bank.*

Same starting point — a trip to the post office — but のみ shuts the door on anything else, while ついでに props it open for one more stop. If you catch yourself reaching for 'only,' ついでに is not what you want.

```jp
病[びょう]院[いん]に行[い]くついでに、薬[やっ]局[きょく]で薬[くすり]をもらう。
```

*While I'm going to the hospital, I'll get medicine at the pharmacy.*

The hospital visit is settled; the pharmacy is a few steps out of the way and costs you nothing extra. That is the situation ついでに is built for.

## Closing

ついでに = one trip you were making anyway, plus a small extra thing you fold into it. Attach it to a dictionary-form verb directly, or to a noun with の.

Hold onto this 'in the middle of an action' feeling. Soon you'll meet 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に, which sounds close in English but runs the other way — it's about being caught right in the thick of something, not about picking up a bonus errand on the side.
caution_notes: ついでに only fits when the two actions belong to the same outing — it cannot link errands done on separate trips.
The tacked-on action must be the minor one; if it is your real goal, ついでに sounds wrong.
Attach ついでに straight to a dictionary-form verb — writing 行くのついでに with an extra の is an error, since only nouns take の.
Keep one subject across both halves; ついでに never means two people acting at the same time.

items.explanation_markdown:
You are three days from moving into a new apartment. The agent slides a contract across the table, taps the signature line, and asks for your decision right now. You are not going to say yes on the spot. You want to read every clause first — the deposit, the notice period, the penalty for leaving early — and commit only once you have seen all of it. In a message to a friend you would use a plain, casual 'after' for this and move on. But a rental office is a formal room, and Japanese keeps a separate, more buttoned-up tool for exactly this thought: 'I will do the real thing, but only once this first step is properly finished.' That tool is 〜た上[うえ]で.

```jp
書[しょ]類[るい]を全[ぜん]部[ぶ]読[よ]んだ上[うえ]で、決[き]めます。
```

*I will decide after I have read all the documents.*

Everything about the pattern is sitting in that one line. There is a finished first action — reading the documents — then the connector 上[うえ]で, then the action the sentence is really about: deciding. The first half is preparation you take on yourself. The second half is the payoff. 上[うえ]で tells your listener that the second thing is not happening loosely or by luck; it happens on the foundation of the first thing being done.

It helps to know where the phrase comes from. 上[うえ] is the word for 'up' or 'on top of', and this pattern is that image made abstract: the second action stands on top of the completed first one, the way a next floor stands on the one below. Once you see that picture, the formal 'on the basis of' sense stops feeling arbitrary.

## How it works

Put the first action into the plain past — the ta-form — and attach 上[うえ]で directly to it. The main clause follows.

```jp
読[よ]む → 読[よ]んだ上[うえ]で
```

```jp
話[はな]し合[あ]う → 話し合[はなしあ]った上[うえ]で
```

Here is the same move in slow motion:

- Start with the verb for the preparatory action: 読[よ]む.
- Shift it to the plain past: 読[よ]んだ.
- Attach 上[うえ]で with nothing in between: 読[よ]んだ上[うえ]で.
- Add the main clause — the decision, the reply, the purchase.

The join is tight: no comma inside 読[よ]んだ上[うえ]で, no particle, no breath.

Why the ta-form specifically? Because 上[うえ]で treats that first action as complete — not in progress, not skipped over, but genuinely wrapped up — and then stacks the second action on top of it. That is exactly why a dictionary form (`読む上で`) or a te-form (`読んで上で`) will not carry this meaning: neither of them says 'this part is already done.'

Since the first clause is groundwork, the two halves belong to the same person, and both are things that person chooses to do. Think of yourself giving a careful answer to something that matters — a job offer, an expensive purchase, a decision that affects your family. You do the checking first, on purpose, and your answer waits for it.

```jp
家[か]族[ぞく]とよく話し合[はなしあ]った上[うえ]で、お答[こた]えします。
```

*I will give you my answer once I have talked it over properly with my family.*

```jp
医[い]者[しゃ]に聞[き]いた上[うえ]で、薬[くすり]を飲[の]みます。
```

*I will take the medicine after checking with the doctor.*

The main clause does not have to point at the future. It often does, because you are usually laying out a plan, but you can just as easily report something you have already finished in this same deliberate, step-by-step way.

```jp
説[せつ]明[めい]を聞[き]いた上[うえ]で、申[もう]し込[こ]みました。
```

*I applied after hearing the explanation.*

There is also a noun version, for nouns that name a process — a discussion, a survey, an application, an inspection. Add の, then 上[うえ]で.

```jp
調[ちょう]査[さ]の上[うえ]で、結[けっ]果[か]を伝[つた]えます。
```

*We will report the results after the investigation.*

## Rules and exceptions

What can sit in front of this 上[うえ]で is narrow: a ta-form verb, or a process noun plus の. Nothing else fits the slot.

> `読む上で` and `読んで上で` are both wrong for the 'having done X' meaning. It has to be 読[よ]んだ上[うえ]で.

Both actions have to be deliberate and within your control, because the entire point of 上[うえ]で is that you arranged the order on purpose. It falls apart when the first 'action' is really something that happened to you — the weather turning, a train running late, a mistake you never meant to make. For those you want an ordinary 'after' or 'because', not this pattern.

```jp
試[し]験[けん]を受[う]けた上[うえ]で、結[けっ]果[か]を待[ま]ちます。
```

*Having sat the exam, I will wait for the results.*

Sitting the exam is a chosen step; waiting is what follows from it. That is the shape 上[うえ]で is built for.

One more limit worth naming: the first clause is a single completed action, not an ongoing state. You would not use it for something like being tired or knowing a fact — those are conditions, not steps you finish and move on from. If you cannot picture a clean moment where the first action is over and the second one begins, the pattern is probably the wrong choice, and a simpler 'after' or 'because' will serve you better.

Register matters here as well. This construction is formal, and it leans written: contracts, official notices, business email, a measured spoken reply in a meeting. Part of why formal Japanese reaches for it is that it makes the groundwork explicit — it says the decision rests on a proper basis, that the right step was taken before the outcome. Drop the same phrase into a relaxed conversation and it sounds starched. Among friends, a plain 'after' gives you the same sequence with none of the stiffness.

> Do not mix this 上[うえ]で up with the plain, everyday 上[うえ]で that means 'on top of a surface' — 机[つくえ]の上[うえ]で書[か]く, 'to write on the desk'. That one needs a physical place and carries no sense of one action ending before another begins. Same two characters, unrelated grammar.

## Against ついでに

You already know ついでに, the 'while I am at it' pattern. It also lines up two actions, but it faces the opposite way. With ついでに, the first action is already happening for its own reasons, and you tack the second one on because it costs you almost nothing — you would never make a special trip just for it.

```jp
買[か]い物[もの]のついでに、郵[ゆう]便[びん]局[きょく]で切[きっ]手[て]を買[か]います。
```

*While I am out shopping anyway, I will buy stamps at the post office.*

上[うえ]で is the mirror image. The first action is a step you take on purpose, precisely so the second one can be done properly.

```jp
値[ね]段[だん]をよく考[かんが]えた上[うえ]で、買[か]います。
```

*I will buy it after thinking the price over carefully.*

Swap the two patterns and the meaning lurches. 買[か]い物[もの]をした上[うえ]で、切[きっ]手[て]を買[か]います comes out sounding as though you treated a whole shopping trip as a formal precondition for buying stamps — a strange thing to claim. If the second action is a small add-on, you need ついでに. If the first action is a real prerequisite that you completed deliberately, you need 上[うえ]で.

There is a tone difference too. ついでに is light and a little informal — it works fine in casual speech, and it often carries a shrug, as if the extra task barely counts. 上[うえ]で is the opposite: it is weighty and careful, the language of someone signalling that they did not rush. Reaching for 上[うえ]で when you mean ついでに makes a trivial errand sound like a solemn procedure, and the reverse makes a serious step sound careless. Matching the pattern to how much the first action actually mattered is most of getting this right.

## One line to keep

A ta-form plus 上[うえ]で means 'having finished that, and on the strength of it, now this' — deliberate groundwork, then the real move, in a formal voice. Hold onto the timing, because the next pattern you will meet, 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に, marks the opposite moment: not once a step is done, but right in the middle of one that is still going.
caution_notes: Use only a plain-past (ta-form) verb or a process noun plus の before this 上で; a dictionary form or te-form is wrong for the 'having done X' meaning.
Both clauses must share one subject and be deliberate, controllable actions, not accidents or events like weather or delays.
The pattern is formal and mostly written; in casual conversation a plain 'after' is used instead.
This sequence 上で is unrelated to the everyday 上で meaning 'on top of a surface' despite the shared characters.

items.explanation_markdown:
You are three minutes into your slot at the weekly meeting. People have finally put their laptops down, you have reached the part that actually matters, and your phone goes off in your pocket — loudly, so everyone hears it. That exact feeling, an action already rolling along and something barging straight into it, is what 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に is built to describe.

```jp
会[かい]議[ぎ]の最[さい]中[ちゅう]に、携[けい]帯[たい]が鳴[な]った。
```

*My phone rang right in the middle of the meeting.*

最[さい]中[ちゅう] (さいちゅう) on its own is a noun. It is written with the characters for *most* and *middle*, and that is a good picture of it: not the start, not the end, but the busiest, most-in-it middle of something that is underway. Add に and you get a time expression that frames one action as getting interrupted — you were deep in the middle of X, and then Y happened.

## How it works

Only two things attach to 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に, and both of them describe something that is genuinely in progress. Very often the same situation can be built either way; the noun version is shorter, and the verb version pins down exactly which part of the activity you were in.

**A noun plus の.** Pick a noun that names an activity with a clear beginning and end — a meeting, a meal, a class, an exam, a phone call — and join it on with の.

```jp
食[しょく]事[じ]の最[さい]中[ちゅう]に、社[しゃ]長[ちょう]から電[でん]話[わ]が来[き]た。
```

*A call from the company president came in right in the middle of dinner.*

The noun carries the whole span by itself. 食[しょく]事[じ] already means the act of having a meal, so 食[しょく]事[じ]の最[さい]中[ちゅう]に is at the busiest point of that meal. No verb needed.

**A verb in its ている form.** ている is the shape Japanese uses for an action in progress — the piece that works like the *-ing* in an English word like eating. 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に insists on that shape, and the reason is simple: 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に points at a midpoint, and only an ongoing action *has* a midpoint you can stand inside. A dictionary form is the whole action as an idea; a past form is the action already finished. Neither one has a middle to be in. So take the plain verb, move it into ている, then add 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に.

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べている最[さい]中[ちゅう]に
```

*eat → in the middle of eating*

```jp
昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べている最[さい]中[ちゅう]に、部[ぶ]長[ちょう]が来[き]た。
```

*The department head showed up right in the middle of my lunch.*

```jp
映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ている最[さい]中[ちゅう]に、地[じ]震[しん]が起[お]きた。
```

*An earthquake hit right in the middle of the movie.*

Look at how each of these sentences ends: 来[き]た, 起[お]きた, 鳴[な]った. Every time, something lands on the scene from outside. That is not a coincidence — it is the heart of the pattern, so it gets its own section.

## The interruption rule

The grammar note for this point is one word: *interruption*. 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に does more than place two things at the same time. It says the first action was cruising along and the second one cut across it — nearly always as a surprise, and usually as a nuisance.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]と電[でん]話[わ]している最[さい]中[ちゅう]に、赤[あか]ちゃんが泣[な]いた。
```

*The baby cried right in the middle of my phone call with a friend.*

You were on the call. The crying was not on your schedule. That gap — between what you were calmly doing and what suddenly grabbed your attention — is what a listener hears the moment you say 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に. Picture the same shape anywhere: mid-exam and a phone starts ringing two desks over; halfway through cooking dinner and someone is at the door. The pattern is waiting for the thing that breaks in.

> If the second half of your sentence is calm and expected — you drank your tea, you carried on reading your book — 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に is the wrong tool. The pattern promises that a disruption is coming. If nothing disrupts anything, choose another way to say while.

## Rules and exceptions

**The front part has to be genuinely ongoing.** This is where people slip first. You cannot hang 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に off a plain dictionary form or a plain past form — `食べる最中に` and `食べた最中に` are both wrong. For a verb it is always the ている form: 食[た]べている最[さい]中[ちゅう]に. For a noun it is always noun + の: 食[しょく]事[じ]の最[さい]中[ちゅう]に.

**It marks one stretch of activity, not a long era.** 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に fits an afternoon of work, a single conversation, one exam. It does not fit the whole of summer or your years at university. Stretch the span that wide and a native speaker simply will not use 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に here — it sounds like you are trying to fold a whole season into one afternoon.

**Both halves share one timeframe.** The interrupting event has to fall *inside* the span of the first action — not in the seconds before it begins, not just after it wraps up. If your friend called the moment the meeting ended, that is not 会[かい]議[ぎ]の最[さい]中[ちゅう]に.

**The pattern never bends for politeness.** 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に sits in the middle of the sentence and stays frozen. All the politeness work happens on the final verb: 鳴[な]った in casual writing, 鳴[な]りました in polite speech, with 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に unchanged in between.

## Contrast with what you already know

**ついでに — while I'm at it.** You met this one recently, and it is the pattern most likely to be confused with 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に, because both land in English as while.

```jp
買[か]い物[もの]のついでに、銀[ぎん]行[こう]にも行[おこな]った。
```

*While I was out shopping, I also went to the bank.*

ついでに means: I am already doing A, so I will attach B and knock both out in one trip. B is a bonus, and *you* chose it. 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に has the opposite temperament — you did not choose the second event, it landed on you and broke your flow. Swap them in the sentence above (買[か]い物[もの]の最[さい]中[ちゅう]に、銀[ぎん]行[こう]に行[い]った) and it turns odd, as though going to the bank were an ambush that wrecked your shopping. ついでに is tidy multitasking; 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に is your activity getting hijacked.

**上[うえ]で — after / on the basis of.** Also recent, also about two events, but 上[うえ]で lines them up in a deliberate order.

```jp
よく考[かんが]えた上[うえ]で、答[こた]えます。
```

*I'll give you an answer after I've thought it over carefully.*

上[うえ]で takes a た-form and says: A is finished, and standing on that result I now do B. It is planned and sequential. 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に is neither — the two events overlap, and the second one shows up with no warning. One pattern is A is done, therefore B; the other is B crashed into A while A was still going.

A quick field test: if you can retell the sentence in English as *just as I was doing X — and then, bang — Y*, 最[さい]中[ちゅう]に fits. If the natural English is and also, or and then as planned, it does not.

## Recap

最[さい]中[ちゅう]に = a ている verb or a noun + の, followed by something that jolts that action from outside. Build the first half as an action still in motion, and make the second half land hard. If nothing gets interrupted, you want a different pattern.
caution_notes: Attach 最中に only to a verb in its ている form or to a noun plus の, never to a plain dictionary or past form.
The clause after 最中に should be a sudden, usually unwelcome event, not a calm or planned action.
Use 最中に for a single ongoing activity, not for a long span such as a whole season or several years.
The interrupting event must fall inside the first action's timeframe, not just before it starts or after it ends.

items.explanation_markdown:
You are at a counter filling out a form, and the clerk taps two empty boxes: one for your name, one for your address. In conversation you would say 名[な]前[まえ]と住[じゅう]所[しょ] and be done. But the printed label on the sheet says 名[な]前[まえ]および住[じゅう]所[しょ]. Same meaning — "name and address" — just wearing a suit.

および is the word formal written Japanese uses to join two nouns into a pair. Think of it as the と of contracts, public notices, instruction sheets, and announcements: the register where every word is chosen with care.

```jp
名[な]前[まえ]および住[じゅう]所[しょ]を、ここに書[か]いてください。
```

*Please write your name and address here.*

Drop that line onto a government form and nobody would blink.

## How it works

The shape is exactly what it looks like: **Noun + および + Noun**. A noun on the left, a noun on the right, and および welds them into a single unit that the rest of the sentence then handles as one thing.

The conjugation information you were handed is only `{"formal_conjunction": true}`. That is the system's way of saying there is nothing to conjugate. および has one form, および, forever — no past, no negative, no politeness levels. The formality is baked in and never moves.

One consequence of "the pair acts as one unit" is worth slowing down for. The particle that says what the pair is doing in the sentence — は for the topic, が for the subject, を for the object, に for the target — lands **after the second noun**, never between the two. The nouns join first; the particle comes second.

```jp
会[かい]議[ぎ]の場[ば]所[しょ]および時[じ]間[かん]は、まだ決[き]まっていません。
```

*The meeting's location and time have not been decided yet.*

場[ば]所[しょ] and 時[じ]間[かん] clip together, and then a single は makes the whole pair the topic. Writing `場所は および 時間は` would be like saying "the location is and the time is" — the particle has been let loose too early.

For a longer formal list, および usually links just the final two items while 、 separates the ones before it — the same slot English keeps for its last "and".

```jp
試[し]験[けん]の結[けっ]果[か]および説[せつ]明[めい]は、金[きん]曜[よう]日[び]に伝[つた]えます。
```

*The exam results and the explanation will be given on Friday.*

The same structure carries notices that address people rather than things:

```jp
学[がく]生[せい]および先[せん]生[せい]は、この入[いり]口[ぐち]から入[はい]ってください。
```

*Students and teachers, please enter through this entrance.*

```jp
書[しょ]類[るい]および荷[に]物[もつ]は、受[うけ]付[つけ]に出[だ]してください。
```

*Please hand in your documents and luggage at the reception desk.*

Read those two aloud and notice how official they sound. That tone is not an accident — it is the whole reason および exists as a separate word from と.

## Rules and exceptions

**および joins nouns, full stop.** It will not connect two verbs, two adjectives, or two complete sentences. Formal Japanese links actions and clauses with other tools — the て-form, し, and more you have yet to meet — but never with および. Trying to bolt it onto a verb is the mistake almost everyone makes first.

> `食べるおよび飲む` for "eat and drink" is not a thing — および cannot touch a verb. You join the nouns instead: 食[た]べ物[もの]および飲[の]み物[もの].

**This is a register choice, not a grammar rule.** および is not *incorrect* in speech, but out loud it sounds like you are reading from a printed manual. When you are actually talking, と joins a closed pair ("exactly these two") and や joins an open-ended set ("these among others"). および steps in only when the sentence is written and wants to be taken seriously.

**Personal relationships sit awkwardly with it.** Because および is so stiff, using it for your own family can sound like a legal filing:

```jp
父[ちち]および母[はは]も、この意[い]見[けん]に反[はん]対[たい]です。
```

*My father and my mother are both against this idea, too.*

That sentence is fine in a written report or a formal statement. Said to a friend over lunch, 父[ちち]と母[はは] is what you would use — および there would make your parents sound like line items on a form.

## のみ versus および

You have already met のみ, the formal word for "only". のみ and および feel like siblings: both are bookish, both belong to the same careful written register, both would look at home on the same official page. But they move in opposite directions. および **adds** a second item to what you are talking about; のみ **strips everything away** except one.

```jp
学[がく]生[せい]および先[せん]生[せい]が来[き]ます。
```

*Students and teachers are coming.*

```jp
学[がく]生[せい]のみ来[き]ます。
```

*Only students are coming.*

One word changed, and the room either doubles or empties out. When you are drafting something formal and reach for one of these, say the sentence back to yourself and check which you meant: "these two groups together" points to one word, "this group and no one else" to the other.

## Closing

および is how a form or a contract says two nouns belong together: **Noun + および + Noun**, no conjugation ever, and the marking particle waits until after the second noun. In speech, と does the same job without the suit.

Coming up is に対[たい]して, another formal piece that attaches straight to a noun — but rather than tying two nouns together as equals, it stands one thing opposite another. Keep this "careful written register" feeling nearby; に対[たい]して lives in the same neighbourhood.
caution_notes: および joins nouns only — it can never connect two verbs, two adjectives, or two whole clauses.
および belongs to written and formal notices; in ordinary conversation と or や is what you actually say.
Put the sentence particle (は, が, を, に) after the second noun, not between the two nouns joined by および.
Do not mix up および, which adds a second item, with のみ, which restricts you to one — they push the meaning in opposite directions.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're in a meeting and a colleague finally says out loud the thing everyone was thinking. Another colleague pushes back, hard. Afterward you want to describe what happened: her reaction wasn't floating in the air, it was aimed squarely at one thing, the opinion that had just been raised. English reaches for "to," "toward," or "in response to" here. Japanese has a dedicated connector that clamps a reaction, an attitude, or a contrast onto the exact thing it targets: に対[たい]して.

```jp
私[わたし]の意[い]見[けん]に対[たい]して、彼[かの]女[じょ]は反[はん]対[たい]しました。
```

*In response to my opinion, she objected.*

The opinion is the target; 反[はん]対[たい]しました is the response pointed straight at it. Keep that frame and swap the noun, and you can describe almost any directed stance: kindness toward a stranger, strictness toward a child, an answer that argues back against a question.

## How it works

The structure is as short as it looks: Noun + に対[たい]して. The noun sits directly in front, with no の and no verb form to remember. Whatever comes after it describes how someone acts, feels, or responds in the direction of that noun. The connector's whole purpose is to keep that direction unambiguous.

```jp
彼[かれ]は動[どう]物[ぶつ]に対[たい]してとても優[やさ]しいです。
```

*He is very gentle toward animals.*

優[やさ]しい is an attitude, and 動[どう]物[ぶつ] is who that attitude is aimed at. に対[たい]して is doing exactly one job here: marking 動[どう]物[ぶつ] as the target, not as the subject and not as a place.

The noun in front doesn't have to be a living thing. に対[たい]して is very common with abstract targets, questions, opinions, proposals, plans, because those are precisely the things people respond to.

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]は生[せい]徒[と]の質[しつ]問[もん]に対[たい]して丁[てい]寧[ねい]に答[こた]えます。
```

*The teacher answers students' questions politely.*

The teacher's politeness is directed at the questions the students raise, and に対[たい]して makes that link explicit. You can also attach も to the end, giving に対[たい]しても, for the sense "toward every" or "toward anyone at all."

```jp
あの店[てん]員[いん]はどのお客[きゃく]さんに対[たい]しても親[しん]切[せつ]です。
```

*That clerk is kind toward every customer.*

### に対[たい]する before a noun

Sometimes the "directed at" phrase has to modify a noun rather than lead into a verb or an adjective. In that spot, に対[たい]して swaps its tail and becomes に対[たい]する. It's the same shift you already know from plain-form verbs: 食[た]べる keeps its -る ending when it sits in front of a noun. に対[たい]して is the shape that runs into a predicate; に対[たい]する is the shape that runs into a noun.

```jp
彼[かれ]の子[こ]供[ども]に対[たい]する態[たい]度[ど]は厳[きび]しいです。
```

*His attitude toward the children is strict.*

態[たい]度[ど] is a noun, so the phrase in front of it has to end in に対[たい]する. Leave it as に対[たい]して and it dangles, still waiting for a verb or an adjective that never arrives.

## Rules and exceptions

The mistake that catches nearly everyone in the first week: に対[たい]して is not the everyday に that marks who receives something. When you give, lend, send, or say something to a person, plain に is correct and に対[たい]して is wrong.

- Natural: `弟に辞書を貸しました。`
- Unnatural: `弟に対して辞書を貸しました。`

に対[たい]して is reserved for a stance or a response, kindness, strictness, an objection, an answer that argues back, not for a plain handover. A rough test: if the English could be "handed to," you want に; if it could be "in response to" or "in dealing with," you want に対[たい]して.

> に対[たい]する has to sit directly in front of the noun it modifies. You cannot end a sentence or a clause on に対[たい]する; if nothing follows, the form you need is に対[たい]して.

Register is worth a note too. に対[たい]して carries a formal, written flavor. It belongs in opinions, reports, essays, and careful speech. Talking with a friend, most people just use に or rebuild the sentence around an ordinary verb. に対[たい]して over a bowl of ramen sounds like you're reading aloud from a memo.

One last caution about the "in contrast to" half of the meaning. That sense works when one side genuinely reacts to, or stands opposite, the other. For a flat "A is like this, B is like that" with no tension between the two, other patterns fit better; に対[たい]して always keeps a faint charge of one thing being set against another.

## Contrast with によって

You've met によって for cause, means, and "it depends." に対[たい]して lives right next door, because both clip straight onto a bare noun with no の. The difference is direction. によって looks back toward whatever produced the result; に対[たい]して looks forward toward whatever the action is aimed at.

```jp
彼[かれ]の説[せつ]明[めい]に対[たい]して、みんなは質[しつ]問[もん]しました。
```

*In response to his explanation, everyone asked questions.*

The explanation is the target the questions are fired at. Now hold the noun and the speaker steady and switch only the connector:

```jp
彼[かれ]の説[せつ]明[めい]によって、みんなは問[もん]題[だい]が分[わ]かりました。
```

*Thanks to his explanation, everyone understood the problem.*

This time the explanation is the cause of the understanding. The same opening phrase, a completely different relationship: に対[たい]して makes 説[せつ]明[めい] a target, によって makes it a reason.

```jp
地[じ]震[しん]によって家[いえ]が壊[こわ]れました。
```

*The earthquake caused the house to break.*

に対[たい]して could never stand in for によって there, because a house breaking is not a stance directed at the earthquake. Quick check: if the noun is doing something to you, reach for によって; if you are doing something toward the noun, reach for に対[たい]して.

## In one line

に対[たい]して pins a reaction, an attitude, or a contrast onto the noun it targets; switch the tail to に対[たい]する the moment the next word is a noun.
caution_notes: に対する must come directly before the noun it modifies; if no noun follows, use に対して instead.
Do not use に対して for the plain recipient of giving, lending, sending, or saying something to a person, where に by itself is the correct particle.
Keep に対して apart from によって: に対して marks what an action or attitude is aimed at, while によって marks a cause, a means, or what something depends on.
に対して sounds formal and written, so in casual conversation people usually use に or rephrase the sentence.
